f: Run by the Generalitat Valenciana's culture department. It bought 16 works by 14 women artists for about EUR 1M.

f: Private foundation set up in Geneva in 1983 by collector Dakis Joannou, a construction and hotel businessman.
w: Runs the Athens space and the Slaughterhouse Project Space on Hydra, granted by the island's municipality in 2008.

f: Nicosia Municipality and the Pierides Foundation run it under a cooperation agreement. Shows credit the Deputy Ministry of Culture, A.G. Leventis Foundation and European University Cyprus.
w: A 2026 show with Emin Cizenel, who designed the north's flag, drew a small protest and a deputy mayor's call to cancel.

f: Greek state museum. The ministry assured EUR 42M of the EUR 59M expansion (2021). The Stavros Niarchos Foundation gave EUR 13M in 2017.

f: Produced by Kampala Arts Trust and Afriart Gallery. KAB20 (2020) was co-funded by the EU and Pro Helvetia. TotalEnergies Foundation backed the 2018 mentoring programme.
w: Founded in 2014 by Daudi Karungi. No edition since the virtual KAB20 in 2020; the site is now an archive.

f: Produced by Desta for Africa, directed by Aida Muluneh. The last sponsor list is from 2018: Swiss Embassy, Canon, National Geographic Society, Marriott and others.
w: Founded 2010. The fifth edition opened 6 December 2018. A sixth was announced for December 2020.

f: Owned and run by the Rwanda Cultural Heritage Academy, the government body that runs Rwanda's national museums.
w: Opened in 2009 in the former presidential palace at Kanombe and renamed the Rwanda Art Museum in 2018.
nodes: Hong Kong Museum of the War of Resistance and Coastal Defence

f: Artist-run centre founded in 2012 by painter brothers Innocent Nkurunziza and Emmanuel Nkuranga.
w: Ten resident-artist slots at KG 563 St, Kacyiru.

f: Won Culture Resource's Abbara Program grant (round 7, 2022). The Australian Government and Creative Australia support its Qubit fellowship (2026). The Spanish Embassy is a named partner.
w: Opened Muse Gallery in Khartoum in 2022; since the April 2023 war it works between Sudan and Egypt and runs the Sudan Art Archive.

n: Institute of Contemporary Art Indian Ocean (ICAIO)
f: Founded in 2015 by Salim Currimjee, a painter, architect and collector (Lonely Planet France).
w: Exhibitions change each quarter, showing Mauritian, Indian and South African artists, at 51 Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam Street, Port Louis.

f: Operates under the Women's Gallery Arts and Research Trust. Its March 2023 show had support from the Swiss and Australian embassies and UN Women.
w: Gallery Delta was founded in 1975 by Derek Huggins and Helen Lieros, who died in 2021; Nhaka presents itself as continuing that legacy.
nodes: Fundación Casa de los Tres Mundos

f: Founder Victor Mutelekesha's household paid for the building. Pro Helvetia paid for shelving. OCA, a Norwegian arts body, part-financed the 2023 opening show. The late artist Jan Groth donated.
w: Opened 6 January 2023 in New Chamba Valley with a gallery, library and artist residency; first show Prospice, Kwacha!

f: Artists' association with over 100 members. State funding ended in the civil war; a late-1990s profile names Hivos as donor.
w: Official foundation 1948; reopened in 1993 by young artists. Maputo's council and the CTA led a 2021 mural project with 40 of its members.
nodes: State funding ended in the civil war

f: Funded by Wissam and Hiba Nesr. Wissam is chief executive of Webcor Group, a Swiss-based food importer and distributor with most African revenue in Angola.
w: Opened in 2021 with a residency for Angolan and Lusophone African artists; the artistic committee is chaired by Paula Nascimento.

f: Binational centre under Namibian law, funded by the French government. Namibia gave the land and France paid for the building; foundation stone laid in 1998.

n: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
f: Statutory museum set up by Act of Parliament in 1967 and run by the Department of National Museum and Monuments (Wikipedia). Government funded its P33 million refurbishment, begun in 2020.
w: Includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery. Opened to the public in 1968.

n: Musée des Cultures Contemporaines Adama Toungara (MuCAT)
f: Built on the initiative of Adama Toungara, then mayor of Abobo; the director says it was built from own funds.
w: Stands opposite Abobo town hall on 3,500 m², designed by architect Issa Diabaté. Opened with the pan-African show Prête-moi ton rêve.

n: Festival International des Arts du Bénin (FInAB)
f: Run by Groupe Empire's events arm with Benin government support through its arts fund (FDAC). MTN partnered the 2026 edition, Canal+ Impact 2025. Other partners unnamed; no budget published.
w: Festival in Cotonou, Porto-Novo and Ouidah. The fourth edition closed in early March 2026, with days for Nigeria, Togo, Lebanon and Morocco.

f: Founded by Andrew Munuwa with Valentin Rudloff.
w: Launched in 2023. The 2025 edition showed 15 artists from Congo, Sudan, Kenya and Tanzania in Dar es Salaam and Zanzibar (Musée Magazine, February 2025).

f: Texaf, listed on Euronext Brussels, is founder and head sponsor of the centre. Its income is 85% Kinshasa real estate, 12% a sandstone quarry and 3% digital.
w: Texaf is 62.9% held by Société Financière Africaine and 10% by the Cha family. Bilembo covers over 1,000 m² of exhibition and workshop space.

f: Burkina Faso's culture ministry organises it and pays professional artists' fees, flights and stay, per its 2024 call for applications.
w: Founded 1989 by Siriki Ky, 35 km from Ouagadougou. The 15th edition runs 2 to 23 November 2026 under President Traoré's patronage.
nodes: Burkina Faso's culture ministry organises it

f: Eastern Cape government, Sarah Baartman District Municipality, National Lottery Commission, Standard Bank. National government gave R5.5 million for 2022 to 2024, nothing in 2025, a smaller grant in 2026.
w: Minister McKenzie says it lost an open call. A January 2026 petition of 302 artists cites the cut among his refusals to renew funding.

n: Javett Art Centre at the University of Pretoria (Javett-UP)
f: University of Pretoria gave the land and funding. The Javett Foundation funded construction and pledged ten years of annual gifts for running costs and an endowment.
w: Opened September 2019; an independent trust runs it. In October 2019 sex workers' group SWEAT petitioned it to remove a Zwelethu Mthethwa work.

f: Private firm of Nadine Abdel Ghaffar. Egypt's foreign and tourism ministries and UNESCO sponsor Forever Is Now. Partners: LMD, Suez Canal Bank, BMW (2026); TotalEnergies, Afreximbank (2024).
w: In October 2026 a petition of 500 to 700 signatories made it drop sculptor Bernar Venet over Israeli ties; artists and galleries withdrew.
why: Private firm of Nadine Abdel Ghaffar. Egypt's foreign and tourism ministries and UNESCO sponsor Forever Is Now. Partners: LMD, Suez Canal Bank, BMW (2026); TotalEnergies, Afreximbank (2024).

f: Primarily funded by the Yinka Shonibare Foundation at its 2019 launch. Donors include Terra Foundation, Deutsche Bank, Afreximbank, Still Earth Holdings, British Council and Pro Helvetia.
w: Founded 2019 by Yinka Shonibare, who started the London residency Guest Projects. Patron Still Earth Holdings owns drilling contractor Tirex, an oil-services supplier.

f: Art network and incubator tied to the KNUST painting and sculpture department in Kumasi.
w: Ranked 69 in ArtReview's 2025 Power 100 and invited to the 2026 Venice Biennale main exhibition.

f: Founded with private money by Boubacar Koné and actress CCH Pounder; Koné gave it to the Senegalese state in December 2014.
w: Ngor museum of contemporary African art with artist studios and a residency. A conservator from the Ministry of Culture took office in March 2015.

n: Contemporary Art Museum of the Kasbah
f: Run by the National Foundation of Museums. Restoration and design cost 13 million dirhams; the Wilaya of Tangier supervised it, with the Ministry of Culture, APDN and the Foundation contributing.
w: Opened in December 2021 in the former Kasbah prison to mark the Foundation's tenth anniversary. Opening show: The School of the North.
nodes: Cap Moderne (Villa E-1027 and Le Cabanon)

f: The Free State of Bavaria and the Friends of Haus der Kunst are shareholders. The Alexander Tutsek Foundation is the major supporter. The Kai and Beisheim foundations also give.
w: A Bavarian ministry official chairs its supervisory board. 2024 attendance was nearly 440,000.

f: Closed 1990. The GDR state owned it and the last GDR government's Council of Ministers dissolved it. Its holdings and the Zeughaus passed to the Deutsches Historisches Museum.
w: The Zeughaus on Unter den Linden now houses the Deutsches Historisches Museum.

f: Closed in 1993 by order of the Russian president. The State Historical Museum, a federal museum, took over the collection and the building on Revolution Square.
w: Part of the building now holds the 1812 Patriotic War museum.

n: State Museum of the History of Religion
f: Federal state museum under the Russian Ministry of Culture since 1991. It moved from Kazan Cathedral to Pochtamtskaya Street 14 in 2000.
w: Its antireligious displays ended in the 1990s.

f: The Humanitarian Projects Foundation runs it and gets most of its money from Gazprom, per RFE/RL in 2019. Gazprom co-financed parks from 2016. Federal and Moscow bodies are partners.
w: Archimandrite Tikhon Shevkunov heads the foundation's expert council. The Education Ministry recommended the parks as teaching material in 2017.
why: The Humanitarian Projects Foundation runs it and gets most of its money from Gazprom, per RFE/RL in 2019. Gazprom co-financed parks from 2016. Federal and Moscow bodies are partners.

f: Azerbaijani state project. President Ilham Aliyev ordered it built in January 2021 and opened it on 12 April 2021, according to the presidential website.
w: The Council of Europe human rights commissioner, the European Parliament and Armenia objected. Wax figures and helmets left the main display in October 2021.

n: Museum of the Communist Party of China
f: Built on a 2017 Communist Party Central Committee decision, with support from the National Development and Reform Commission, Finance Ministry and Beijing city. Entry is free.
w: Opened 18 June 2021. Xinhua reported more than 3.5 million visits by 30 June 2024.

f: Funded by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism as a level-1 public welfare institution. The Art Newspaper counted 7.4 million visitors in 2019.
w: Formed 2003 by merging the Museum of the Chinese Revolution and the National Museum of Chinese History. Building opened 1959.

f: Founded 1985 by the Nanjing Municipal Government; the Jiangsu provincial government added a research institute in 2016. The Standard reported about 6 million visitors in 2025.
w: The Victory Exhibition Hall opened 7 December 2015. Admission is free with prior registration.
nodes: Jiangsu provincial government added a research institute

n: Museum of the War of Chinese People's Resistance Against Japanese Aggression
f: Budget unit in the Beijing government's published accounts: 809 million yuan of public funding in 2025, 711 million of it project spending.
w: Inside Wanping Fortress near the Marco Polo Bridge. Beijing opened a patriotic education base there for Hong Kong and Macau youth in August 2025.

f: Run under county-level administration since 1984. Provincial permission was needed for exhibit changes in 1988 (Ho and Li, Modern China, 2016).
w: The 114 clay figures were made in 1965 by Sichuan Fine Arts Institute artists. Tens of millions visited in the Mao era.

f: Run by Cambodia's Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts, which lists it among its institutions. Foreign adults pay $5 and Cambodians enter free, the museum states.
w: Former Khmer Rouge prison S-21. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025 as part of the Cambodian Memorial Sites.

n: National Museum of the Islamic Revolution and Holy Defense
f: Tehran municipality built it, and its statute makes the municipality responsible for the budget and staff.
w: Opened in 2012 in Tehran's Abbas-Abad district; about 300,000 visitors a year (AFP, 2018). The Armed Forces General Staff published its statute amendments in 2021.

n: Museo Casa sobre el Arroyo (Casa del Puente)
f: The national state bought the house in 2012 and passed it to the city. The Ministry of Public Works paid over ARS 72M for the restoration, reopened April 2023.
w: Amancio Williams's house of 1943 to 1945 over the Las Chacras stream. Its restoration won the 2024 World Monuments Fund/Knoll Modernism Prize.

f: Lothar Trierenberg, of an Upper Austrian paper family, bought the house for EUR 5M and spent twice that restoring it. Stadt Wien gave EUR 700k, the Monuments Office about 200k.
w: Josef Frank and Oskar Wlach's 1930 villa, open since March 2026. Lothar Trierenberg co-owns delfortgroup, a specialty paper maker whose lines include cigarette paper.
why: Josef Frank and Oskar Wlach's 1930 villa, open since March 2026. Lothar Trierenberg co-owns delfortgroup, a specialty paper maker whose lines include cigarette paper.

f: Owned by the NSW Government and run by Museums of History NSW (successor to the Historic Houses Trust), a statutory body with a 2024-25 budget of A$73.6M.
w: Harry Seidler's 1950 house for his parents, handed to the state in 1988 and open to the public since 1991.

f: Robin Boyd Foundation revenue AUD 435k in 2023-24: donations 137k, grants 36k, partnerships 30k. Partners include Brickworks, Maddocks and Arup; donor trusts include Mori Provan and Isaacson Davis.
w: Robin Boyd's own 1959 house in South Yarra. A private ancillary foundation, unnamed, lent AUD 1.8M interest free against the title.

f: Verein Margarete Schütte-Lihotzky Club is funded by Stadt Wien, Bezirk Margareten, the federal arts ministry, GESIBA and arching. ORF named Wertinvest, the building's owner, a financial backer in 2021.
w: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.
why: The architect's flat, open since October 2022. Wertinvest's Heumarkt tower put Vienna's historic centre on UNESCO's red list, 2017 to 2026.

n: Das Rote Wien im Waschsalon Karl-Marx-Hof
f: Run by Verein Sammlung Rotes Wien. Stadt Wien gives an annual subsidy and the insurer Wiener Städtische supports it. Wien Tourismus shows as a partner logo.
w: Exhibition on Red Vienna, 1919 to 1934, in a laundry of the 1930 Karl-Marx-Hof, open since 2010. Students and volunteers guide.

f: The Bulgarian state bought the house in 1975 and runs it as the Bulgarian Cultural Institute, the embassy's cultural department. Both countries' culture ministries backed its 2024 Wittgenstein exhibition.
w: Paul Engelmann and Ludwig Wittgenstein's house of 1928, a protected monument since 1971. It hosted a Wittgenstein exhibition in November 2024.

f: STEINHAUS Günther Domenig Privatstiftung receives subsidies from Land Kärnten (culture) and the Federal Ministry for Arts, Culture, the Civil Service and Sport. Gemeinde Steindorf and HTL Villach give in-kind sponsoring.
w: Günther Domenig's own house. In 2008 he put it into the foundation with his artistic, legal and material estate.

f: The commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961. The museum's EUR 800k renewal is paid by Urban Brussels, the commune, Fonds Baillet-Latour, museum resources and an unnamed patron.
w: Victor Horta's house and studio of 1898 to 1901, a museum since 1969. The first phase of facade and reception works ends in November 2026.
nodes: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)

f: Run by the Boghossian Foundation, created in 1992 by the jewellers Robert Boghossian and his sons, which bought and restored the villa. The Circle of the Villa adds donors.
w: Michel Polak's villa of 1930, an art centre since 2010. Circle donors include Jan-Leonard Moortgat (Duvel) and Claude Moët (Moët & Chandon).
nodes: Circle of the Villa adds donors
Armenian Center for Contemporary Experimental Art (ACCEA/NPAK)

f: Owned by the Arthur Erickson Foundation, a charity that takes donations and tour fees. Canadian Heritage gave CAD 17,800 in 2024. Patrons include Michael Audain and Yosef Wosk.
w: Garden tours run April to October and the house interior is closed. Phyllis Lambert chairs a board of 16 directors.

f: Donations were CZK 4.48M in 2025: CZK 4.40M from founder Bata Schuh Stiftung, CZK 30k from Continental Barum. Subsidies: City of Zlín CZK 195k, Zlín Region CZK 35k.
w: Thomas J. Bata recovered the villa by restitution and donated it to the foundation. Rosemarie Bata Blyth chairs the board, which includes Zlín's mayor.

f: The National Heritage Institute runs it. Transfers, mostly from the Ministry of Culture, were 69 percent of 2024 revenue. EU's ERDF paid 85 percent of a CZK 179M restoration project.
w: Built 1927 to 1929 for textile owner Alfred Stiassni and later used for state visits, including Fidel Castro's. Opened to the public in December 2014.

f: The Brummel family owns the house. Plzeň - TURISMUS, a City of Pilsen organisation, runs the tours. The Adolf Loos Plzeň project credits Ministry for Regional Development state-budget money.
w: Jan and Jana Brummel commissioned Loos to remodel the house in 1929. Their nephew Michal took it over in 1991.

f: Herita vzw, a heritage non-profit, runs it with the City of Antwerp. The Flemish Government set EUR 6.3M for Herita's 2025 operating year under a one-year agreement.
w: Renaat Braem left the house to the Flemish Community in 1999. Herita has worked since 2024 to open it to the public.

f: Lombard Odier is the structural partner. urban.brussels, Loterie Nationale and Uccle are institutional partners. Friends pay EUR 150 a year, patrons from EUR 2,000.
w: Belgium's National Lottery, a public-law company, has run Scooore sports betting since January 2013.
why: Belgium's National Lottery, a public-law company, has run Scooore sports betting since January 2013.

f: Branch of the Moravian Gallery, founded by the Ministry of Culture, which paid CZK 140.9M of its CZK 168.0M 2025 income. A Norwegian Financial Mechanism grant supported the villa.
w: Dušan Jurkovič's own villa of 1906 in Brno-Žabovřesky, with a permanent exhibition on the architect and seasonal shows. Tickets must be booked in advance.

f: Plzeň Region owns the building and gave the Gallery of West Bohemia CZK 37M of its CZK 39M 2024 budget. Region and EU funds helped pay the EUR 4.5M restoration.
w: Apartment of Oskar Semler, remodelled 1932 to 1934, with interiors by Heinrich Kulka to a concept by Adolf Loos. Fully open since September 2022.

f: Ministry of Culture paid CZK 38.4M in 2025 for the villa and furniture; the Museum of Decorative Arts runs it. An EEA grant covered EUR 348k of the earlier restoration.
w: Josef Gočár's 1914 cubist villa, bought from the Czech Cubism Foundation, which had restored it and opened it. Tours since July 2025.

f: Run by the Prague City Gallery, which the City of Prague founded and pays: CZK 122.8M operating contribution in 2024, against CZK 10.8M own revenue. Four patrons gave CZK 360,000.
w: František Bílek's home and studio, built 1911 to his own design. A new permanent exhibition opened in June 2022; about 8,000 visitors in 2024.

f: Owned by the City of Prague and run by the Museum of Prague, a city organisation that received a CZK 227.9M city subsidy in 2024.
w: Adolf Loos's 1930 villa. Closed in February 2025 for failed terrace waterproofing, it reopened in 2026 after a reconstruction costing about CZK 20M.

f: Run by the Museum of Prague, which the City of Prague funds with a CZK 227.9M subsidy (2024). The museum site also names the Education Ministry and Erasmus as supporters.
w: Architect Otto Rothmayer's own villa of 1929 in Prague 6, with 3,558 visitors in 2024. Its garden opened free to the public in May 2026.

f: Brno City Museum, funded by the City of Brno: CZK 108.3M of CZK 199.2M income in 2025. State budget and funds CZK 4.6M, South Moravian Region CZK 0.35M.
w: Mies van der Rohe's 1930 villa, on the UNESCO list since 2001, with 57,036 tour and exhibition visitors in 2025.

f: Foundation set up by owner Čestmír Vančura. 2025 income CZK 4.2M: gifts 2.1M (including his foundation, NAVI CZ, ZULIP, MEJTA, Edhouse, PSG Construction), grants 1.0M, mainly EEA and Norway Grants.
w: Traveller Miroslav Zikmund owned the villa from 1953 until he sold it to Čestmír Vančura in 2020. The foundation opens it for guided tours.

f: The Akseli Gallen-Kallela Museum Foundation runs it. 2024 income EUR 0.80M: state subsidy 39%, municipal grants 26% (Espoo is a named supporter), tickets 21%, services and sales 14%.
w: Akseli Gallen-Kallela's studio at Tarvaspää, completed 1913 and protected as built heritage. Espoo's cultural committee granted EUR 70,000 for its restoration in 2024.

f: The City of Järvenpää, owner since 1998, runs it. The first restoration phase, budgeted at EUR 425,000, drew on city investments and a EUR 105,000 culture ministry grant.
w: Alvar Aalto's 1969 home for the composer Joonas Kokkonen. Open May to September on guided tours. A 2024 city paper proposed a second phase.

f: The Didrichsen Art Foundation, set up by the founders in 1963, runs it. 2024 income EUR 1.30M: tickets 50%, state subsidy 17%, other grants 16% (grantors not named), services 15%.
w: The founders' home, designed by Viljo Revell and completed in 1957.

f: State money. A site of the National Museum of Finland, a department of the Finnish Heritage Agency under the Ministry of Education and Culture. Adult ticket EUR 15.
w: Studio home of the architects Gesellius, Lindgren and Saarinen, completed 1903. Open May to September.

f: The Alvar Aalto Foundation runs it. The foundation's Alvar Aalto Museum reported 2024 income of EUR 2.73M: state subsidies 38%, tickets 19%, services and sales 19%, municipal grants 14%.
w: Alvar and Elissa Aalto's self-designed studio and summer home, built 1952-54. Open for guided tours in summer. Tickets are sold through Aalto2.

f: The Villa Mairea Foundation runs it. A. Ahlström Kiinteistöt Oy owns and maintains the building.
w: Designed by Aino and Alvar Aalto and completed in 1939 for Maire and Harry Gullichsen. The foundation dates from 1980. Guided tours cost EUR 30.

f: The Christine and Göran Schildt Foundation owns and runs it, and Christine Schildt sits on its board. Tickets cost EUR 22.
w: Alvar Aalto's last and smallest house, built 1969-70 for his friends Christine and Göran Schildt. Open to the public since December 2020, on guided tours.

f: The City of Nancy, owner since 2003, runs it through the Musée de l'École de Nancy. With the Fondation du patrimoine it has opened an appeal for the 2026-28 restoration.
w: Henri Sauvage's house of 1901-02 for the cabinetmaker Louis Majorelle, a listed monument. Open Wednesday to Sunday by booking.

f: A public-utility foundation created by decree in 1994 runs it. Its subsidiary HB Projet hires the site out for events and filming.
w: Home and studios of the painters Hans Hartung and Anna-Eva Bergman, open to the public since May 2022. Closed until the spring 2027 exhibition.

f: The City of Le Havre bought the flat in 2005 for EUR 220,000 and fitted it out for EUR 150,000. The Pays d'art et d'histoire service runs the guided visits.
w: A reconstruction of the model homes Auguste Perret showed in 1947 and 1949-53, inaugurated in 2006. Guides took 24,000 visitors through it in 2025.

w: 2018: ICAIC moved one film to a 24-seat room; the director withdrew it. 2020: ICAIC cut a documentary and at least six filmmakers withdrew works.

n: Escuela Internacional de Cine y Televisión (EICTV)
c: San Antonio de los Baños, Cuba
f: The Cuban government supported it at founding. Tuition was 5,000 euros a year in 2011 (AFP). EU-financed UNESCO Transcultura supplied equipment and courses valued at 600,000 euros in 2024.
w: The school's site lists the Ministry of Culture and ICAIC as supporters. In 2026 it also runs a donation campaign for energy autonomy.

f: Founded in 1899 by Santiago's mayor Emilio Bacardí, this state museum got its building in 1927 from his widow Elvira Cape. The Ministry of Culture's provincial heritage centre oversees it.
w: National Monument since 1999. OnCuba reports more than 23,000 items in three halls and an art annex.

n: Museo Castillo del Morro San Pedro de la Roca
f: Cuban state property; UNESCO names the Consejo Nacional del Patrimonio Cultural as responsible agency. A museum opened in the fortress on 23 July 1978. State bodies began repairs in 2020.
w: UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997. Granma, quoted by OnCuba in April 2021, reported the repairs would continue through 2021.

f: Private studio-gallery founded in Havana in 1995 by curator Cristina Vives and photographer José A. Figueroa. It describes itself as self-financed; the Norwegian Embassy in Cuba is a named collaborator.
w: Dialogue with state institutions has been on and off and one-way (IPS, 2020).
nodes: CRAC Valparaíso (Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo)

f: Open as a museum since 1974, the Palacio Brunet is an 1808 mansion restored from 1964. The Sancti Spíritus heritage centre's 2024 summer programme includes this state museum.
w: The Asociación Pro Trinidad bought the palace in 1945. Trinidad's historic centre has been on the UNESCO list since 1988.

f: Opened in 1955 in a former cavalry barracks, Camagüey's provincial museum is a state institution. A private Patronato Pro Museo assembled its first collection.
w: Holds Cuban painting including Wifredo Lam and Amelia Peláez, plus natural history and decorative arts rooms.

f: State theatre in Cienfuegos, a National Monument. Built 1887 to 1890 with 115,000 gold pesos set aside by the heirs of slave-owning sugar planter Tomás Terry.
w: The building won the National Conservation Prize in 2008. Spanish Wikipedia lists it among eight large colonial-era theatres.

f: Matanzas state theatre, a National Monument since 1978, closed 2010 to 2018 for restoration (EcuRed: 2019). Its main hall closed mid-2024; ACN said in July 2025 it would reopen.
w: The state heritage council gave the restoration its 2020 National Restoration Prize. Seating is 775.

c: San Antonio de los Baños, Cuba
f: Opened 17 March 1979 per EcuRed (14ymedio: 1948) in an 1830 house in San Antonio de los Baños; the Ministry of Culture is its parent body, per EcuRed.
w: Hosts the Bienal Internacional del Humor, whose 24th edition ran in April 2025 (Cubaperiodistas). EcuRed counts over 10,000 works from 40 countries.

n: American Museum of the Cuban Diaspora
f: Non-profit Cuban Museum Inc. A $10 million Miami-Dade County bond grant (2004) built it and county funds support it. The City of Miami added $175,000 in American Rescue Plan money.
w: In September 2017 seven of 13 county commissioners moved $550,000 from the Pérez Art Museum to this museum; Jorge Pérez called it punishment.
why: In September 2017 seven of 13 county commissioners moved $550,000 from the Pérez Art Museum to this museum; Jorge Pérez called it punishment.

f: Florida non-profit run by a volunteer board that says donations and volunteers maintain the building. State of Florida grants of $2.8 million paid for the restoration reopened in 1992.
w: Founded in 1871 by Cuban exiles. Cuba's government gave $80,000 for the 1920s rebuilding and paid a teacher's salary until 1959.

f: Independent art institute founded in 2015 and set up by a crowdfunding campaign of 915 backers. In 2024 its whole income, $95,283, came from Estudio Bruguera, the founder's studio.
w: Cuban authorities detained founder Tania Bruguera in December 2014 and January 2015; INSTAR says the street outside was drilled during its 2015 reading.

f: Non-profit educational institution founded in 1972 that runs the Cuban Art Space gallery. Its 2024 revenue was $296,120, of which $194,216 was contributions and $86,374 program services (Form 990).
w: Founded in 1972 to counter US policy toward Cuba. A bomb wrecked its New York premises on 28 March 1973; its letter named no perpetrator.

f: A building of 1860 to 1868 on Parque Calixto García houses Holguín's state provincial history museum, whose heritage centre lists six rooms; EcuRed says one is mounted.
w: National Monument since 10 October 1978. Spanish Wikipedia dates the museum to 1980, EcuRed to 25 July 1976.

n: Museo Provincial de Pinar del Río
f: State provincial history museum in a building that housed the provincial government from 1892 to 1959. It belongs to the Pinar del Río provincial heritage centre.
w: Opened with one room on 14 December 1979 and the rest in 1981. Rooms cover archaeology, history, decorative arts and local musicians.

n: Museo Provincial de Granma Manuel Muñoz Cedeño
f: Bayamo's provincial museum opened on 19 October 1982 as the Museo Histórico de Bayamo, in the city's historic centre. It belongs to the Centro Provincial de Patrimonio Cultural en Granma.
w: Armando Hart, then minister of culture, attended the opening. Bayamo's historic centre has been a National Monument since 1935, ratified in 1978.

n: Victory Museum (Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War)
f: Federal museum under Russia's Ministry of Culture. Its director Alexander Shkolnik was honoured by Putin in 2021 for patriotic education and sanctioned by the UK and Australia in 2022.
w: Opened on Poklonnaya Hill on 9 May 1995 in Anatoly Polyansky's building; the 2022 exhibition Ordinary Nazism drew 150,000 visitors in its first month.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Papua New Guinea National Museum and Art Gallery

f: Built and funded by Russia's Defence Ministry, which allocated over 20 billion rubles in 2015. Its head Vyacheslav Akhmedov was arrested for fraud in August 2024 with a ministry general.
w: A 5,414 hectare site with a 3,530 hectare military base, hosting the ministry's Army forum; conceived by Sergei Shoigu and opened from 2015 to 2016.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Mária Schmidt's public foundation ran it from 2002 to 2026 on government money, 5.5 billion forints in 2019. Since September 2026 a culture ministry company, Kulturális Vagyonkezelő Kft, runs it.
w: At Andrássy út 60, once Arrow Cross and ÁVH headquarters. Culture Minister Zoltán Tarr dismissed Schmidt on 15 September 2026 and ordered a content review.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Museum of the Second World War
f: A state institution financed by Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage, which appoints its director. In March 2024 the minister replaced PiS appointee Grzegorz Berendt with Rafał Wnuk.
w: Opened 23 March 2017 in a 23,000 square metre building with a 40 metre leaning tower by the Kwadrat studio; 601,000 visitors in 2024.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A public institution of the Ho Chi Minh City government under its Department of Culture and Sports, funded from the city budget and ticket income.
w: Opened 4 September 1975 at 28 Võ Văn Tần; about 500,000 visitors a year, two thirds of them foreigners.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A public service unit under Vietnam's Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism, which by Decision 2372/QD-BVHTTDL of 2025 sets its propaganda and education tasks and lets it collect fees.
w: Founded by a 1970 Party resolution and opened 19 May 1990, Ho Chi Minh's centenary, in Garon Isacovich's lotus-shaped building; over 40 million visitors.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Owned and run by Kültür A.Ş., the Istanbul Metropolitan Municipality's culture company, which built it from 2005 and opened it in January 2009. Financed by the municipality and ticket sales.
w: Built at Topkapı where the Ottomans breached the walls in 1453; opened after three years with praise from Prime Minister Erdoğan.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Hong Kong Museum of the War of Resistance and Coastal Defence

f: Maintained by Yasukuni Shrine, a private religious corporation since 1946, when the Occupation's Shinto Directive ended state sponsorship of Shinto. The revamped museum reopened in July 1986.
w: Japan's first Western-style museum, opened February 1882 on the shrine grounds; scholars criticise its revisionist account that omits the experiences of China and Korea.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Owned by Roma Capitale and run under a city service contract by Azienda Speciale Palaexpo, a 1998 municipal body that also runs the Scuderie del Quirinale and Casa del Jazz.
w: Opened 1883 on Via Nazionale to a design by Pio Piacentini; reopened in 2007 after restoration.

f: Run and funded from the central budget by an agency of Taiwan's Ministry of Culture, which directs its transformation and negotiated the 2024 honour guard change with the defence ministry.
w: Built from 31 October 1976 and opened 5 April 1980 with a 6.3 metre bronze statue of Chiang; the changing of the guard draws tourists.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Museo Nacional de Arte de Bolivia

f: State-owned, controlled by the Ministry of Defense and the Bolivarian National Militia, based there since 2008. The state organises visits and an honour guard watches the sarcophagus.
w: Built 1904 to 1906 in 23 de Enero. Acting president Delcy Rodríguez renewed her oath at the tomb on 6 January 2026 after Maduro's capture.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War
f: A state museum financed from the state budget under the Ministry of Culture, which renamed it in July 2015 under the decommunisation laws. Its director general is Yurii Savchuk.
w: The 102 metre Motherland Monument houses the main exhibition; in 2023 the Soviet emblem on its shield gave way to the Ukrainian trident.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Run by the Stiftung Deutsches Hygiene-Museum, a non-profit foundation funded by matching annual contributions from Saxony and the City of Dresden, with further grants from federal bodies, businesses and foundations.
w: Founded 1912 by Odol manufacturer Karl August Lingner. Dresden mayor Annekatrin Klepsch chairs its trustees and Iris Edenheiser has directed it since 2022.

n: Museum of Contemporary History of Russia
f: A federal state budgetary institution under Russia's Ministry of Culture, funded from the federal budget. It was the Museum of the Revolution of the USSR until 1998.
w: In the former English Club mansion at Tverskaya 21; the 2022 exhibition NATO, Chronicle of Cruelty drew almost 20,000 visitors in under two months.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A Georgian state museum, funded by the Ministry of Culture and Monuments and listed as a heritage monument; restoration tenders run through the State Procurement Agency. Lia Okroperidze is director.
w: The 1957 complex by Archil Kurdiani holds about 40,000 items; Gori counted roughly 162,000 visitors in 2018. A room on repressions was added in 2010.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery

f: A state institution of Serbia, whose government appoints its director with the Ministry of Culture's consent. Formed in 1996 from the Tito Memorial Centre and the Museum of the Revolution.
w: Serbia's most visited museum, with 100,000 to 120,000 visitors a year; the complex includes Mihailo Janković's 1962 building and the House of Flowers, Tito's tomb.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A state institution under Albania's Ministry of Economy, Culture and Innovation. Its 2024 to 2028 reconstruction is funded by the state Public Investment programme (606 million lek) and EU4Culture.
w: Albania's largest museum, opened 28 October 1981; a Communist Terror pavilion was added in 2012 and it closed in March 2024 for four years.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: In the state Pancasila Sakti complex at Lubang Buaya, jointly managed by the Indonesian military (TNI) and the Education and Culture Ministry. Admission is 5,000 rupiah.
w: Opened by President Suharto on 1 October 1992 with 34 dioramas; tens of thousands of visitors a year, mostly schools. A wing opened in 2013.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: In the state Pancasila Sakti complex at Lubang Buaya

f: The 12 million dollar memorial was paid mostly by Phnom Penh Municipal Hall, the rest by tycoon Ly Yong Phat, who gave the land. The Defence Ministry solicited public donations.
w: Inaugurated by Hun Sen on 29 December 2018 in Chroy Changvar; General Nem Sowath's construction committee runs the site and its museum.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Established on 8 October 1976 by joint decision of the CCP Central Committee, the NPC Standing Committee, the State Council and the Central Military Commission. Entry is free.
w: Opened 9 September 1977 in Tiananmen Square; 240 million visitors, among them over 190 heads of state. Memorial rooms for Mao and five other leaders.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Hong Kong Museum of the War of Resistance and Coastal Defence
f: Owned and run by the Hong Kong Government's Leisure and Cultural Services Department. Admission to its thematic exhibitions is free.
w: In the 1887 British Lei Yue Mun Fort; opened in 2000 as the Museum of Coastal Defence and renamed on 3 September 2024.

f: Owned by the Spanish General State Administration, one of the national museums attached to the Ministry of Culture, under the education and later culture ministries since its creation.
w: Created by decree in April 1941, shown in the Archaeological Museum from 1944; its Ciudad Universitaria building part-opened in 1965 and fully in 1994.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Fondazione La Quadriennale di Roma is funded by its partners: the Ministry of Culture, Roma Capitale's Department of Culture, the Lazio Region and the Rome Chamber of Commerce.
w: Founded by Rome's Governorate in 1927, first held in 1931 at the Palazzo delle Esposizioni, an autonomous body since 1937; based at Villa Carpegna.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Property of the Czech Ministry of Defence since 1 June 2024, administered by the Military History Institute Prague. From 2000 to 2024 the National Museum ran and renovated it.
w: Built 1928 to 1938 by Jan Zázvorka for the Czechoslovak legionaries, with the Unknown Soldier's tomb; state ceremonies and military parades are held there.

f: A Portuguese state museum, run with the Museu Nacional de Etnologia by the Directorate-General for Cultural Heritage until Decree-Law 79/2023 passed national museums to Museus e Monumentos de Portugal E.P.E.
w: In the popular life pavilion of the 1940 Portuguese World Exhibition in Belém; closed in 2003 and reopened in December 2016 after a citizens' campaign.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Military Museum of the Chinese People's Revolution
f: A People's Liberation Army institution, a deputy corps-level unit under the General Political Department, whose propaganda bureau supervises it. Admission is free; the state rebuilt it from 2012 to 2017.
w: One of the Ten Great Buildings, opened 1 August 1960; since the 2017 rebuild, 159,000 square metres, 43 halls and over 160,000 relics.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Memorial of the Site of the First National Congress of the CPC
f: The Shanghai Party committee bought the site in 1952 and shows it free. The state built the hall across the street, opened by Party secretary Li Qiang in June 2021.
w: Xi Jinping took the Politburo Standing Committee there in October 2017 to renew the Party oath; China Daily counts 12 million visits since June 2021.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A state museum founded on 1 July 1950, rated a national first-class museum by the National Cultural Heritage Administration in 2008. Admission free since the building opened in August 2009.
w: The building holds over 38,000 relics and draws nearly 4 million visits a year; Xi Jinping took the Politburo Standing Committee there in October 2022.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Memorial Hall of the War to Resist US Aggression and Aid Korea
f: A state memorial built in 1958 and moved to its site in 1993. Closed in December 2014 for a centrally approved expansion, it reopened in September 2020 with free admission.
w: The 182,000 square metre site has a 53 metre tower and a national defence education park; 12 million visits before the 2014 closure.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: Museo de la Revolución Democrática y Cultural
f: Built by the Fondo Nacional de Inversión Productiva y Social (FPS) for nearly 50 million bolivianos. In 2023 the culture minister said the FPS and Andamarca municipality still administer it.
w: Opened in 2017 in Evo Morales's birthplace, a village of about 163 people; 17,000 visitors in its first year, and closed since 2020.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Built with non-refundable Vietnamese aid on a 1992 Politburo decision and opened in December 2000; in 2014 Vietnam funded a 14 billion dong refurbishment. The Lao state runs it.
w: A bronze statue of Kaysone stands outside; the Party's Propaganda and Training Board stages its anniversary exhibitions, opened by General Secretary Thongloun Sisoulith in 2025.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: The Bangabandhu Memorial Trust ran it from 1994; banks gave it 1,360 million taka in 2017 and Standard Bank 100 million in 2020. The Yunus government revoked its tax exemption.
w: The house where Mujib was killed in 1975, with a six-storey extension from 2011; burned on 5 August 2024 and demolished in February 2025.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Yunus government revoked its tax exemption

f: A state museum created by Ordinance 66-72 of 1972, opened 5 July 1982 and under the Ministry of Mujahideen since 1993. Entry costs 20 dinars, free for mujahideen and soldiers.
w: Beneath the Maqam Echahid esplanade, with wings on the 1830 resistance, the 1954 to 1962 war and independence; Lavalin built it to Bachir Yelles's design.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Run by the defence ministry and the army's General Department of Political Affairs under the Central Military Commission; the state funded the 2,500 billion dong building, opened in November 2024.
w: A 64,640 square metre building on a 74 hectare site with a 45 metre Victory Tower and over 150,000 artefacts, four of them national treasures.

f: A branch of the state National Historical Museum of Belarus, created by the Ministry of Culture and opened in 2012. State bodies lent exhibits to its 4,000-item collection.
w: Six halls on Belarus since 1990, with the first presidential decrees, gifts to Alexander Lukashenko and models of state buildings, in the Presidential Administration building.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Self-financed: paid announcements bought by museums, biennials and fairs, among them Russian, Chinese and Gulf state bodies, plus books, Index and Bar Laika, and two forgiven federal PPP loans.
w: Artist-run company of Moscow-born Anton Vidokle; its Russian state and oligarch-funded clients stopped posting after the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

f: One of Belgium's ten federal scientific institutes, under the Secretary of State for Federal Science Policy. Two thirds of staff and budget go to research. Bart Ouvry is director general.
w: The museum had 106,000 visitors in 2024, down from 132,000 in 2023; it occupies the Charles Girault palace inaugurated by King Albert I in 1910.

n: Palais de la Porte Dorée (Musée national de l'histoire de l'immigration)
f: Run by a public body under four ministries (integration, culture, education and research), formed in 2012 by merging the Cité nationale de l'histoire de l'immigration with the Aquarium.
w: The immigration exhibition opened in October 2007 and was reinstalled in June 2023 after a three year closure, in Albert Laprade's 1931 Art Deco palace.

f: Run by Stichting Nationaal Museum van Wereldculturen, named Wereldmuseum since 2023 and under the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science since the 2014 merger. VriendenLoterij is a supporting partner.
w: In the Colonial Institute building, opened by Queen Wilhelmina in 1926 and shared with the Royal Tropical Institute (KIT) until 2014; 317,572 visitors in 2022.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Managed since April 2003 by EGEAC, the Lisbon city company that runs the municipal cultural venues. The Portuguese Republic holds title to the monument.
w: The 56 metre slab was remodelled in 1985 with exhibition halls and a rooftop viewpoint; EGEAC's 2025 programme centres on empire and colonial memories.

f: A Section 21 non-profit company since 1993; tourism gave 56 to 60 percent of its revenue in 2011 (PMG, 2011).
w: Gerard Moerdijk's monument stands in a nature reserve with a 20,000-seat amphitheatre from 1949; retired Major General Gert Opperman led it as CEO from 2000.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: A state agency under the Executive Yuan, Taiwan's cabinet. The Legislative Yuan froze NT$350 million for renovation in December 2024 and over 20 percent of the 2025 budget.
w: Visits fell from 6.14 million in 2016 to 2.87 million in 2024 across both branches; Hsiao Tsung-huang has been director since January 2023.

f: The General Staff of Turkey's armed forces, in control since the 1980 coup, runs it as a military installation with free entry. A 1981 law declared it a national monument.
w: The mausoleum, built from 1944, opened in 1953 and its museum in 1960; 6,550,480 visitors in 2024, 1,092,000 of them on 10 November alone.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

n: VDNKh (Exhibition of Achievements of National Economy)
f: Owned by the City of Moscow, which took the controlling stake from the federal government after a 2013 decision by Putin, and run as a state joint-stock company.
w: The 2.4 million square metre site holds about 400 buildings, 49 of them listed heritage; Mayor Sobyanin reports more than 30 million visitors a year.

f: A public cultural institution under the Ministry of Culture (Government Decision 90/2010), financed by state budget subsidies plus its own revenue; the subsidy was 19,490,552 lei in 2024.
w: Former Palace of the Posts; a restoration of over 100 million euros, on a Council of Europe Development Bank loan, was announced in October 2024.

f: A National Institution established on 31 July 2008. The Skopje 2014 accounts record 2,110,940 euros of public money spent on its building. The Ministry of Culture heads its partner list.
w: The government counted over 200,000 visitors in its first five years; visits are by compulsory guided tour past 109 wax figures and 85 history paintings.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.
nodes: Ministry of Culture heads its partner list

n: State Museum of the History of the Temurids (Amir Timur Museum)
f: A state museum under the Academy of Sciences of Uzbekistan, built under Cabinet Resolution 99 of 14 March 1996 and rebuilt under a presidential decree of 5 February 2026.
w: The building with a blue cupola, modelled on Samarkand's Gur-e-Amir, faces the Timur statue; President Mirziyoyev reopened it on 9 April 2026 with interactive exhibits.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Run by the Tatmadaw, Myanmar's armed forces: the museum and its Historical Research Institute sit under the Commander-in-Chief's office. Soldiers control its gates and active-duty units supply its docents.
w: The 603 acre site in Zeyathiri Township has twelve display halls of about 540,000 square feet; civilian visitors are rare and staff often outnumber them.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Created by the Ministry of Home Affairs under Than Shwe's State Peace and Development Council; the ministry still pays a skeleton staff and a police major runs it.
w: Three floors of exhibits on a 15.11 acre former cemetery; visitors are mostly students on free field trips, and others pay 4,000 kyat.
tn: No reason for the flag is recorded.

f: Tate group income £167.2M (2024-25), £53.9M of it government grant-in-aid. Supporters: Burberry, The Bukhman Foundation, Gucci, Hyundai Motor, The Julia and Hans Rausing Trust, Blavatnik Family Foundation.
w: A 2025 restructure brought redundancies and closed the staff canteens; PCS members struck over pay from 26 November to 2 December 2025.

f: Rotterdam municipality subsidy, with €15.1M in government subsidies in 2025, plus admissions, funds and companies. Renovation: city credit of €280M approved December 2025, Droom en Daad foundation €80M.
w: Building closed since 2019. Renovation budget rose from €223M to about €359M; a prosecutor's inquiry into Rotterdam building contracts touches its asbestos removal.

f: 2025 income €64.5M: €30.1M federal base payment, €25.6M admissions and education, €1.2M sponsoring and donations. OMV is general partner.
w: General partner OMV is an oil and gas company. Appointed director Eike Schmidt withdrew in October 2019, a month before taking office.
why: The KHM-Museumsverband annual report for 2023 names OMV Aktiengesellschaft as general partner of the Kunsthistorisches Museum; The Art Newspaper (15 November 2022) describes OMV as the Austrian oil, gas and petrochemical company.
nodes: The KHM-Museumsverband annual report for 2023 names OMV Aktiengesellschaft as general partner of the Kunsthistorisches Museum; The Art Newspaper (15 November 2022) describes OMV as the Austrian oil, gas and petrochemical company.

f: 2024 accounts: federal base payment €11.6M, sales revenue €28.9M, donations and other contributions €0.9M. Sponsors are not listed by name.
w: Director Agnes Husslein-Arco's contract was not renewed in July 2016 after an external audit confirmed breaches of compliance rules.

f: Part of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin under the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, financed by the federal government and the states. Second-phase building work: €722.4M plus €295.6M for risks.
w: Closed since 23 October 2023. North wing and Pergamon Altar hall reopen on 4 June 2027; the south wing stays closed until 2037.

f: Public-law foundation. 2025: sales revenue €5.5M, other operating income €22.8M. The Förderstiftung der Hamburger Kunsthalle is its private supporters' foundation.
w: The 2025 income statement shows a loss for the year of €574,656 and a deficit not covered by equity of €574,162.

f: The Free State of Bavaria owns the collections and buildings. The Stiftung Pinakothek der Moderne and a friends' association of 900 members support it.
w: Director general Bernhard Maaz was removed on 2 April 2025 after reports on Nazi-looted art. A 2026 plan ends the State Painting Collections from 2029.

f: Run under the Governorate of Vatican City State, with about 700 employees.
w: In May 2024, 49 employees petitioned the Governorate over pay, conditions and visitor safety; their lawyer raised a first class action before a Vatican court.

f: State museum of the Italian Ministry of Culture with special autonomy. Donors named for Palazzo Citterio: Fondazione Giulio e Giovanna Sacchetti, Amici di Brera and Salone del Mobile Milano.
w: Palazzo Citterio, bought in 1972, opened on 8 December 2024; the museum's unions had called a strike for the inauguration day.
nodes: State museum of the Italian Ministry of Culture

n: Musée du quai Branly – Jacques Chirac
f: 2025 operating receipts €57.3M: State subsidies €44.4M, ticketing €4.6M, patronage and sponsorship €1.2M from 25 patron companies and foundations.
w: Emmanuel Kasarhérou was reappointed president in July 2026. Returned 26 works to Benin and the Djidji Ayôkwé drum to Côte d'Ivoire in 2025.

f: 2023 receipts €25.1M: Ministry of Culture operating subsidy €18.3M, ticketing €2.2M, patronage €1.3M. Caisse d'Epargne CEPAC and Digital Realty are founding patrons.
w: President Pierre-Olivier Costa and general manager Véronique Haché were suspended from 1 July 2026 after a harassment complaint and a prosecutor's investigation; Costa denies wrongdoing.

f: Partners and funders listed: the Belgian federal government, the National Lottery, BNP Paribas Fortis, Proximus, Denys and NextGenerationEU. No amounts are given.
w: The board removed director Paul Dujardin on 5 February 2021 after 18 years and two staff motions of no confidence.

n: Royal Museums of Fine Arts of Belgium
f: 2022 income €22.4M: federal funding €13.4M, own revenue €7.3M, gifts and sponsoring €0.8M.
w: Director general Michel Draguet left on 30 April 2023 after a public conflict with staff. Kim Oosterlinck took over on 1 July 2024.

f: Danish state institution. 2024 budget: net state appropriation DKK 83.3M, other income DKK 72.7M. Named foundations: A.P. Møller Fonden, Ny Carlsbergfondet, Bikubenfonden, Nordea Fonden.
w: More than 40 per cent of its budgeted spending must come from income other than the state appropriation.

f: Public body funded by the Irish government department for the arts. Its café contract with Aramark is worth €7.5M over three years.
w: Artists withdrew works and over 100 people protested the Aramark café contract in February 2022. A €124,805 X-ray system sat unused for eight years.
why: The Irish Times reported on 25 February 2022 that more than 100 people protested outside the gallery, and that three artists asked for their work to be removed, over its €7.5 million café contract with Aramark, a caterer to three direct provision centres.

f: FY2023 Form 990: revenue $114.4M, contributions $44.0M, expenses $77.9M. The City of Philadelphia gave $2.6M in fiscal 2025 and $2.3M in fiscal 2026.
w: The board dismissed director Sasha Suda on 4 November 2025; she sued and the case went to arbitration. Unionised staff struck in September 2022.

f: FY2023 Form 990: revenue $99.6M, contributions $62.4M, expenses $123.3M, net assets $1.22B. The Massachusetts Cultural Council is credited.
w: Laid off 33 employees, about 6.3% of staff, in January 2026, citing an unsustainable deficit; 16 posts were union roles.

f: A 0.2 mill property tax in three counties covered about 65% of the operating budget in 2020. FY2023 Form 990: revenue $71.2M, expenses $57.6M.
w: Whistleblower Aid complained in 2020 about loans of paintings owned by the then director's family; the museum said a law firm's inquiry found no misconduct.

f: Cuyahoga Arts & Culture public grant and the Ohio Arts Council. FY2023 Form 990: revenue $102.9M, contributions $53.8M, expenses $68.7M, net assets $1.14B.
w: A bronze bought in 1986 was ordered seized in 2023 as looted from Bubon, Turkey; the museum agreed to return it in February 2025.

f: FY2023 Form 990: revenue $148.0M, contributions $33.8M, investment income $35.3M, expenses $121.3M, net assets $2.04B. Past gifts from the Brown and Cullen foundations.
w: Heirs of Max Emden sued in 2021 for a Bellotto painting; the Fifth Circuit upheld dismissal of the claim on 29 May 2024.

f: Part of the Woodruff Arts Center, whose FY2023 Form 990 shows revenue $99.8M, contributions $67.8M and expenses $108.4M.
w: The Woodruff Arts Center accused its former chief operating officer of misappropriating about $600,000 and referred the matter to the U.S. Attorney's Office.

f: FY2023 Form 990: revenue $27.6M, contributions $20.1M, expenses $41.6M. Operating support from the City of Baltimore, Maryland State Arts Council, Baltimore County and Howard County; Stoneridge Foundation gave over $10M.
w: In October 2020 it paused a planned $65M sale of works hours before auction, after former trustees objected and $50M in pledges was rescinded.
nodes: Named in the record: Henry and Marie-Josée Kravis were among the lead sponsors of the 2025 BMA Ball, which raised over $1.1 million.

f: City support as a Cultural Institutions Group member. FY2023 Form 990: revenue $47.2M. Its October 2026 gala raised $4M; Lafayette Square and HarbourView Equity were lead sponsors.
w: Opened its $300M Adjaye Associates building on 125th Street on 15 November 2025, a public-private project with the city.

f: FY2025 Form 990: revenue $52.6M, contributions $25.7M, expenses $45.4M, net assets $587.1M. A campaign raised $242M by November 2023, led by $35M from trustee Stephen A. Schwarzman.
w: Reopened on 17 April 2025 after a $220M renovation by Selldorf Architects.

f: A Smithsonian museum. Federal appropriation $5.6M for fiscal 2023, beside $4.8M in donor and sponsor funds. The $68M sculpture garden had $46.7M of prior federal funding.
w: Director Melissa Chiu left on 31 August 2026. The redesigned sculpture garden opened in October 2026 after objections from the Cultural Landscape Foundation.

f: Nearly half its operating budget comes from a Hennepin County tax levy, $19.7M certified for 2024. Its filer, the Minneapolis Society Of Fine Arts, reports FY2025 revenue of $57.7M.
w: An Italian magistrate ordered the return of its Roman marble Doryphoros in February 2022; Italy has since stopped state museum loans to it.

f: Ontario Ministry of Culture, City of Toronto, Department of Canadian Heritage and Canada Council for the Arts. Ken Thomson gave $50M in capital; Dani Reiss C$35M to the expansion.
w: Curator Wanda Nanibush's 2023 departure drew open letters with over 3,400 signatories. Over 400 OPSEU members struck in March 2024, closing it for a month.

An open letter published on 29 November 2023, with more than 3,300 signatures, called for a boycott of the gallery over the departure of curator Wanda Nanibush, and a letter of 28 November from 44 Governor General Award-winning artists called it political censorship (The Art Newspaper, 1 December 2023); the gallery called the departure a mutual decision.

f: A federal Crown corporation: parliamentary appropriations $55.9M in 2024-25, earned revenue $7.7M, its Foundation $2.4M. Scotiabank gave $10M over ten years to the photography programme.
w: Four senior staff, including the chief curator and the senior curator of Indigenous art, were let go on 18 November 2022 under an interim director.

f: Year to March 2025: revenue $57.7M. Quebec's culture ministry $16.7M, Canada Council for the Arts, Conseil des arts de Montréal, its Foundation $8.5M, admissions and events $4.7M.
w: The board dismissed director Nathalie Bondil in July 2020; she sued for C$2M and the sides settled in January 2022.

f: City of Vancouver, Province of British Columbia, BC Arts Council and Canada Council for the Arts; BMO and Canada Life fund programmes. Michael Audain pledged C$100M for a new building.
w: Scrapped its Herzog & de Meuron building in December 2024 after costs reached C$600M. About 30 staff were laid off after a C$32.1M deficit.

f: Year to March 2025: revenue $103.7M, Province of Ontario grants $41.5M, its Foundation $12.6M, admissions $15.3M. Hennick Family Foundation gave C$50M to OpenROM.
w: In October 2023 it asked Palestinian American contributors to change wording and cropped a painting, then apologised after an overnight sit-in.

n: Art Gallery of New South Wales
f: 2024-25 revenue $147.9M: NSW Government recurrent grants $54.7M, donations $28.0M. Corporate partners include ANZ, Aqualand, Macquarie Group, Bank of China and Optus.
w: Director Maud Page announced 51 of 382 jobs would go to save AUD 7.5 million a year; staff protested outside on 27 August 2025.
why: ArtAsiaPacific reported on 29 August 2025 that more than 100 gallery staff and supporters held a midday protest outside the gallery on 27 August 2025 over 51 planned job cuts, the first industrial action there in more than a decade.

f: Year to June 2025: government operating grants $89.5M, trading revenue $62.7M. Partners include Mercedes-Benz, MECCA, Telstra, Country Road, Deakin University, Macquarie Group, Qantas, HSBC Australia and EY.
w: NGV Foundation members include Crown Resorts Foundation, Tabcorp and Rio Tinto. The precinct project with its new gallery rose from $1.41B to $1.57B.

f: Privately funded by founder David Walsh, a professional gambler, who paid the A$75M cost himself. Admission is $45 for visitors from outside Tasmania.
w: Its festival Dark Mofo cancelled Santiago Sierra's Union Flag in March 2021. The women-only Ladies Lounge faced a discrimination case in 2024.
why: The Art Newspaper reported on 21 June 2026 that founder David Walsh, a professional gambler, paid the A$75m cost of the museum himself; Al Jazeera reported on 25 January 2015 that he made his millions gambling.

f: FY25/26: State Government income $12.3M, 52% of the total. Wesfarmers Arts is principal partner; others include Healthway, Seven West Media, JCDecaux and Singapore Airlines.
w: Wesfarmers Arts, its longest-standing corporate partner, has a gallery and the daily guided tours carrying its name.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: National museum funded by government money and its own income. Group budget for fiscal 2025: JPY 13.5B, of which government operating funding JPY 9.6B, self-generated income JPY 2.2B.
w: The Agency for Cultural Affairs wants national museums to earn 65% of exhibition costs by 2030; it says restructuring does not assume closure.

f: National institution under the National Museum of Art, funded by government money and its own income.
w: One of 12 national museums told to earn 65% of exhibition costs by 2030, with higher prices planned for foreign tourists.

f: Privately funded through the Samsung Foundation of Culture. It houses the Lee family's collection of more than 15,000 objects.
w: Director Hong Ra-hee resigned in 2008 during a Samsung slush fund investigation, returned in 2011 and resigned again in March 2017 after her son's indictment.

f: Government museum of the Leisure and Cultural Services Department. 2025/26: expenditure HK$146.2M, revenue HK$96.7M.
w: Asked in 2019 whether it shows political art, a government spokesman said only that curating follows the museum's strategic positioning.

f: State project financed largely by Japanese loans. Tickets are EGP 200 for an Egyptian adult and EGP 1,450 for other nationalities.
w: A public-private partnership: Hassan Allam's subsidiary Legacy runs it. President Sisi appointed Major General Atef Moftah to lead the project in 2016.

f: Run and paid for through Qatar Museums, under the Amir's patronage. Hyundai won a $434M construction contract in 2011; Microsoft, Cisco and droppGroup are digital partners.
w: Qatar Museums is chaired by the Amir's sister, Sheikha Al Mayassa. The building's total cost was not disclosed.
why: Qatar Museums' own about page, read on 14 November 2026, says it operates under the patronage of the Amir and is chaired by his sister Sheikha Al Mayassa; The Art Newspaper reported on 27 March 2019 that Qatar Museums Authority let the $434m building contract.

f: An autonomous institution, by its own account un-aided by government. Donors of Rs 10 crore and above: Ministry of Culture, Citibank, Bank of America, TCS Foundation, J. Paul Getty Trust.
w: Established by Act III of 1909 as the Prince of Wales Museum of Western India; now governed under the CSMVS Act.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Run by INAH within the federal culture secretariat. Its ethnographic galleries were reinstalled from the federal Chapultepec Forest project, whose budget reached 10bn pesos.
w: Closed early on 3 June 2025 and reopened on 5 June after a private security firm did not supply enough guards.

f: Run by a trust with Banco de México, the central bank, as trustee. Tickets are $320 MXN general, $160 for Mexican residents.
w: A former director said in April 2025 that works and diary pages had gone missing and trustees ignored the evidence; the trust disputes it.

f: Privately funded from an endowment set up by Unibanco and enlarged by the Moreira Salles family.
w: The family's wealth comes from Unibanco, merged into Itaú Unibanco in 2008, and stakes in niobium supplier CBMM.

f: Budget from the national General Appropriations Act. Endowment: ₱250M a year each from the Philippine Charity Sweepstakes Office and the Philippine Amusement and Gaming Corporation for five years.
w: Its 2019 charter feeds the endowment from the state lottery and the state gaming corporation; a 15-member board has eight private-sector presidential appointees.

f: Run by Banco de la República, Colombia's central bank, which received the collection as a gift from the artist. Admission is free.
w: Holds the 208 works Fernando Botero donated to Banco de la República in 2000: 123 of his own and 85 by other artists.

f: Privately funded by a French family, Mission Local reported on 3 September 2025; its Americas director said the closing of its San Francisco space that month had nothing to do with funding. Its own site names no funder: it lists co-founders Vincent Worms (president) and Sandra Terdjman (vice-president) and says it operates through the endowment fund AKAT – KADIST in France and two US 501(c)(3) entities, Artnow International Inc and KADIST Collection Manager Inc. Their Form 990-PF returns, as shown on ProPublica's Nonprofit Explorer: Artnow International, year to December 2024, revenue USD 1.42M, nearly all of it contributions, expenses USD 1.46M, Vincent Worms chairman; KADIST Collection Manager, total assets USD 41.6M at December 2024, after contributions of USD 44.7M in 2023. The pages read did not name the contributors.
w: A non-profit contemporary art organisation with a collection its site puts at over 2,600 works by 1,400 artists; it runs exhibitions, residencies and loans to museums. The collection was started in 2001 and the Paris space opened in 2006 (Wikipedia). A second space at 3295 20th Street in San Francisco's Mission District, opened in 2011, closed on 6 September 2025 after 14 years; the director said the work had shifted to international collaborations and that no one would be laid off (Mission Local).

f: A joint project of the art collective teamLab and the Tokyo developer Mori Building Company, which carries its name in the title (Tokyo Metropolitan Government's Tokyo Updates, 7 April 2023); the Japanese title also carries the name Epson (Good Luck Trip listing, updated 4 March 2026). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: A ticketed digital art venue by the collective teamLab in the basement of Mori Building's Azabudai Hills development; it opened in Odaiba in June 2018, closed in August 2022 and reopened at Azabudai Hills on 9 February 2024 (Time Out Tokyo). It is a commercial venue inside a property developer's complex, and no accounts for it were found.

f: Part of Benesse Art Site Naoshima, the collective name for the art activities of Benesse and the Fukutake Foundation (Benesse Art Site Naoshima website). The Peak reported on 22 December 2016 that the project is funded by Soichiro Fukutake's foundation, which runs on dividends from its shares in Benesse Holdings. Admission is JPY2,500 to JPY3,000 (museum website); the pages read did not state amounts.
w: A museum built underground on Naoshima, designed by Tadao Ando and opened in July 2004, holding works by Claude Monet, James Turrell and Walter De Maria (Benesse Art Site Naoshima website). The Fukutake Foundation is chaired by Hideaki Fukutake, who also chairs the board of Benesse Holdings, with Soichiro Fukutake as honorary chairman (Fukutake Foundation press release, 22 October 2024).

n: The National Museum of Modern Art, Tokyo
f: One of the museums of the Independent Administrative Institution National Museum of Art, which received a state operating grant of about ¥8.46 billion in FY2026; operating grants and facility subsidies were more than 60% of its income when its 2026 objectives were set (Institute for Social Vision Design, 26 September 2026, citing the Agency for Cultural Affairs and the education ministry). Earned income is tickets and the MOMAT Passport (¥1,200), with a donation page run by the parent body (museum website).
w: Japan's first national art museum, established in 1952, in Kitanomaru Park. Objectives the education ministry set on 27 February 2026 require the parent body to cover at least 65% of exhibition costs from its own revenue by FY2030, and MOMAT's collection admission rises from ¥500 to ¥1,000 on 9 February 2027 (Institute for Social Vision Design, 26 September 2026).

n: Jorge B. Vargas Museum and Filipiniana Research Center
f: A museum of the University of the Philippines, a state university, on its Diliman campus; the pages read did not state who pays its budget. Admission is P20 for students, P50 for non-UP visitors and P40 for UP staff, faculty and alumni (Quezon City Government website).
w: A university museum of Philippine art holding the collection Jorge B. Vargas was also Mayor of Manila in 1942 and ambassador to Japan from 1943 to 1945 (ASEF culture360).

f: Paid for by the Government of Punjab: it allocated Rs240 million in January 2025 to equip the museum with modern technology (Dawn, 24 January 2025), and in February 2025 the chief minister directed the cabinet to approve $8 million (Rs2 billion) for an upgrade under a UNESCO master plan (Dawn via Asia News Network, 22 July 2026). Tickets are Rs50 for adults, Rs20 for students and children and Rs1000 for foreigners (museum website).
w: A provincial museum on The Mall, opened to the public in 1894, run by a board of governors headed by the chief secretary of Punjab as an allied department of the Tourism, Archaeology and Museums department (Dawn via Asia News Network, 22 July 2026). Dawn reported that no museum specialist has headed it since 2001 and that five rare manuscripts were stolen that year.

f: Mainly the Victorian Government: government grants of $30,507,620 from the Department of Jobs, Skills, Industry and Regions out of total revenue of $37,264,194 in 2024-25, with self generated revenue of $6,756,574 (annual report 2024-25). Named partners include Blackmagic Design, Panasonic, RMIT University, Big Ant Studios, the Gandel Foundation, the Naomi Milgrom Foundation and the 6a Foundation; sponsorship and grants came to $1,359,195.
w: A museum of screen culture at Fed Square, established under Victoria's Film Act 2001 and one of the Victorian Government's nine public cultural institutions; Seb Chan is Director and CEO (annual report 2024-25; museum website). The 2024-25 grant 'includes additional solvency operating funding' and the net result from transactions was a deficit of $4,863,902 after depreciation (annual report 2024-25).

f: Owned by the NSW Government, which gave $26.2m of the $147.5m general operations revenue in FY25, including an $18.5m annual operating endowment and $3.1m of COVID-19 tourism support, plus a $39.3m building maintenance grant; 82% of operating revenue was self-generated from performances, the precinct and private funding (annual report 2024-25). Mastercard is Major Partner and Honeywell is Global Goals Partner; private funding was $6.9m.
w: A performing arts centre on Bennelong Point, opened in 1973 and run for the NSW Government by the Sydney Opera House Trust under the Sydney Opera House Trust Act 1961 (annual report 2024-25). What is projected on its sails is decided by the state government and has been fought over since 2018, when the premier overruled the chief executive to allow a horse race promotion (SBS News, 9 October 2018).
why: More than 1,000 people with torches and phones protested on the forecourt on 9 October 2018 against the projection of the Everest horse race draw on the sails, and a petition of over 300,000 signatures went to state parliament (SBS News, 9 October 2018). A pro-Palestine rally at the forecourt follow
