f: Funded entirely by the central government; under the National Finance Act its revenue goes to the national treasury (The Korea Times, 12 January 2026). Its annual operating budget exceeds 80 billion won against revenue of 2.3 billion won, a figure raised at a National Assembly audit (The Asia Business Daily, 3 November 2025).
w: The state museum of Korean art and archaeology in Yongsan, opened in 1945, with free admission to permanent galleries since 1 May 2008 and more than 6.5 million visitors in 2025 (The Korea Times; The Asia Business Daily). The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism is considering bringing back admission fees as early as 2027, at about 5,000 won for adults (The Korea Times, 12 January 2026).

f: An autonomous organisation under the Ministry of Culture, Government of India, with a Board of Trustees; the ministry paid for its modernisation, sanctioning ₹99.76 crore in June 2013 and ₹ nine crore in March 2013 out of ₹109.42 crore available (Comptroller and Auditor General of India, Report No. 6 of 2020). The pages read did not state its annual grant.
w: Founded in 1814 as the Asiatic Society Museum and opened in its present building in 1878 as the Imperial Museum (Comptroller and Auditor General of India, Report No. 6 of 2020). The auditor found that the modernisation for the 2014 bicentenary was awarded to NBCC (India) Ltd. on nomination, cost ₹105.70 crore against ₹83.66 crore sanctioned for the works done, and damaged artefacts including the Lion Capital.

f: A municipal exhibition company: the City of Frankfurt pays for the building works, a renovation of the Römerberg building costed at 35.6 million euros with a KfW grant of 2,020,000 euros (entwicklungsstadt.de, 9 February 2026). The Schirn says its exhibitions are also carried by partners and sponsors, which the pages read did not name. The pages read did not state the annual city grant.
w: An exhibition hall for modern and contemporary art without a collection of its own on the pages read, run as SCHIRN KUNSTHALLE FRANKFURT am Main GmbH under director Sebastian Baden, with the city's culture councillor Ina Hartwig chairing the supervisory board. Since September 2025 it shows in the former Dondorf printing works in Bockenheim while its 1986 building on the Römerberg is renovated; the return is given as 2027 by hessenschau and the completion as 2028 by entwicklungsstadt.de.

f: A museum of the City of Frankfurt am Main (museumsufer.de); its contact address is a city address. The pages read did not state amounts or name sponsors.
w: The city's museum of art from the 1960s to today, in a 1991 building by Hans Hollein with two further sites, ZOLLAMT and TOWER; museumsufer.de lists the main building as closed for fire-safety renovation. In 2022 about 80 per cent of staff signed an anonymous letter to director Susanne Pfeffer describing a toxic work culture (ArtReview, 18 May 2022), and in May 2023 the city's culture department told the city assembly that a mediation had been declared failed by staff.

f: The museum calls itself 'the publicly funded state museum of North Rhine-Westphalia'; it is a private-law foundation. Named partners include KPMG (since 2002, free evenings), Linklaters (since 2010, family days) and Stiftung der Sparda-Bank West (since 2010), with a longer list of companies and foundations. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The state art museum of North Rhine-Westphalia in two houses, K20 on Grabbeplatz (opened 1986) and K21 in the former state parliament building (opened 2002), founded in 1961 after the state bought 88 works by Paul Klee; Susanne Gaensheimer has been director since 1 September 2017. Its partner list names Audi, Bayer, Emirates, Henkel, HSBC Deutschland, Volkswagen and several law firms without saying what each pays for.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Deichtorhallen Hamburg GmbH is wholly owned by the Free and Hanseatic City of Hamburg and is financed for the most part by a city operating grant, 6.5 million euros in business year 2025, with total city grants of 7.02 million euros (Hamburg Beteiligungsbericht 2025). The Körber Foundation paid for the restoration of the halls before they were handed to the city in 1988 (Deichtorhallen website).
w: Exhibition halls for contemporary art and photography in two former market halls, opened on 9 November 1989, with the Falckenberg Collection in Harburg since 2011; directors are Dirk Luckow and Bert Antonius Kaufmann and the culture senator Carsten Brosda chairs the supervisory board. The Haus der Photographie has been closed for renovation since August 2021; the reopening planned for 2024 is now given as spring 2028 and the city pays compensation for the lost income (Hamburg Beteiligungsbericht 2025).

f: The Province of Styria and the City of Graz finance it under a fixed commitment in a 55:45 ratio; Kunsthaus Graz GmbH is owned in equal parts by the City of Graz and Universalmuseum Joanneum GmbH, a company of the Province of Styria (Kunsthaus website). A 2019 state press release put the annual budget from state and city at about 6.4 million euros and the construction cost at 38.4 million euros, shared by the state, the city and the Republic of Austria.
w: An exhibition house for contemporary art opened in 2003, run by Kunsthaus Graz GmbH with Universalmuseum Joanneum GmbH managing the company under a service agreement. Until the 2019 restructuring about 2.2 million euros of its yearly money went to leasing payments on the building, leaving 4.2 million euros for operations (Land Steiermark, 14 October 2019).

f: The basic financing of the Museen der Stadt Linz (Lentos and Nordico) for 2026 is 4.9 million euros, the same as 2025: a donation of 4.0 million euros from LINZ AG and a grant of 0.9 million euros from the City of Linz, in a total budget of 5.8 million euros (City of Linz press paper, annual programme 2026). Raiffeisenlandesbank OÖ and UNIQA are corporate partners; business sponsors and 'building block' buyers covered about 10 per cent of the 33 million euro construction cost (Lentos website).
w: The City of Linz's museum of modern and contemporary art, opened on 18 May 2003 in a building by Weber+Hofer as successor to the Neue Galerie der Stadt Linz, which grew from the holdings of the Berlin art dealer Wolfgang Gurlitt; Hemma Schmutz has been director since 2017. The museum has reviewed its holdings for Nazi-era losses since 1998 and lists restitutions from 1999 to 2015, among them works by Schiele, Klimt, Corinth and Nolde (Lentos website).

f: The concert programme is run by HamburgMusik gGmbH, 95.20 per cent City of Hamburg and 4.80 per cent Stiftung Elbphilharmonie, which gets a fixed city grant of 6.0 million euros, a subsidy share of 14 per cent this season (Hamburg Beteiligungsbericht 2025). Principal sponsors are Kühne Stiftung, Julius Baer and Rolex, with about 20 'classic sponsors' and several foundations (Elbphilharmonie website).
w: Hamburg's concert hall, opened on 11 January 2017; the city founded the operating and marketing company in December 2008 and owns it outright. Construction was first estimated at about 186 million euros and ended at about 866 million euros after almost ten years (spot on news via leinetal24.de, 7 September 2026).

f: A dependent institution of the State of Berlin, paid from the state budget: 25.14 million euros according to the Bund der Steuerzahler Berlin (9 September 2026). Berlin cut 2 million euros from its 2025 budget (taz, 27 November 2024) and set savings of 1.25 million euros for the first season of the new director (taz, 4 August 2026).
w: A Berlin state theatre, legally 'eine nichtrechtsfähige Anstalt des Landes Berlin', led since the 2026/2027 season by Matthias Lilienthal, appointed by culture senator Joe Chialo on 7 February 2025 after René Pollesch's death. Its 2026 pop-up pool cost about 410,000 euros, of which Speedo paid 27,500 euros and the rest came from the theatre's budget (Berlin Senate answer, 26 August 2026), and the taxpayers' association called it a misuse of funds.

f: A private theatre partly funded by the Berlin Senate: it earns about a quarter of its budget itself and last received 21 million euros of Senate funding; the 2025 cut was 1.8 million euros, softened by 700,000 euros for wage rises (Berliner Zeitung, 5 December 2024). Its partner page shows logos of Pentanex, Goethe-Institut, Bundeszentrale für politische Bildung, Hertie-Stiftung, Steinway & Sons and GEODIS, without amounts.
w: A theatre founded in 1962 by a group of students around Jürgen Schitthelm, at Lehniner Platz since 1981, run as a non-profit GmbH whose associates are Schitthelm, Friedrich Barner, Thomas Ostermeier and Tobias Veit; Ostermeier has been artistic director since 2009. In December 2024 it said the Berlin cut left it threatened with insolvency in 2025, raised top ticket prices by almost 100 per cent, closed its Studio stage and cut two productions a season (Berliner Zeitung, 4 and 5 December 2024).

f: The City of Hamburg has been sole shareholder since May 2020 and its culture authority pays the operating subsidy; the company is 'highly dependent' on city grants, which included a deficit cover of 1.884 million euros in 2023/24, and it closed 2024/25 with a loss of 888,000 euros (Hamburg Beteiligungsbericht 2025). The federal government and Hamburg each pledged 60 million euros for the general renovation (Kampnagel website); project funders include Kulturstiftung des Bundes, Fonds Darstellende Künste, Goethe-Institut and the EU's Creative Europe programme (Kampnagel website).
w: A performing arts venue on a former crane factory site, used by independent theatre groups from 1982, a GmbH since 1993 and a state theatre since 2020, led since 2007 by Amelie Deuflhard. The city's holdings report records a structural deficit and negative equity before a rebuild by Lacaton & Vassal planned for 2026 to 2029; in January 2024 Hamburg's antisemitism commissioner demanded that it disinvite the speaker Zamzam Ibrahim, and the keynote was moved online.

f: A cultural company of the City of Frankfurt, which funds it with over 4 million euros a year; in November 2025 the federal government ended its funding of the Bündnis internationaler Produktionshäuser, of which the Mousonturm's share was 600,000 euros a year (hessenschau, 20 November 2025). Project money comes from the Hessian Ministry of Science and Art, Kulturfonds Frankfurt RheinMain and Frankfurt foundations such as Crespo Foundation and Stiftung Polytechnische Gesellschaft (Mousonturm website).
w: A production house for dance, performance and international theatre in Frankfurt's Ostend, run as Künstlerhaus Mousonturm Frankfurt am Main GmbH by Anna Wagner and Marcus Dross, with the city's culture councillor Ina Hartwig chairing the supervisory board. The loss of 600,000 euros of federal alliance money in 2025 was criticised by Hartwig, who said the city would keep supporting the house.

Museo de la Solidaridad Salvador Allende

f: Funded by Berlin's Senate Department for Culture and Social Cohesion (Sophiensæle website); the Senate lists it among 15 concept-funded private houses that shared about 3.1 million euros of extra money for pay in the 2024/2025 budget (Berlin Senate press release, 15 December 2023). The pages read did not state amounts for the house itself.
w: A production house for independent dance, performance and theatre in the former Craftsmen's Association House of 1904/05 in Berlin-Mitte, founded in 1996 by Sasha Waltz, Jochen Sandig, Jo Fabian and Dirk Cieslak and led since 2023/24 by Jens Hillje and Andrea Niederbuchner; Sandig, Waltz and Amelie Deuflhard are the associates of Sophiensæle GmbH. In November 2024 it called on its public to protest the Berlin culture cuts.

f: Funded by the State of Saxony-Anhalt, the Federal Government Commissioner for Culture and the Media and the City of Dessau-Roßlau (foundation website). The state's financing agreement for 2022 to 2026 gives the foundation about 22.6 million euros over the period (Staatskanzlei Sachsen-Anhalt, 27 December 2021); the pages read did not state the federal or city amounts.
w: A foundation under public law set up in 1994 that keeps the Bauhaus Building, a museum opened in 2019 and a collection of over 50,000 objects; Barbara Steiner has been director since 2021. In October 2024 the AfD group in the Saxony-Anhalt parliament tabled a motion calling the Bauhaus a wrong path of modernism, which was rejected, and in July 2026, six weeks before a state election the AfD led in polls, the federal culture minister said the state remains bound to fund the foundation (Tagesspiegel/dpa, 24 July 2026).

f: It receives institutional funding from the Senate Department for Culture and Community of the State of Berlin (Kunsthaus Dahlem website). The pages read did not state amounts; other sponsors appear on its site only as logos.
w: An exhibition house for post-war modernism in Germany, mainly sculpture from 1945 to 1961, opened in 2015 in the state studio built from 1939 to 1942 for the Nazi-era sculptor Arno Breker on a site the City of Berlin provided 'at the request of the Führer'. It is run by Atelierhaus Dahlem gGmbH, sole subsidiary of the Bernhard Heiliger Foundation, with Dorothea Schöne as managing director.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Community of the State of Berlin

f: The Ville de Nîmes is the main funder: 927 000 € of the 995 000 € in operating subsidies received in 2023, with 40 000 € from the Conseil régional (Occitanie) and 28 000 € from the DRAC (activity report 2023). The same report gives an annual budget of close to 1.4 M€ and 85 000 € from the city plus 17 625 € from the FRAM for acquisitions in 2023.
w: Contemporary art museum of the city of Nîmes, in a building by Norman Foster opened on 8 May 1993, run since 2000 by a municipal régie autonome created by the city council. The city has cut its operating subsidy by 50 000 € since 2021, a cut Objectif Gard reported in December 2021 as part of the 2022 municipal budget.

f: The Ville de Lyon lists the museum among its facilities and in 2018 placed it with the Musée des Beaux-Arts in its Pôle des musées d'art; private support comes through Cercle 21, a patrons' group created to support the museum. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Contemporary art museum created in 1984 in a wing of the Palais Saint-Pierre and moved in 1995 to a Renzo Piano building at the Cité internationale; its artistic director also heads the contemporary art side of the Biennale de Lyon, for which it is a venue.
nodes: Musée des Beaux-Arts in its Pôle des musées d'art

f: Its site lists four public partners, the Ministère de la Culture, the Région Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, the Métropole de Lyon and the Ville de Lyon, then Groupe Partouche, Grand Casino de Lyon Le Pharaon as 'partenaire historique', Esker as 'mécène officiel' and Société Générale and LPA Mobilités as 'mécènes associés'. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: An association (SIREN 315 605 535) that stages one biennial a year, alternating contemporary art and dance; the 18th art edition runs from 19 September to 13 December 2026. In 2022 the Région Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes under Laurent Wauquiez cut its support by more than 250 000 € according to figures from the regional Green group reported by Lyon Mag, and the Métropole de Lyon protested.
nodes: Grand Casino de Lyon Le Pharaon as 'partenaire historique

f: Its statutes split the cost between the Région Hauts-de-France (8/10), the Département du Pas-de-Calais (1/10) and the Communauté d'Agglomération Lens-Liévin (1/10): 9 991 840 €, 1 061 650 € and 1 248 980 € in 2025. The state pays 500 K€ a year under a three-year agreement, ticketing brought 1,08 M€ and patronage and space hire 873 K€ in 2025, with 150 K€ from Crédit Mutuel and 100 K€ from AXA for exhibitions (budget report CFU 2025, BP 2026).
w: An établissement public de coopération culturelle opened on 4 December 2012 on a former coal pit in Lens, showing works lent by the Musée du Louvre, which holds 10 of the 30 board seats while the region holds 9. Its 2026 budget report says the statutory contributions, unchanged in cash, are worth 10,4 M€ in 2014 prices and that the Pas-de-Calais department paid less than its tenth in 2025.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Local authorities pay operating contributions of 5 150 000 € (Eurométropole de Metz), 4 000 000 € (Région Grand Est) and 550 000 € (Ville de Metz); the state and the Centre Pompidou pay nothing and lend works. In 2019 patronage brought 705 000 € and ticketing 971 991 €, the Département de la Moselle gave 300 000 €, and Groupe Wendel is the founding patron (museum website; annual report 2019).
w: An établissement public de coopération culturelle opened in 2010 as the first decentralised branch of the Centre Pompidou, chaired by Centre Pompidou president Laurent Le Bon and directed by Chiara Parisi. On 6 May 2024 two women wrote 'Me Too' on the glass over Courbet's L'Origine du monde, on loan from the Musée d'Orsay, in an action claimed by the artist Deborah de Robertis (ArtReview, 8 May 2024).

f: A national public establishment under the Ministère de la Culture: in 2023 its own resources were 6,40 M€, 56% of total revenue, of which 4,20 M€ ticketing, and public financing was 5 M€, including an exceptional end-of-year subsidy of 500 000 € from the ministry (annual report 2023). Patrons thanked in the 2023 report include the Ford Foundation, the Terra Foundation for American Art, Farrow & Ball, Phillips and the Fondation Almine et Bernard Ruiz-Picasso pour l'Art.
w: State museum in the Hôtel Salé, opened in October 1985 around works given to the state by Picasso's heirs in lieu of inheritance tax, and a public establishment since a decree of 18 June 2010, with a president named by the Council of Ministers. In 2023 its president Cécile Debray answered critics of Picasso's treatment of women by saying some readings of his life were 'completely perverse' (The Art Newspaper, 3 July 2023).
nodes: Fondation Almine et Bernard Ruiz-Picasso pour l'Art
Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA)

f: The museum states that it is the only national public museum to finance itself at 100%: it sells original bronze casts made from Rodin's moulds, in editions limited to 12, which bring between 30 and 35% of its annual budget (museum website). The Art Newspaper put normal annual revenue at about €11m, roughly €8m from tickets, shop, restaurant and space hire and about €3m from bronzes (8 July 2020).
w: National museum under the Ministère de la Culture in the Hôtel Biron, open since 1919, founded on Rodin's 1916 gift of his works, moulds and copyrights to the French state, and holder of the artist's moral right. In 2020 a deputy told the culture minister the sale of bronzes abroad to cover Covid losses was 'insupportable'; the ministry replied that such sales are a traditional resource of the museum and concern editions made for sale, not the inalienable collection (Assemblée nationale, written question 31232).

f: A museum of the Ville de Paris run by the public establishment Paris Musées, which received a city operating subsidy of 55,5 M€ in 2025 for its fourteen museums and drew 43% of operating revenue from its own resources (Paris Musées annual report 2025). Named patrons in 2025 were the BPCE group, 'grand mécène du Petit Palais', for the peristyle fresco restoration, and Chanel for the Worth exhibition.
w: Fine arts museum of the City of Paris in a building by Charles Girault made for the 1900 Exposition universelle, a museum since 1902, with free entry to the permanent collection and 1 455 790 visitors in 2025. Its accounts are not published separately from those of Paris Musées, created in 2013.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A museum of the Ville de Paris run by Paris Musées, which received a city operating subsidy of 55,5 M€ in 2025 for its fourteen museums and drew 43% of operating revenue from its own resources (Paris Musées annual report 2025). Named patrons in 2025 were Forvis Mazars for 'Matisse et Marguerite', the Würth group, 'mécène régulier du MAM', for Gabriele Münter, Sfil for Otobong Nkanga and the Fondation Famille Jean-Pierre Aubin for George Condo.
w: The City of Paris's museum of modern and contemporary art, inaugurated in 1961 in a building made for the 1937 international exhibition, with close to 16 000 works; director Fabrice Hergott. In June 2025 the dealer Kamel Mennour announced a gift of 180 works by 45 artists from his gallery's stock and his own collection, with a 1,700 sq m exhibition planned for 2027 (The Art Newspaper, 13 June 2025).
nodes: Fondation Famille Jean-Pierre Aubin for George Condo

f: A private foundation: for its 4 million euro extension, the Région, the Département and the state gave 500,000 euros each, Groupe Dassault 1 million euros, president Adrien Maeght 500,000 euros, ten individual patrons 500,000 euros together, Triverio Construction 150,000 euros, the Société des Amis 65,000 euros and Saint-Gobain 20,000 euros (The Art Newspaper France, 9 January 2023). The pages read did not state its operating budget for recent years.
w: Modern art foundation created by the Paris dealers Aimé and Marguerite Maeght, opened in 1964 in buildings by Josep Lluís Sert, presided for four decades by their son Adrien Maeght, with his daughter Isabelle Maeght, director of Galerie Maeght, on the board. Its largest extension donor is Groupe Dassault, whose Dassault Aviation makes military aircraft, and the new main hall is named after Nicole Dassault.
why: Groupe Dassault gave 1 million euros to the foundation's extension, whose large hall is named after Nicole Dassault (The Art Newspaper France, 9 January 2023); the group's site, read on 14 November 2026, says Dassault Aviation 'conçoit, fabrique, vend et soutient des avions militaires'.
nodes: Groupe Dassault gave 1 million euros to the foundation's extension, whose large hall is named after Nicole Dassault (The Art Newspaper France, 9 January 2023); the group's site, read on 14 November 2026, says Dassault Aviation 'conçoit, fabrique, vend et soutient des avions militaires'.

f: The state's operating subsidy was 99,8 M€ in 2023, within revenue of 241,4 M€ against 239,1 M€ of expenses, of which 155,1 M€ payroll; patronage and partnerships brought 23,6 M€ in 2023 (Cour des comptes, 24 October 2024). Sponsors named by the Cour are EY, Paprec, Chanel, Crédit agricole and Rolex, with funds collected through the friends' association AROP.
w: France's national opera and ballet company, working at the Palais Garnier and the Opéra Bastille under director general Alexander Neef. The Cour des comptes reported on 24 October 2024 that it ran deficits until 2022 and needs at least 200 M€ of building works by 2030; the works plan later announced is costed at 450.8 million euros, a quarter from the state, and the Garnier stage is now expected to stay closed until at least 2032 (Sortiraparis citing AFP, updated 3 July 2026).

f: A museum of Sabancı University, to which the Sabancı family gave the mansion and its collections in 1998. Its support page lists Sabancı Holding, Akbank and Sabancı Vakfı (the Sabancı Foundation) as supporters, with American Express, Jotun, Norde, Medline, Kale, IKEA, Kastamonu Entegre, Jung Türkiye, Faber-Castell and others as programme and in-kind sponsors. Adult admission is 450 TL; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: A museum in the Atlı Köşk, a 1920s villa on the Bosphorus at Emirgan that the industrialist Hacı Ömer Sabancı bought in 1951 and his family gave to Sabancı University in 1998; it opened to the public in 2002. Its named supporters are the Sabancı group's own holding company, bank and foundation, so the family that founded it still pays for it.
nodes: Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts

f: A state museum presented on the site of Egypt's Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities; the Supreme Council of Antiquities speaks for its plans. Tickets are EGP 550 for foreign adults and EGP 30 for Egyptian adults. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The archaeological museum on Tahrir Square, in a building by Marcel Dourgnon inaugurated in 1902 by Khedive Abbas Helmy II. Its Tutankhamun treasures have gone to the Grand Egyptian Museum and its director said daily visitors fell from 7,000 to 8,000 to 1,000 to 2,000 (Al-Monitor, 22 August 2026); in January 2016 eight of its staff were sent to a disciplinary tribunal over the 2014 gluing of Tutankhamun's mask (The Irish Times, 25 January 2016).

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or any amounts. About 300 of Iran's museums are overseen by the Ministry of Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts, whose deputy minister ordered the closures and removals of June 2025 (The Art Newspaper, 18 June 2025).
w: Iran's archaeology museum in Tehran, made up of the Museum of Ancient Iran, opened in 1937, and the Museum of Islamic Archaeology and Art of Iran, opened in 1972, holding more than 300,000 finds. Its portable objects were moved into its cellars when Israeli strikes began on 13 June 2025, and in September 2026 most of Iran's leading museums were still shut with their holdings boxed in storage (The Express Tribune, 3 July 2025; The Art Newspaper, 4 September 2026).

f: A private collection, described by the foundation as an independent, UAE-based initiative of its founder Sultan Sooud Al Qassemi, a member of Sharjah's ruling family (Apollo, 7 September 2017). The pages read did not state who pays for it or any amounts.
w: A collection of modern and contemporary Arab art, 1,800 works in May 2024, founded in Sharjah in 2010 by Sultan Sooud Al Qassemi and shown since 2018 in a wing of the Sharjah Art Museum under a contract with the Sharjah Museums Authority. Its public display therefore rests on a ruler's relative lending to a Sharjah museums body, and in May 2024 the founder asked on social media for more UAE buildings to take works on loan (The Art Newspaper, 14 May 2024).
nodes: UAE-based initiative of its founder Sultan Sooud Al Qassemi

f: The Bahrain Authority for Culture and Antiquities (BACA), which has a Director of Museums, answers for the museum; the pages read did not state its budget. In October 2025 the European Union and BACA agreed a joint plan to upgrade the museum and Qal'at al-Bahrain under the EU-GCC Outreach Facility, with the EU giving technical expertise and no amounts published (The Daily Tribune, 26 October 2025).
w: Bahrain's national museum of archaeology and tradition, opened in December 1988 by the late Amir Shaikh Isa bin Salman Al-Khalifa on an artificial peninsula facing Muharraq. Its Documents and Manuscripts hall shows papers of the ruling Al Khalifa family (Bahrain Confidential, 14 May 2026).

f: In 2024 the theatre received 6.7 billion rubles from the federal budget as subsidy for its state assignment and other purposes, plus 629 million rubles in presidential grants, and earned 6.3 billion rubles itself, according to Russia's Accounts Chamber (Expert, July 2025). A 2019 Forbes ranking put charitable and sponsorship contributions at 976.6 million rubles of 8.628 billion rubles total income (Afisha Daily, 6 December 2023).
w: Russia's state opera and ballet house in Moscow, a separate line in the federal budget, headed since 1 December 2023 by Valery Gergiev, appointed by order of Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin while remaining head of the Mariinsky. In May 2022 it cancelled productions by Kirill Serebrennikov and Timofey Kulyabin, both critics of the war in Ukraine, and the general director who had signed an anti-war letter, Vladimir Urin, left in November 2023 (The Moscow Times, 2 May 2022 and 1 December 2023).
why: On 1 May 2022 the Bolshoi cancelled Serebrennikov's ballet 'Nureyev' and Kulyabin's 'Don Pasquale', both by directors who had criticised the war in Ukraine, giving no reason (The Moscow Times, 2 May 2022). The Moscow Times Russian service reported on 1 December 2023 that Urin said in summer 2022 tha
nodes: On 1 May 2022 the Bolshoi cancelled Serebrennikov's ballet 'Nureyev' and Kulyabin's 'Don Pasquale', both by directors who had criticised the war in Ukraine, giving no reason (The Moscow Times, 2 May 2022). The Moscow Times Russian service reported on 1 December 2023 that Urin said in summer 2022 that works by authors who had spoken against the war were removed from the repertoire by the theatre and the Culture Ministry.

f: A state cultural institution paid from the Bulgarian state budget; its finance department accounts for the state subsidy and other funds, and the Minister of Culture appoints the director after a public competition (gallery website). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Bulgaria's largest art museum, established in 1948, with more than 42,000 works across Kvadrat 500, the Palace, the Museum of Christian Art, the Museum of Socialist Art, Sofia Arsenal and three house museums. The culture minister appoints its director after a public competition; the director named on its site, and by BTA in December 2025, is Aneliya Nikolaeva Angelova.

f: A private museum created and run by the MARe Foundation, whose president and founder is Roger Akoury, a Lebanese-born pharmaceutical entrepreneur who paid for the building and assembled the collection; it takes no public funding (The Art Newspaper, 22 October 2018). Kaufland Romania pays for free Monday entry for under-25s to the end of 2026 and Banca Transilvania cardholders get 15% off; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: A private museum of Romanian art since the 1960s and international contemporary art, opened on 9 October 2018 in a new building by the Lebanese architect Youssef Tohme in Bucharest's Primăverii district. One collector's money stands behind it, and its first director Erwin Kessler said it does not want public funds, to keep its curatorial independence (The Art Newspaper, 22 October 2018).

f: A federal venue run by the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL), which has its seat in the building. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Mexico's national theatre and museum building, inaugurated on 29 September 1934, home to INBAL, the Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional, the Compañía Nacional de Ópera and the Ballet Folklórico de México. In December 2019 farm-worker groups entered it demanding the removal of Fabián Cháirez's painting 'La Revolución', and the culture ministry and INBAL then agreed with Zapata's family to keep the work on show beside a label stating the family's objection and to withdraw it from official publicity (Expansión Política, 12 December 2019).
why: On 10 December 2019 farm-worker organisations, among them the Unión Nacional de Trabajadores Agrícolas, protested in the Palacio against Fabián Cháirez's painting of Emiliano Zapata and attacked LGBT activists there (Expansión Política, 12 December 2019). On 11 December 2019 INBAL workers closed the

On 10 December 2019 farm-worker organisations, among them the Unión Nacional de Trabajadores Agrícolas, protested in the Palacio against Fabián Cháirez's painting of Emiliano Zapata and attacked LGBT activists there (Expansión Política, 12 December 2019). On 11 December 2019 INBAL workers closed the building over unpaid wages (La Razón, 11 December 2019).

f: A museum of the Instituto Nacional de Bellas Artes y Literatura (INBAL), with a Patronato created in 1988 to help protect, conserve and enlarge the collection; the Patronato page shows Interceramic and Fundación José Cuervo. General admission is $95.00; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: Mexico's national museum of art, opened in 1982 in the former Secretaría de Comunicaciones y Obras Públicas building of 1904 to 1911 by the Italian architect Silvio Contri, holding about 10,000 pieces. Its money comes through INBAL, whose unions said in January 2021 that a 25% cut to the culture sector hit the upkeep of museums (El Universal, 26 January 2021).

f: A federal museum of the Instituto Brasileiro de Museus (Ibram), with free entry. For the renovation begun in 2020 the Fundo de Defesa dos Direitos Difusos of the justice ministry paid for the dome, BNDES is to pay for the electrical system, and Shell, described as an oil company and the museum's master sponsor, for air conditioning, education and the long-term display; no amounts were given (Jornal do Brasil with Agência Brasil, 14 January 2025).
w: Brazil's national fine arts museum, created by Decreto-Lei 378 of 1937, with about 70,000 items in a 20,958 m² building on Avenida Rio Branco. It has been closed for renovation since 2020 and is reopening by rooms: full reopening was expected in 2026 in January 2025 and is now expected in April 2027 (Jornal do Brasil, 14 January 2025; Diário do Rio, 9 November 2026).
why: Jornal do Brasil, with material from Agência Brasil, reported on 14 January 2025 that the oil company Shell is the museum's master sponsor and will pay for air conditioning and the renewal of its education work and long-term exhibition.

Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity

f: The gallery is part of the Courtauld Institute of Art, a college of the University of London, and has no separate accounts. The institute's financial statements for 2024/25 give total income of £45,552,000: donations and endowments £18,318,000, tuition fees and education contracts £9,716,000, funding body grants £7,247,000 and other income £8,075,000, which includes £2,922,000 from gallery admissions and events and £2,269,000 from the gallery shop. The same accounts record a pledged donation of £30 million from the Reuben Foundation announced in October 2025, and pledges from the Blavatnik Family Foundation and the Rothschild Foundation for a new Strand campus.
w: The public gallery of the Courtauld Institute of Art in the north wing of Somerset House, with a collection held in trust by the Samuel Courtauld Trust, a registered charity (No. 802109). The Art Newspaper reported that the gallery reopened with its collection undamaged after a fire in the roof of Somerset House on 17 August 2024.
nodes: Rothschild Foundation for a new Strand campus

f: Tate Liverpool has no separate accounts, it is funded through the Tate group. Tate's Annual Report 2024-25 gives group income of £167,150,000, of which grant-in-aid revenue £41,442,000 and grant-in-aid capital £12,461,000 from government, fundraising £41,679,000, trading income £32,550,000 and admissions £9,132,000. For the rebuilding of its Royal Albert Dock home, Tate lists £18.6m from the DCMS Public Bodies Infrastructure Fund, £10m from MHCLG, £3m from the Garfield Weston Foundation and £1.25m from the Wolfson Foundation; The Art Newspaper (11 June 2025) reports the project is costed at £35m.
w: One of the four Tate galleries and part of the same body as Tate Modern and Tate Britain, which have their own records in the atlas; it opened in May 1988 in a warehouse on the Albert Dock converted by James Stirling. The dock building has been closed since October 2023, the reopening first due in 2025 is now set for 2027, and the forecast cost rose from £29.7m to £35m (The Art Newspaper, 11 June 2025); until then it is housed at RIBA North on Mann Island.

f: Tate St Ives has no separate accounts, it is funded through the Tate group. Tate's Annual Report 2024-25 gives group income of £167,150,000, of which grant-in-aid revenue £41,442,000 and grant-in-aid capital £12,461,000 from government, fundraising £41,679,000, trading income £32,550,000 and admissions £9,132,000. The same report records £2.8 million from The National Lottery Heritage Fund to restore the Palais de Danse, Barbara Hepworth's St Ives studio, and lists Tate St Ives supporters including the British Council, the Jane and Aatos Erkko Foundation, The Mildred Fund and the galleries Pace, White Cube and Galerie Max Hetzler.
w: One of the four Tate galleries and part of the same body as Tate Modern and Tate Britain, which have their own records in the atlas; it opened in June 1993 on the site of a former gasworks above Porthmeor Beach and also runs the Barbara Hepworth Museum and Sculpture Garden. Unlike the other Tate galleries it charges for entry (£14 without donation), and commercial galleries appear among the supporters of its exhibitions.
nodes: Tate St Ives has no separate accounts

f: Run by Glasgow Life (Culture and Sport Glasgow, charity SC037844) for Glasgow City Council, which pays it an annual service fee; entry is free. The Scottish Charity Register gives Glasgow Life's income as £152,761,000 and expenditure as £154,064,000 for the year to 31 March 2026, with no figure for Kelvingrove alone. A programme of stonework, roof and window repairs that began in September 2025 is funded by Glasgow City Council.
w: The city's museum of art, natural history and human history, opened in 1901 and under the same body as GoMA and Tramway, which have their own records in the atlas. After the council cut Glasgow Life's service fee in its 2023/24 budget, 37 of 128 posts in the museums and collections service were proposed for removal (Museums Journal, 30 May 2023), and a five-day Unison strike closed Kelvingrove in October 2023 (STV News, 23 October 2023).
nodes: Glasgow Life for Glasgow City Council

f: Its 2025 policy plan names ticket sales, friends, sponsorship from the VriendenLoterij, Heineken, Aegon, ELJA Foundation and ABN AMRO, funds such as Fonds 21, the Cultuurfonds and the VSBfonds, and rent from the building it owns. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: An exhibition museum without a collection of its own in the 17th-century Amstelhof, formerly the Hermitage Amsterdam; it cut ties with the State Hermitage Museum in St Petersburg after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and took the name H'ART Museum on 1 September 2023, with the British Museum, Centre Pompidou and Smithsonian American Art Museum as partners (AP, 26 June 2023). Its site lists the VriendenLoterij as founder.

f: A privately owned exhibition business, not a public museum: The Art Newspaper (13 December 2019) reports that its main source of income is admission fees, supplemented by an academy, a bookshop, a restaurant and a bar. A PR Newswire release names investor Yoram Roth as majority owner after a $35MM capital raise that merged Fotografiska with the members' club NeueHouse under a holding company, CultureWorks, valued at $165MM. The pages read did not state current accounts.
w: A photography exhibition venue in the Stora Tullhuset customs house, founded in 2010 by brothers Jan and Per Broman, with branches in Berlin, Tallinn, Shanghai and other cities; Yoram Roth is executive chairman. The New York branch closed its Park Avenue South building on 29 September 2024 ahead of a planned move (The Art Newspaper, 24 May 2024).

f: A Swedish government authority funded mainly by a state appropriation: its annual report for 2023 gives appropriation income of SEK 244,255 thousand, fees and other income of SEK 50,773 thousand (of which sponsorship SEK 500 thousand) and grants of SEK 11,244 thousand. The acting director general wrote in September 2023 that the museum needed a budget increase of SEK 40 million to balance the books.
w: Sweden's museum of art and design, founded in 1792 and run as a government authority under a director general; its building on Blasieholmen reopened in October 2018 after a renovation costing around SEK 1.3 billion. SVT reported on 17 March 2026, from a compilation by the union DIK, that premises take 46 percent of its budget, the highest share of any Swedish state agency; in 2023 the museum saved SEK 24 million by cutting exhibitions and closing on Tuesdays.

f: One of the three museums of the Finnish National Gallery, a foundation under public law in the administrative branch of the Ministry of Education and Culture, which appoints its council and board. Standard admission is €23 at the ticket office, and the museum seeks corporate partners and receives bequests. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Finland's national museum of older and modern art, in a building completed in 1887, part of the Finnish National Gallery with Kiasma and the Sinebrychoff Art Museum. After a five-month artists' boycott of Kiasma over patron Poju Zabludowicz, the gallery's board adopted ethical funding guidelines for all three museums that rule out donations from sanctioned entities and from organisations tied to oil and gas, tobacco, weapons manufacturing or environmentally hazardous chemicals (ArtReview).

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts.
w: The museum built to house the finds from the Acropolis and its slopes, with a Parthenon Gallery that shows the frieze, metopes and pediments; Greece wants the Parthenon sculptures held by the British Museum reunified here. To Vima (23 September 2026) and iefimerida (24 September 2026) relayed a Daily Telegraph report that talks between Greece and the British Museum, begun in 2021, have stalled over ownership, while the British Museum says discussions remain constructive.

f: Established and endowed by Antonis Benakis and given to the Greek nation; the pages read name state funding, corporate and private donations, tickets, shops, educational programmes, events and rent as its income, without amounts. Its chief executive said in 2020 that it broke even for the first time in 2016 after serious difficulties in 2012-15 and was creating a trust fund; the Qualco Foundation supports its technology infrastructure (Qualco Group, 25 May 2022).
w: A museum of Greek culture in the Benakis family mansion in central Athens, established by Antonis Benakis and inaugurated in 1931, with branches including the Pireos Street building and the Ghika Gallery. Angelos Delivorias, director for 41 years, said on stepping down in October 2014 that state funding had diminished 'year after year' (Newsbomb).

f: A Portuguese state museum, listed and ticketed on the site of the public body Museus e Monumentos de Portugal. Its current works programme drew 8.5 million euros from the Plano de Recuperação e Resiliência (PRR), and it seeks patronage, sponsorship and donations alongside its friends group, the Grupo dos Amigos do MNAA. The pages read did not state amounts for its annual budget.
w: Created in 1884 in the Palácio Alvor, it holds more than 40,000 items. Directors have said in public that staff shortages closed rooms: António Filipe Pimentel announced in January 2019 that he would leave for 'lack of conditions' (Diário de Notícias), and Joaquim Caetano told a parliamentary committee in October 2022 that 20 staff covered 84 open rooms (Notícias ao Minuto).

f: Run by the Fundació Museu Picasso de Barcelona, set up on 6 March 2013 by Barcelona City Council and the Fundació Barcelona Cultura (museum website). Its 2026 budget is 10,822,777.35 euros, of which 8,946,777.35 euros is fees, public prices and other income and 1,876,000.00 euros is income from property, with no current transfers.
w: Opened in 1963 on Carrer de Montcada around the Picasso collection of Jaume Sabartés, it holds about 5,000 works from the artist's formative years. Its front-of-house service was outsourced to MagmaCultura, whose staff struck in April 2018 over subcontracting and pay (betevé, 3 April 2018).

n: Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona
f: A local consortium of the Diputació de Barcelona and Barcelona City Council, which pay 75% and 25% of its operating costs. In 2024 public bodies contributed 13,583,893.00 euros of 16,352,029.67 euros of executed income, with 725,205.34 euros of direct income from activities (annual report 2024).
w: A public centre for exhibitions, debates and festivals in the former Casa de Caritat in the Raval, open since 1994. Its visitor services were outsourced to MagmaCultura, whose staff struck in April 2018 over subcontracting (betevé, 3 April 2018).

n: Museo de Bellas Artes de Bilbao
f: Owned by Bilbao City Council, the Diputación Foral de Bizkaia and the Basque Government, which each give 2,400,000 euros for ordinary running in 2026 and fund the expansion works and the loan behind them. Patrons and collaborating companies give more than two million euros a year; the board includes Fundación Bancaria BBK, Fundación BBVA, Iberdrola, Petronor, Metro Bilbao and Fundación Banco Santander (plan de actuación 2026; museum website).
w: Founded in 1908 and opened in 1914, it holds more than 19,000 works and is finishing the Agravitas expansion by Norman Foster and Luis María Uriarte, financed by a Kutxabank loan that the three public owners repay. Petronor, a trustee since 2017 and an exhibition sponsor, describes itself on the museum's site as an energy company built on petrochemical products.
why: Petronor has sat on the museum's board of trustees since 2017 and sponsors an exhibition in the 2026 plan; the museum's own patron page, read on 14 November 2026, describes Petronor as an energy company founded in 1968 whose industrial activity rests on technology, innovation and petrochemical produ
nodes: Petronor has sat on the museum's board of trustees since 2017 and sponsors an exhibition in the 2026 plan; the museum's own patron page, read on 14 November 2026, describes Petronor as an energy company founded in 1968 whose industrial activity rests on technology, innovation and petrochemical products.

n: Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Castilla y León (MUSAC)
f: Run entirely by the Junta de Castilla y León through the Fundación Siglo para el Turismo y las Artes de Castilla y León, a public-sector foundation attached to the regional culture department. elDiario.es reported on 3 August 2026 that the Fundación Siglo is endowed with more than 30 million euros plus other public grants, ticket sales and other income. The pages read did not state amounts for the museum itself.
w: The regional contemporary art museum, opened in León on 1 April 2005. Former director Manuel Olveira, dismissed in 2021, accused the Fundación Siglo of interference and took the culture department to court (Diario de León, 12 October 2021); in August 2026 the Vox-led department chose a former Vox regional deputy to head the foundation (elDiario.es, 3 August 2026).

f: An administrative agency of the Junta de Andalucía under the regional culture department. The Junta's 2026 budget gives it 7,716,199 euros under programme 45G, promotion of contemporary art.
w: Created in February 1990 and housed since 1997 in the former Cartuja monastery in Seville, where it absorbed the Conjunto Monumental de la Cartuja and the Museo de Arte Contemporáneo de Sevilla; since 2018 it also runs the C3A in Córdoba.

f: Its 2026 budget is 14,620,557 euros: 7,315,000 euros from visitors' fees, 4,848,557 euros from grants, donations and legacies, 1,640,000 euros from sales and 697,000 euros from sponsors and promotions. The Junta de Andalucía authorised a nominative grant of 4,378,557 euros to the foundation for 2024 (Junta de Andalucía, 25 June 2024).
w: Opened on 27 October 2003 in the Palacio de Buenavista by the will of Christine and Bernard Ruiz-Picasso, the artist's daughter-in-law and grandson, who donated 233 works, and of the Junta de Andalucía, which bought the palace in 1997. A private foundation owns the collection and the building while the regional government is its main grant-giver and sits on its board; the Fundación Almine y Bernard Ruiz-Picasso lends works to the displays.

f: In 2024 the state gave 35.874 million euros, the City of Milan 4 million euros and the Lombardy Region 3.308 million euros, 33.2% of the budget; other founders gave 18.9%, sponsors 9.3%, donations 4.2% and tickets and subscriptions 34.1 million euros, 26.2% (Il Giorno, 15 June 2025). Private contributions passed 43 million euros in 2024 (Il Sole 24 Ore, 27 November 2024); Intesa Sanpaolo is main sponsor of the season.
w: Milan's opera house, opened on 3 August 1778 and a foundation under private law since 1997, chaired by the mayor of Milan, Giuseppe Sala, with Fortunato Ortombina as chief executive since February 2025. In May 2025 it dismissed an usher who shouted 'Palestina libera' as prime minister Giorgia Meloni entered the royal box; a labour court ruled the dismissal unlawful in November 2025 (Open, 27 November 2025).

f: Run by a foundation whose founders are the Ministry of Culture, Regione Piemonte, the City of Turin, Compagnia di San Paolo and Fondazione CRT. In 2025 its value of production was 19,137,193 euros: 10,710,759 euros from sales and services and 3,506,488 euros of operating grant from the founders, with releases from renovation funds given by Compagnia di San Paolo, Regione Piemonte, Fondazione CRT and the City (accounts 2025).
w: Founded in 1824 around the Drovetti collection and open to the public since 1832, it has been run since 2004 by the Fondazione Museo delle Antichità Egizie di Torino. In September 2023 Lega vice-secretary Andrea Crippa called on director Christian Greco to resign over a 2016 two-for-one offer for Arabic speakers and a Fratelli d'Italia regional councillor said he would not confirm him (AGI, 21 September 2023).
nodes: Castello di Rivoli Museo d Arte Contemporanea
GAM - Galleria Civica d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino

f: A museum under Italy's Ministry of Culture, on whose site it is listed, with tickets at 13.00 euros plus 2.00 euros booking. It names as donors Bank of America, Mattia De Luca, Enel, Fendi, ICS Galleria Borghese, Pousaz Philanthropies, Prada, Vy Capital and Webuild. The pages read did not state amounts, except a feasibility study of about 900,000 euros paid by the engineering firm Proger (The Art Newspaper, 20 May 2026).
w: The seventeenth-century villa of Cardinal Scipione Borghese in Rome with his collection of Caravaggio, Bernini, Raphael and Titian, limited to 360 visitors per two-hour slot. A feasibility study for an added building, sponsored by Proger, whose art and culture division is headed by former culture minister Francesco Rutelli, drew objections from Italia Nostra Roma and other heritage groups in May 2026 (The Art Newspaper; Wanted in Rome).
why: Heritage groups Italia Nostra Roma, Amici di Villa Borghese and the Bianchi Bandinelli Association objected in May 2026 to a privately sponsored feasibility study, worth about 900,000 euros and paid by the engineering firm Proger, for new construction beside the villa (The Art Newspaper, 20 May 2026
nodes: Heritage groups Italia Nostra Roma, Amici di Villa Borghese and the Bianchi Bandinelli Association objected in May 2026 to a privately sponsored feasibility study, worth about 900,000 euros and paid by the engineering firm Proger, for new construction beside the villa (The Art Newspaper, 20 May 2026; Wanted in Rome, 19 May 2026).
Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea

f: Form 990 data for the year to June 2025 show revenue of $33,749,714, of which $20,191,732 was contributions, $3,865,906 program service revenue and $3,793,444 investment income, against expenses of $30,073,540 and net assets of $245,027,793 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). Lifetime donors of $5 million or more named in the FY25 annual report include the City of Philadelphia, the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, the Annenberg Foundation, Comcast NBCUniversal, The Pew Charitable Trusts, the William Penn Foundation and the Neubauer Family Foundation.
w: An educational institution chartered in 1922 by collector Albert C. Barnes, who made his fortune in pharmaceuticals, it moved from Merion to a new building on the Parkway in 2012 (museum website). In August 2023 the Montgomery County Orphans' Court let it alter Barnes's trust indenture to lend paintings, a step cultural journalist Lee Rosenbaum called a further departure from the donor's intent (CultureGrrl, 25 August 2023).

f: A family-run museum showing the collection of Don and Mera Rubell; the museum says its Miami and DC sites are 501(c)3 non-profit organisations and asks for memberships and donations. The Rubells bought buildings and land in Allapattah worth more than $12m and planned to sell their Wynwood building as part of the move (The Art Newspaper, 6 December 2017). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Don and Mera Rubell began collecting in 1965, moved to Miami in 1992 and with their children Jason and Jennifer developed hotels alongside an art foundation, which opened in Wynwood in 1993 and moved to Allapattah in December 2019 (museum website). No accounts were found under its names on ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, so the family's share of the costs is not on the public pages read.

f: Owned and operated by the Kimbell Art Foundation, to which Kay Kimbell left his collection and his fortune and Velma Kimbell gave her share of their property (Texas State Historical Association). The foundation's Form 990 for 2024 shows revenue of $53,175,895, of which $5,272,732 was contributions, expenses of $47,546,617 and net assets of $689,750,432 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: A museum of about 350 works in a 1972 building by Louis I. Kahn, with a second building by Renzo Piano opened in 2013, founded on the bequest of Fort Worth businessman Kay Kimbell, who died in 1964. In May 2025 it bought Chardin's The Cut Melon from the Rothschild family after a 2024 Christie's sale at €26.7m fell through when the buyer did not pay; the price was not disclosed (The Art Newspaper, 23 May 2025).

f: Audited accounts for the year to 30 April 2026 show support and revenue of $62,271 thousand: contributions $34,712 thousand, investment return designated for current use $16,827 thousand, membership $4,854 thousand and auxiliary activities $5,064 thousand, against expenses of $51,931 thousand; pooled investments stood at $458,850 thousand (consolidated financial report, 30 April 2026). A planned expansion costed at $160 million to $170 million is to be funded entirely by private donations (KCUR, 2 October 2024).
w: A free-admission museum of more than 40,000 works run by the Nelson Gallery Foundation, a charitable trust created in 1954 by the trustees of the William Rockhill Nelson Trust, with one board over both (consolidated financial report, 30 April 2026). It carries $98,463 thousand in bonds and notes and booked $14,000 thousand from the sale of collection items in the year to April 2025.

f: One of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh, which file together as Carnegie Institute: 2024 revenue of $115,993,787, of which $67,146,141 was contributions, $20,255,466 program service revenue and $6,498,351 investment income, with expenses of $83,369,019 and net assets of $627,791,876 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The pages read did not give figures for the art museum alone.
w: Andrew Carnegie, steel magnate, founded the Carnegie Institute in 1895 and the exhibition now called the Carnegie International was first held in 1896 (museum website). Staff across the four museums unionised with the United Steelworkers in 2020 and took 18 months to win a first contract, ratified in May 2023 (The Art Newspaper, 12 June 2023).
nodes: One of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh

f: One of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh, which file together as Carnegie Institute, with 2024 revenue of $115,993,787 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The museum's press office lists the Pennsylvania Council on the Arts, the National Endowment for the Arts, The Heinz Endowments and the Allegheny Regional Asset District as funders, and its Pop District site names the Richard King Mellon Foundation, the Henry L. Hillman Foundation, PPG Foundation and Dell Technologies; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: A single-artist museum in Warhol's birthplace holding the largest collection of his art and archives, part of Carnegie Museums. Director Patrick Moore's exit, set for 31 May 2024, was announced after a December 2023 WESA report that some staff were unhappy with his leadership and with the Pop District, a ten-year, $80m plan for the blocks around the museum; Carnegie Museums said rumours tying his exit to the controversy were untrue (The Art Newspaper, 20 March 2024).
nodes: One of the four Carnegie Museums of Pittsburgh

f: A public museum paid for mainly by property tax: support from the Zoo-Museum District was $28,086,651 in 2025, from a levy of 6.27 cents per $100 of assessed valuation in the City of St. Louis and St. Louis County, and the St. Louis Art Museum Foundation, which manages the endowment, gave $12,334,737; operating expenses were $48,644,512 (combined financial statements, 31 December 2025). Admission is free.
w: Founded in 1879 and tax-supported since 1909, it is the Art Museum Subdistrict of the Metropolitan Zoological Park and Museum District, a political subdivision of Missouri (museum website). It bought the Egyptian mummy mask of Ka-Nefer-Nefer from Phoenix Ancient Art in 1998; Egypt says the mask was stolen, and a federal judge dismissed the US government's forfeiture suit on 31 March 2012 (St. Louis Public Radio, 5 April 2012).

f: Form 990 data for the year to June 2025 show revenue of $30,590,585: program service revenue $10,513,234, contributions $7,907,710 and investment income $4,446,554, against expenses of $49,494,532, with net assets of $488,591,937 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The pages read did not name its funders.
w: A 152-acre campus holding the Indianapolis Museum of Art, founded as the Art Association of Indianapolis in 1883, on the Oldfields estate given by Ruth Lilly and Josiah K. Lilly in 1966 (museum website). President Charles Venable resigned in 2021 after a job posting spoke of keeping the museum's 'traditional, core, white art audience', and his successor Colette Pierce Burnette left in November 2023 after 15 months with no reason given, followed by three trustee resignations and a protest (Indianapolis Business Journal, 10 and 21 November 2023).

f: Form 990 data for the year to June 2025 show revenue of $37,991,971: contributions $25,033,316, program service revenue $5,010,131 and investment income $3,373,790, against expenses of $37,200,095, with net assets of $420,453,286 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). Art purchases draw on funds left by the founders, the Libbeys, whose wills allow works bought with them to be sold if the proceeds buy other art (BG Independent News, 8 April 2022).
w: A free-admission museum opened in 1901 by glass industrialist Edward Libbey and a group of charter members, on a 37-acre campus (BG Independent News, 7 April 2026). In May 2022 it sold paintings by Cézanne, Matisse and Renoir at Sotheby's for about $59.7 million with fees to pay for a more varied collection, a sale critic Christopher Knight called 'unconscionable' (Art History News, 11 May 2022; CultureGrrl, 26 May 2022).

f: Run by the Cincinnati Museum Association, whose Form 990 for the year to August 2025 shows revenue of $29,466,364: contributions $15,590,811, investment income $8,781,057 and program service revenue $512,745, against expenses of $24,100,368, with net assets of $317,447,912 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The museum names ArtsWave, the Ohio Arts Council, the City of Cincinnati and its members as operating supporters, and free general admission is paid for by the Rosenthal Family Foundation.
w: The Cincinnati Museum Association was incorporated on 15 February 1881 and the museum opened in Eden Park on 17 May 1886; it holds more than 73,000 works (museum website). General admission has been free since May 2003 through a gift of the Lois and Richard Rosenthal Foundation, and the city's mayor, Aftab Pureval, is listed on its board (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).

n: Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco
f: The City of San Francisco provides about 20% of its funding, $24.2 million proposed for fiscal 2025-26 (KQED, 22 July 2025). The Corporation of the Fine Arts Museums, its private arm, reported revenue of $53,329,543 in the year to June 2025, of which $41,683,139 was contributions and $8,818,495 program service revenue, against expenses of $57,481,779 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: The city's two fine arts museums, the de Young in Golden Gate Park, established in 1895, and the Legion of Honor in Lincoln Park, opened in 1924, run with a private corporation beside the city department. It cut 12 posts in July 2025 citing lower attendance, after proposing in March to drop 23 of 99 city-funded positions (KQED, 22 July 2025; The Art Newspaper, 10 March 2025); long-time board chair Diane 'Dede' Wilsey, lead donor to the $206m de Young building, stepped down in 2019 after criticism of her control (The Art Newspaper, 4 June 2019).
nodes: Corporation of the Fine Arts Museums

f: Form 990 data for the year to June 2025 show revenue of $14,713,652: contributions $6,509,494, investment income $1,327,353 and program service revenue $1,185,558, against expenses of $8,796,439, with net assets of $149,647,247 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). Two related Pasadena bodies, the Norton Simon Art Foundation and the Norton Simon Foundation, file separately; the pages read did not state who gives the contributions.
w: In 1975 industrialist Norton Simon, who ran the Hunt-Wesson Foods conglomerate, took over the financially troubled Pasadena Art Museum, which took his name and housed his collection in return for financial support (LAist, 21 December 2025; Apollo, 7 February 2025). It kept Cranach's Adam and Eve, appraised at about $24 million, after the US Supreme Court in May 2019 declined to hear Marei von Saher's claim that they were taken from her father-in-law, the dealer Jacques Goudstikker, in a forced sale to Hermann Göring (The Art Newspaper, 21 May 2019).

f: Part of Yale University; its support page says gifts from members and donors keep admission, membership and public programmes free and that donors invest in its endowment. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Yale's art museum, founded in 1832 and directed by Stephanie Wiles, with a collection of nearly 300,000 objects. On 30 March 2022 it handed 13 antiquities valued at more than $1.2 million to the New York District Attorney's Office, nine of them linked by prosecutors to the dealer Subhash Kapoor (Connecticut Public Radio, 4 April 2022).

f: Part of Harvard University. Free admission is paid for by a contribution from the Estate of David Rockefeller and support from the Office of the President at Harvard, according to its visit page; the Arthur M. Sackler Museum was built with funding from Dr. Arthur M. Sackler. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Three Harvard museums (Fogg, opened 1895; Busch-Reisinger, founded 1903; Arthur M. Sackler, opened 1985) in one building since 2014, led by Sarah Ganz Blythe. In July 2024 the Harvard Corporation kept the Sackler name after a student proposal of October 2022 to remove it (The Harvard Crimson, August 2024).
why: Students submitted a 23-page proposal in October 2022 to remove Arthur M. Sackler's name from the museum, citing his family's company, which became Purdue Pharma, maker of OxyContin; the Harvard Corporation accepted a committee recommendation to keep the name in July 2024 (The Harvard Crimson, Augus
