Students submitted a 23-page proposal in October 2022 to remove Arthur M. Sackler's name from the museum, citing his family's company, which became Purdue Pharma, maker of OxyContin; the Harvard Corporation accepted a committee recommendation to keep the name in July 2024 (The Harvard Crimson, August 2024).
Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery (National Museum of Asian Art)

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $38,992,891, of which contributions were $25,916,030 (66.5%), programme services $6,954,351 (17.8%) and investment income $1,635,747 (4.2%), with net assets of $369,508,438 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: The house museum Isabella Stewart Gardner built and opened in 1903 as Fenway Court; her will forbids permanent changes to the displays. Thirteen works stolen on 18 March 1990 are still missing and the museum says the investigation with the FBI and the US Attorney's Office continues.

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $26,403,862 against expenses of $47,293,444, with contributions of $8,972,691 (34.0%), programme services $2,739,837 (10.4%), investment income $2,409,809 (9.1%) and net assets of $777,342,160 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: A museum of art and culture in Salem whose roots go back to the East India Marine Society of 1799. It laid off 38 of 260 staff in June 2020 and its director Brian Kennedy resigned that December after 17 months (The Art Newspaper, 16 December 2020); Kurt Steinberg has been acting director since 1 July 2026, after Lynda Roscoe Hartigan left for the Smithsonian American Art Museum (WBUR, 22 April 2026).

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $59,357,260, of which contributions were $56,664,621 (95.5%), with net assets of $683,977,199 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). In October 2024 the Aso O. Tavitian Foundation gave 331 works and more than $45m for a curator, care of the collection and a new wing (The Art Newspaper, 28 October 2024).
w: An art museum and research centre in Williamstown, Massachusetts, directed by Olivier Meslay. The Tavitian gift, from the foundation of a former trustee who made his fortune in software, pays for a wing by Selldorf Architects due in 2027 or 2028 (The Art Newspaper, 28 October 2024).

f: A state-supported, privately endowed institution of the Commonwealth of Virginia, in its own words. The General Assembly approved $112 million in 2020 toward its expansion and James W. and Frances Gibson McGlothlin gave $57 million in March 2022 (Richmond BizSense, 26 April 2022); the VMFA Foundation reported revenue of $71,216,972 and net assets of $292,913,230 for the year to June 2025 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: Virginia's state art museum, with more than 50,000 works, free general admission and opening 365 days a year, led by Alex Nyerges. Its campaign has a goal of $471 million, which the museum calls the largest in its 90-year history, and a second McGlothlin wing of about 173,000 square feet is planned.

f: An agency of the North Carolina Department of Natural and Cultural Resources that receives appropriations from the Governor and the General Assembly, supported by the separate NCMA Foundation, which reported revenue of $32,272,133 and net assets of $96,696,903 for the year to June 2025 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The Andrew W. Mellon Foundation gave $750,000 in December 2019 for the reinstallation of the collection (WUNC, 15 September 2026).
w: The state's art museum, begun with a 1947 legislative appropriation of $1 million to buy art and opened in 1956, with a 164-acre park. Director Valerie Hillings left on 19 August 2026 to become the first director of the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi and deputy director Katherine White is interim director (NC Department of Natural and Cultural Resources, 4 August 2026).

f: A private nonprofit in two buildings owned by the City of Charlotte and leased for $1 a year each. Its audited statement for the year to June 30, 2025 shows operating support and revenue of $20,037,339, including gifts of $9,409,949, an endowment allocation of $3,091,384, rental income of $2,136,545, use of City facilities valued at $1,641,852 and grants of $1,413,884.
w: An art and design museum established in 1936 in the former first United States branch mint, with a second building uptown since 2010, led by president and chief executive Todd A. Herman. The museum's own about page acknowledges the unpaid labour of enslaved people of African ancestry who helped build the Randolph Road building.

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to September 2025 shows revenue of $36,326,460, of which contributions were $25,092,482 (69.1%), programme services $3,367,009 (9.3%) and investment income $2,537,637 (7.0%), with net assets of $279,450,476 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The founder left an endowment for buying art, and the 2019 extension is named the Kenneth C. Griffin Building.
w: Founded in 1941 by Ralph Hubbard Norton, who headed the Acme Steel Company in Chicago, and Elizabeth Calhoun Norton; the collection holds more than 8,900 works. A Foster + Partners expansion opened on 9 February 2019; the director and chief executive is Ghislain d'Humières (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer, Form 990 for the year to September 2025).
nodes: Named in the record: The building that opened on 9 February 2019, with new galleries and an auditorium, carries his name.

nodes.b: Ken Griffin gave $75M to $100M+ to Republican groups in the 2022 cycle, according to InfluenceWatch.

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $14,719,095 against expenses of $17,086,410, with contributions of $10,336,866 (70.2%), programme services $1,598,189 (10.9%), investment income $759,434 (5.2%) and net assets of $125,703,417 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer).
w: Founded by Anna Rice Cooke, chartered in 1922 and opened on 8 April 1927 as the Honolulu Academy of Arts; it took in The Contemporary Museum in 2011 and sold that museum's Spalding House in 2023. In April 2020 it laid off a third of its full-time staff and all part-time and seasonal workers (Honolulu Star-Advertiser, 17 April 2020), and in 2021 it eliminated the deputy director's post (Hawaiʻi Public Radio, 6 May 2021).

n: Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA)
f: The art museum and film archive of the University of California, Berkeley. Its supporters page lists, at $100,000 and above, the Eucalyptus Foundation, Walter & Elise Haas Fund, William and Flora Hewlett Foundation, Renate, Hans & Maria Hofmann Trust, Institute of Museum and Library Services, National Endowment for the Humanities, Rotasa Foundation, Terra Foundation for American Art, Andy Warhol Foundation, Mellon Foundation and Henry Luce Foundation. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Its collection began with gifts to the university in the 1870s and the 1881 Bacon Art and Library Building; a 1963 gift from Hans Hofmann of forty-seven paintings and $250,000 led to the University Art Museum that opened on Bancroft Way in 1970. It holds nearly 25,000 works of art and 18,000 films and videos.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $31,022,519, of which contributions were $26,063,233 (84.0%), programme services $2,611,982 (8.4%) and investment income $1,709,325 (5.5%), with net assets of $140,475,104 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). Funders it lists for that year include the Barr Foundation, Mellon Foundation, Mass Cultural Council, The Boston Foundation and Yawkey Foundation.
w: Founded in 1936 as the Boston Museum of Modern Art, a sister institution to New York's MoMA, and renamed in 1948; it moved into a Diller Scofidio + Renfro building on Boston Harbor in 2006 and began a permanent collection that year. Jill Medvedow was director until 31 March 2025 and Nora Burnett Abrams was announced as the next director on 20 November 2024.

n: The Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens
f: A private nonprofit trust. Its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows total revenue of $160,592,538, of which contributions were $94,767,418, program service revenue $17,317,414 and investment income $21,454,656, with net assets of $1,180,013,751 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The pages read did not name individual donors.
w: A research library, art museum and botanical garden on the former San Marino estate of Henry Edwards Huntington, who set it up as a trust in 1919; it opened to the public in 1928 (Encyclopedia.com). The founding fortune came from railroads, land speculation and water and power investments in California (Encyclopedia.com).

f: The Academy Museum Foundation's Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $71,382,463, of which contributions were $61,811,490 and program service revenue $8,333,233, against expenses of $85,368,645 and total liabilities of $434,381,694 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). Haim and Cheryl Saban gave $50 million, the museum's largest gift, and the main building is named after them (TheWrap, 3 June 2024).
w: The film museum of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, a $480 million building that opened in 2021 (TheWrap, 3 June 2024). Critics said the opening displays left out Hollywood's Jewish founders; the exhibition made in answer, Hollywoodland, opened in May 2024 and drew an open letter from more than 300 film workers calling its texts antisemitic, after which the museum changed them (The Art Newspaper, 11 June 2024).
why: An open letter from United Jewish Writers, signed by more than 300 Hollywood workers, accused the museum's Hollywoodland exhibition of a double standard that was antisemitic 'whether intentional or not'; the museum said it would change the exhibition (The Art Newspaper, 11 June 2024).
nodes: An open letter from United Jewish Writers, signed by more than 300 Hollywood workers, accused the museum's Hollywoodland exhibition of a double standard that was antisemitic 'whether intentional or not'; the museum said it would change the exhibition (The Art Newspaper, 11 June 2024).

f: A California state museum. The enacted 2025-26 state budget gives it $4,306,000, of which $3,758,000 is from the General Fund, $373,000 from the Exposition Park Improvement Fund and $175,000 from reimbursements; in 2024-25 the figure was $13,676,000, of which $13,153,000 was General Fund (California state budget 2025-26).
w: A state museum of African American history, art and culture in Exposition Park, chartered by the State of California in 1977 and governed by a seven-member board appointed by the Governor (California state budget 2025-26). It began operations in 1981 in temporary quarters and its own building opened during the 1984 Olympic Games (California Assembly budget subcommittee, 7 April 2015).

n: National Museum of African American History and Culture
f: A Smithsonian museum. The federal government paid half of the $540 million building cost and private donors the rest (Chronicle of Philanthropy, 24 May 2016); the largest gifts were $21 million from the Oprah Winfrey Charitable Foundation and $20 million each from the Lilly Endowment and the investor Robert Smith (Chronicle of Philanthropy, 8 August 2016). The Smithsonian as a whole gets about 53% of its funding from the federal government, $1.09 billion in fiscal year 2024 (The Art Newspaper, 13 August 2025).
w: The Smithsonian's museum of African American history on the National Mall, opened on 24 September 2016. President Trump's executive order of 27 March 2025 named it as promoting ideology, and a White House letter of 12 August 2025 put it among eight museums whose texts are to be reviewed and rewritten where it finds 'divisive or ideologically driven language' (whitehouse.gov; The Art Newspaper, 13 August 2025).

n: National Museum of the American Indian
f: A Smithsonian museum. Of $219 million raised for the building and its opening, Congress gave $119 million and private donors $100 million; the three largest gifts were $10 million each from the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, the Mohegan Tribe and the Oneida Indian Nation of New York (ICT, 22 September 2004). The Smithsonian as a whole gets about 53% of its funding from the federal government (The Art Newspaper, 13 August 2025).
w: The Smithsonian's museum of Native peoples on the National Mall, set up by an Act of Congress of 28 November 1989, with a second site, the George Gustav Heye Center, in the Old U.S. Custom House in New York (20 U.S.C. 80q-5). It is one of eight museums named in the White House review of Smithsonian content of 12 August 2025 (whitehouse.gov).
nodes: Oneida Indian Nation of New York

f: The Carnegie Hall Corporation's Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $101,837,752, of which contributions were $45,525,878 and program service revenue $42,892,955, against expenses of $124,873,288, with net assets of $482,510,845 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). It is one of the 39 members of New York City's Cultural Institutions Group, which sit on City-owned property and receive capital and operating support from the City (NYC Department of Cultural Affairs); the pages read did not state the City's amount.
w: A concert hall opened on 5 May 1891 with $2 million from Andrew Carnegie (Encyclopedia.com) and run by the nonprofit Carnegie Hall Corporation. In September 2015 chairman Ronald O. Perelman left the chair after accusing executive and artistic director Clive Gillinson of a 'troubling lack of transparency'; five vice chairs called his accusations 'totally untrue' (Chronicle of Philanthropy, 21 September 2015; YourClassical, 28 September 2015).

f: The Metropolitan Opera Association's Form 990 for the year to July 2025 shows revenue of $304,122,827, of which contributions were $179,783,313 and program service revenue $101,534,612, against expenses of $325,333,793 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). A September 2025 memorandum with the Saudi Music Commission, reported as worth up to $200 million over eight years, was withdrawn in April 2026 (OperaWire, 23 April 2026).
w: An opera company at Lincoln Center led by general manager Peter Gelb. It has spent about half the principal of its endowment, cut 22 administrative staff in January 2026, lost its Saudi funding deal in April 2026 and plans to sell the naming rights to the house and its two Chagall murals (ABC7 New York, 21 January 2026; OperaWire, 23 April 2026).
why: On 3 September 2025 the Met signed a memorandum of understanding with the Saudi Music Commission to become winter resident company at the Royal Diriyah Opera House near Riyadh (BroadwayWorld, 3 September 2025); the Saudi side withdrew and the Met announced the end of the deal on 23 April 2026 (CBS N
nodes: On 3 September 2025 the Met signed a memorandum of understanding with the Saudi Music Commission to become winter resident company at the Royal Diriyah Opera House near Riyadh (BroadwayWorld, 3 September 2025); the Saudi side withdrew and the Met announced the end of the deal on 23 April 2026 (CBS New York, 23 April 2026).

f: The Seventh Regiment Armory Conservancy's Form 990 for 2024 shows revenue of $28,748,363, of which contributions were $10,262,650 and program service revenue $12,588,881, with net assets of $264,032,707 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The Thompson Family Foundation gave $65 million in July 2015 for a programming endowment, bringing the family's total to nearly $129 million (Antiques and The Arts Weekly, 10 July 2015); New York City gave $1,925,000 toward a $4 million drill hall floor in 2018 (NYC Department of Cultural Affairs).
w: A nonprofit arts venue in the armory built from 1877 to 1881 by the Seventh Regiment of the National Guard, with Rebecca Robertson as founding president; its first production was in September 2007 (Antiques and The Arts Weekly; NYC Department of Cultural Affairs). One family is by far its largest donor: Wade Thompson, described as an 'Airstream trailer mogul', and his foundation, whose name the arts spaces carry for 50 years at the family's request (Chronicle of Philanthropy, 10 July 2015).

f: Built for an estimated $475 million from a $500 million capital campaign: Michael R. Bloomberg gave $75 million and the Bloomberg administration appropriated $75 million of public money before he left office in 2013, with other funding from a small group of billionaires including Stephen M. Ross of Related Companies and Barry Diller (6sqft, 24 May 2017). Founding board member Darla Moore gave $25 million, unrestricted, in April 2026 (GroundBreak Carolinas, 30 April 2026).
w: An independent nonprofit arts centre in Hudson Yards that opened in April 2019, with Dan Doctoroff as founding board chair and Jonathan Tisch as chair now (Attractions Management, 5 April 2019; GroundBreak Carolinas, 30 April 2026). In July 2020 it laid off 26% of full-time staff and cut its budget from $46 million to $26 million; in January 2023 founding director Alex Poots gave up the chief executive role (International Arts Manager, 21 July 2020; BroadwayWorld, 12 January 2023).

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for 2024 shows revenue of $114,814,441, of which contributions were $44,767,255, program service revenue $30,406,582 and investment income $11,879,122, with net assets of $759,038,429 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer). The pages read did not break the contributions down by public body or donor.
w: A natural history museum opened on 2 June 1894 with $1 million from the Chicago merchant Marshall Field (museum website). It holds more than 2,000 skeletal and ceremonial objects awaiting repatriation requests and covered Native American display cases in January 2024 under new federal rules (The Art Newspaper, 29 January 2024); its nearly 300 unionised staff won a first contract in May 2025 after a public wage dispute (WBEZ, 13 March 2025; AFSCME Council 31, 28 May 2025).
why: About 100 union members and supporters picketed the museum on 12 March 2025 over low wages and slow contract talks, with a Cook County commissioner and a state senator among the speakers (WBEZ, 13 March 2025).
nodes: About 100 union members and supporters picketed the museum on 12 March 2025 over low wages and slow contract talks, with a Cook County commissioner and a state senator among the speakers (WBEZ, 13 March 2025).

f: A private nonprofit: its Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $43,143,885, of which contributions were $34,444,595 (79.8%), with net assets of $217,637,217 (ProPublica). Its $175m Tang Wing, opened 18 June 2026, took $75m of public money and $100m of private philanthropy, including $57m from the City of New York, $9.25 million from Empire State Development, $5 million from the New York State Council on the Arts and $20m from Oscar Tang and Agnes Hsu-Tang (The Art Newspaper; New York State governor's release).
w: New York City's first museum and a research library, founded in 1804, renamed from the New-York Historical Society in October 2024. The wing is named for the board chair, Agnes Hsu-Tang, and her husband, the financier Oscar Tang, after their $20m gift (The Art Newspaper, 29 October 2024).
nodes: New York State Council on the Arts

n: Museum of the City of New York
f: A private nonprofit in buildings whose title the City of New York holds. In the year to 30 June 2025 operating revenue was $14,626,259, including $2,438,088 from the New York City Department of Cultural Affairs, $40,000 from the New York State Council on the Arts, $2,326,956 in other grants and contributions, $2,329,010 gross from special events and $1,048,754 in admissions, against operating expenses of $16,785,466 (audited financial statements 2025). Endowments stood at $28,071,766.
w: A city history museum founded in 1923 by Henry Collins Brown, a member of the city's Cultural Institutions Group. It ran an operating deficit of $2,159,207 in the year to June 2025 and booked $577,313 of deaccession income, after $1,299,823 the year before (audited financial statements 2025).

f: The museum depends on the Banco de la República, which runs it as one of the four lines of its cultural work (the Library Network, the Gold Museums, the art museums and music) under Ley 31 de 1992 (Banco de la República). A ticket costs about 2 dollars and Sundays are free (Voz de América). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: A museum of pre-Hispanic goldwork that grew from the Banco de la República's purchase of the poporo quimbaya in 1939, made at the Education Ministry's request to keep such objects out of private hands and the melting pot. Published accounts of that piece's find differ, and one places it in a tomb opened when theft of archaeological pieces was common (My Modern Met; Voz de América).

f: A municipal museum of the Prefeitura do Rio, managed since January 2021 by the Organização dos Estados Ibero-americanos (OEI). The city's funding was in the order of R$1 million a month for salaries and maintenance in 2020, with exhibitions and education paid for through fundraising under culture incentive laws (CIMAM, 11 January 2020). The museum names the Instituto Cultural Vale as its maintainer, Equinor and LATAM as master sponsors and Itaú Unibanco as gold sponsor (museum website).
w: Opened on 1 March 2013 as part of the Porto Maravilha redevelopment, conceived with the Fundação Roberto Marinho and run until 2020 by the Instituto Odeon. In November 2019 Odeon put all 126 staff on notice of dismissal after the city stopped its transfers, and two directors left (The Art Newspaper, 13 November 2019).

f: A museum of the Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro, under the Ministério da Educação, which pledged R$ 13,5 milhões a year for maintenance in July 2023 (Agência Brasil). Its rebuilding after the fire of 2 September 2018 is budgeted at 545,2 milhões de reais, with 369 milhões raised (Projeto Museu Nacional Vive). At 31 December 2024 the money raised came from parliamentary amendments (R$ 56,4 milhões), BNDES (R$ 50 milhões, since raised to R$ 100 milhões), Vale (R$ 50,5 milhões), Bradesco (R$ 50 milhões), MEC (R$ 44,3 milhões), MCTI (R$ 20 milhões), Itaú (R$ 10 milhões), Eletrobras (R$ 5 milhões) and Cosan (R$ 3,1 milhões) (Relatório de Atividades 2024).
w: Brazil's first museum and scientific institution, created in 1818 by d. João VI. The Federal Police found the 2018 fire accidental and held nobody responsible, though firefighters had flagged the fire risk in 2015; the director says the cause was the constant lack of money for upkeep. Full reopening has moved from 2026 to 2029 (O Povo, 6 July 2020; Agência Brasil, 21 July 2023; Projeto Museu Nacional Vive).

f: A state museum, the head of the Unidad Administrativa Especial Museo Nacional of the Ministerio de las Culturas, las Artes y los Saberes, which groups fourteen museums. The unit's budget, all investment money from the national budget, was $ 12.222 millones in 2023, $ 21.060 millones in 2024, $ 14.520 millones in 2025 and $ 15.750 millones in 2026 (Ministry handover report, 29 July 2026). The report also names an alliance with the Fundación SURA and a 2025 donation of an exhibition by the German cooperation agency GIZ.
w: Founded in 1823 and run directly by the culture ministry. On 15 October 2026 the government of President Abelardo de la Espriella had 63 objects on feminist and LGBTQ+ movements, political violence and the 2016 peace agreement taken off display; a Bogotá judge ordered them back and they were reinstalled on 30 October (The Art Newspaper, 20 October and 2 November 2026).
why: The Art Newspaper reported on 20 October 2026 that the government removed more than 30 works from the permanent displays citing 'political indoctrination', that hundreds protested outside on 17 and 18 October and were dispersed by riot police, and on 2 November 2026 that a judge of Bogotá's 24th Fam
nodes: The Art Newspaper reported on 20 October 2026 that the government removed more than 30 works from the permanent displays citing 'political indoctrination', that hundreds protested outside on 17 and 18 October and were dispersed by riot police, and on 2 November 2026 that a judge of Bogotá's 24th Family Court ordered the 63 objects reinstalled.

f: A public museum of the Shanghai municipal government. Its 2025 final accounts, published on the Shanghai government site, show income of 722.13 million yuan: 366.53 million yuan (50.76%) in fiscal appropriations and 355.60 million yuan (49.24%) in its own operating income.
w: Museum of ancient Chinese art founded in 1952, with a building on People's Square and a second, larger one, Shanghai Museum East, in Pudong; a third site, Shanghai Museum North, is planned before 2030. Its charter calls it a national key museum built jointly by the central and local governments, and its organisation chart lists a Party committee beside the director's office.

f: One of the museums of the Independent Administrative Institution National Institutes for Cultural Heritage, whose fiscal 2025 budget of 13.48 billion yen was made up of 9.58 billion yen in government funding for operating expenses, 2.20 billion yen in self-generated income, 0.81 billion yen from commissioned projects and 0.89 billion yen from donations and other sources. The pages read did not give a separate budget for the Kyoto museum.
w: National museum of Japanese and Asian art that opened in 1897 as the Imperial Museum of Kyoto and became a national institution in 1952. The education ministry's sixth medium-term goal, announced on 27 February 2026, sets self-generated revenue targets for the national museums; an Akahata editorial of 30 March 2026 says institutions below 40% by fiscal 2029 face restructuring.

n: The National Museum of Western Art
f: A state museum run by the Independent Administrative Institution National Museum of Art. Kawasaki Heavy Industries signed the museum's first official partnership agreement on 17 March 2023 (Tokyo Art Beat, 13 March 2024). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Japan's national museum of Western art, opened in 1959 in a Le Corbusier building to house the Matsukata Collection, which France had sequestrated as enemy property and returned in 1959. On 12 March 2024 exhibiting artists protested in its lobby against its partner Kawasaki Heavy Industries over the import of Israeli weapons, and from 2026 it falls under state revenue targets.
why: Tokyo Art Beat reported on 13 March 2024 that artists in the museum's exhibition 'Does the Future Sleep Here?' protested at the press preview on 12 March 2024, demanding that Kawasaki Heavy Industries, the museum's official partner, halt the import and distribution of Israeli weapons.

f: A New South Wales state museum under the Museum of Applied Arts and Sciences Act 1945.
w: Australia's largest museum group, of applied arts and sciences, with sites at Parramatta, Ultimo (closed since 4 February 2024), Castle Hill and Sydney Observatory. Its chief executive Lisa Havilah stepped aside ten weeks before the Parramatta opening amid NSW government investigations into governance and procurement (The Conversation, 27 August 2026), after a decade of dispute over moving the museum from Ultimo.
why: The Conversation reported on 27 August 2026 that the 2021 dismantling of Willow Grove, a 19th-century villa on the Parramatta site, drew a union green ban, with construction workers refusing to work on the site in support of a heritage campaign.
