f: Principally funded by the NSW Government: of total revenue of $81.4 million in 2024-25, recurrent grants from the NSW Government were $46.9 million and capital grants $15.3 million. Self-generated revenue was $15.6 million, including $1.455 million in sponsorships, and the Australian Museum Foundation gave $1,116,404 (annual report 2024-25).
w: Natural history and cultural museum founded in 1827, a NSW Government organisation under the Department of Creative Industries, Tourism, Hospitality and Sport, governed by a board of trustees. It holds restricted collections that include human remains and is returning Ancestors and objects to First Nations communities under a policy its trustees approved in May 2025.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Funded mainly by Australian Government appropriation: the 2024-25 federal budget raised government funding by $2 million, offset by lower revenue from other sources, leaving expenses at about $67.4 million (Region Canberra, 15 May 2024). In April 2023 the government announced an extra $535 million over four years for the nine national collecting institutions (The Canberra Times, 6 April 2023).
w: One of Australia's nine national collecting institutions, in Canberra. It told the incoming government in 2022 that efficiency dividends had hit national institutions disproportionately, and it shed jobs in 2020 after a fall in revenue and an expected cut in appropriation (The Canberra Times).

f: Auckland Council is its primary public funder, paying roughly $35 million of ratepayers' money a year under a three-year funding agreement; the museum's draft annual plan projects a need for $46.01 million of public funding in 2027-28 and $47.80 million in 2028-29 (RNZ, 11 February 2026). Asbestos removal had cost $8 million by September 2026 with $4 million more expected (1News, 3 September 2026).
w: Auckland's war memorial museum, in a building it has occupied since 1929, free to Aucklanders. Asbestos dust found in May 2025 closed it, the Māori Court and Pacific galleries are still shut, 31 roles were disestablished, and its request for central government money has the mayor's backing but, RNZ reported on 11 February 2026, the government has no plans to help.

f: A museum under India's Ministry of Culture (Press Trust of India, 3 April 2018). The 1 February 2025 Union Budget allocated 450 million rupees ($5.1m) for museum development under general schemes and named no budget for the museum planned to replace it (The Art Newspaper, 6 February 2025). The pages read did not state the museum's own grant.
w: India's national museum on Janpath, opened in 1949, holding more than 200,000 objects. The government plans to replace it with the Yuga Yugeen Bharat National Museum in the North and South Blocks under the Central Vista project and has not said what happens to the present building; in 2018 the Comptroller and Auditor General found Rs 2.26 crore of its receipts kept outside government accounts.

f: A museum under India's Union Ministry of Culture (Deccan Chronicle, 28 April 2016), governed by the Salar Jung Museum Act, 1961 and overseen by the Salar Jung Board. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Art museum on the Musi river in Hyderabad, opened by Jawaharlal Nehru on 16 December 1951 to show the collection of the Salar Jung family, chiefly that of Salar Jung III. It was among the national-level museums audited in the Comptroller and Auditor General's Report No. 10 of 2022; a fire burnt its auditorium on 3 November 2006.

f: An initiative of the Dubai Future Foundation, a body formed in 2016 by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Ruler of Dubai, and chaired by Dubai's Crown Prince. In 2015 a Dubai law set an 'innovation fee' of AED10 per transaction at several government agencies to fund the planned AED500m (US$136.2m) museum (Attractions Management, 17 August 2015).
w: Exhibition building on Sheikh Zayed Road with immersive displays about possible futures and no historical collection, chaired by the minister Mohammad Al Gergawi. It closed on 1 September 2026 while new experiences are prepared for its fifth anniversary in 2027 (Khaleej Times, 25 August 2026).
why: The museum's own site says it is an initiative of the Dubai Future Foundation, formed in 2016 by the Ruler of Dubai, and Attractions Management reported on 17 August 2015 that a Dubai law imposed an 'innovation fee' on government agencies' transactions to fund it.
nodes: The museum's own site says it is an initiative of the Dubai Future Foundation, formed in 2016 by the Ruler of Dubai, and Attractions Management reported on 17 August 2015 that a Dubai law imposed an 'innovation fee' on government agencies' transactions to fund it.

f: A state museum run by Turkey's Presidency of National Palaces, to which it was transferred from the Ministry of Culture and Tourism by a presidential resolution published on 6 September 2019. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The Ottoman sultans' palace, built from 1460 to 1478 and a museum since 3 April 1924. Since the 2019 transfer to the presidency's National Palaces administration, the Istanbul branch of the Chamber of Architects has said restoration is moving fast with few controllers on site and that conservation boards and the municipality cannot intervene (BirGün, 6 October 2020).

f: A state institution that raises most of its own money: in 2021 the government gave 36% of its budget, commercial activity 5% and private donations and legacies 59% (The Jewish Chronicle, 21 April 2022). Its ongoing budget for 2017 to 2019 was 200 million shekels according to the State Comptroller, it ran a deficit of 25.6 million shekels in 2020, and the government added $9.2 million to its 2022 allocation (Algemeiner, 23 January 2022).
w: Israel's Holocaust remembrance authority, set up by a Knesset law in 1953, whose chairman is appointed by the education minister. It ended a partnership with Roman Abramovich on 10 March 2022, the day Britain froze his assets, after its leaders had asked the US ambassador not to sanction him; in 2023 the education minister's reported bid to remove chairman Dani Dayan was dropped after an international outcry.
why: Jüdische Allgemeine reported on 11 March 2022 that Yad Vashem ended its strategic partnership with Roman Abramovich, announced on 22 February 2022, on the day the British government froze his assets. The Jewish Chronicle wrote on 21 April 2022 that the 'casino moguls' Sheldon and Miriam Adelson beca
nodes: Jüdische Allgemeine reported on 11 March 2022 that Yad Vashem ended its strategic partnership with Roman Abramovich, announced on 22 February 2022, on the day the British government froze his assets. The Jewish Chronicle wrote on 21 April 2022 that the 'casino moguls' Sheldon and Miriam Adelson became its greatest benefactors with a $25 million donation in 2011.

f: A state museum under the Directorate General of Antiquities of Lebanon's Ministry of Culture, repaired with foreign and private money: ALIPH gave $175,000 after the 2020 port explosion, with the Louvre's help (The Art Newspaper, 3 August 2021); the Italian government gave €1.2 million to restore the basement (The National, 23 October 2016); and the National Heritage Foundation with the Es-Said family paid for the pavilion opened in 2024 (The National, 26 December 2024).
w: Lebanon's archaeological museum, built from 1930 to 1937 and opened in 1942, which stood on the Green Line in the civil war and was closed for two decades. The 4 August 2020 blast destroyed its windows and doors and damaged its security system; the Louvre said in 2021 that repairs worth nearly $800,000 were still needed and the air conditioning ran at 30% of capacity.
nodes: Museum of the Second World War

f: A house of the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen, paid for by the Free State of Bavaria: the 2026/2027 state budget sets 139,102.5 thousand euros for 2026 for all 20 state museums in chapter 15 70, with no separate figure for this house. The Pinakotheks-Verein, founded in 1953, supports the Alte and Neue Pinakothek.
w: State gallery of European painting from the 14th to the 18th century, open since 1836 in Leo von Klenze's building. After a Süddeutsche Zeitung report in February 2025 on suspected Nazi-looted works in the state painting collections, the arts minister removed director general Bernhard Maaz on 2 April 2025; restitutions decided since 2023 are still being prepared.

f: The Free State of Bavaria paid for the building and runs the museum as part of the Bayerische Staatsgemäldesammlungen; the Udo und Anette Brandhorst Stiftung pays for additions to the collection. The pages read did not state amounts for the foundation.
w: Museum of contemporary art in Munich's Kunstareal showing the collection of Udo and Anette Brandhorst, put into a foundation in 1993 and opened to the public in 2009. It belongs to the state painting collections whose director general was removed in April 2025 after a report on suspected Nazi-looted works.

f: A state museum run as a Landesbetrieb of Baden-Württemberg: the state grant is 9,498.6 thousand euros for 2024, 10,492.3 thousand euros for 2025 and 10,743.9 thousand euros for 2026 (science ministry report on the 2025/2026 budget). Purchases of about 135,000 euros came from the state's central acquisition fund in 2023 and 2024.
w: The largest art museum in Baden-Württemberg, founded on the order of King Wilhelm I, with a listed postmodern building known as the Stirling building. In August 2019 it returned two drawings to the heirs of the Jewish lawyer Michael Berolzheimer, whose collection was auctioned in Munich in 1938 and 1939.

f: The city art museum of Düsseldorf, run by the Stiftung Museum Kunstpalast, founded in 1998 together with E.ON AG; E.ON ended its permanent funding at the end of 2017 and left the boards. Named supporters include the State of North Rhine-Westphalia's culture ministry, Henkel, ERGO Group, Stadtsparkasse Düsseldorf and Stadtwerke Düsseldorf. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Düsseldorf's city art museum in the Ehrenhof, opened in 1913, holding about 130,000 objects. In July 2017 it withdrew a painting by Andreas Achenbach from an exhibition after the heirs of the Jewish dealer Max Stern filed a claim against its private owner.
nodes: Kunstverein für die Rheinlande und Westfalen

f: A gGmbH owned by the Federal Republic and all 16 Länder and funded by the federal commissioner for culture and media (BKM) under a Bundestag resolution. The pages read did not state amounts; on 26 November 2025 the management cancelled a 2026 exhibition because federal grants had not risen enough to cover costs.
w: Federal exhibition hall in Bonn, open since 1992, with no collection of its own. A Bundesrechnungshof audit in 2007 led to the removal of both directors; in June 2022 the Federal Administrative Court ruled that the former commercial director cannot have statements in that audit report withdrawn.

f: Cologne's city painting gallery: the founding bequest of Ferdinand Franz Wallraf went to the City of Cologne in 1824, the merchant Johann Heinrich Richartz gave 100,000 Taler for the first building in 1854, and the city council decided the present building in 1996. The pages read did not state amounts for the running budget.
w: Cologne's oldest museum, opened on 1 July 1861, renamed in 2001 after Gérard and Marisol Corboud lent over 170 Impressionist paintings in perpetuity. The whole museum is closed until the end of 2028 for a general overhaul and an extension by Christ & Gantenbein; in February 2008 it said a Monet in its holdings was a forgery.

f: Paid for jointly by the City of Hanover and the State of Lower Saxony: the state's 2024 budget plans spending of 9,239 thousand euros and income of 408 thousand euros for the museum, with the gap covered by 5,500 thousand euros from the state and 3,331 thousand euros from other public bodies. Foundations including the Niedersächsische Sparkassenstiftung and the friends' association add works and exhibition funding.
w: Museum of 20th and 21st century art opened in June 1979 after the chocolate manufacturer Bernhard Sprengel and his wife Margrit gave their collection to the City of Hanover in 1969. Since 2024 the state funds it by institutional grant, replacing a 2010 agreement with the city that was dissolved in 2023.

f: Part of the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden, paid for by the Free State of Saxony: in 2024 the state gave the Kunstsammlungen 35,013,691.96 euros for running costs and 2,901,015.00 euros for investment (state accounts 2024). There is no separate figure for the Albertinum.
w: Home of the Galerie Neue Meister and the sculpture collection from 1800 of the Dresden state art collections, reopened in 2010 after a rebuild. In 2017 the art historian Paul Kaiser accused director Hilke Wagner in the Sächsische Zeitung of sending East German art to the depot; she received hate mail, held a public discussion and showed the GDR holdings in 2018.

f: A museum of the City of Leipzig, whose mayor's office decides the director's contract; the collection grew from the Leipziger Kunstverein of 1837 and citizens' bequests such as Adolf Heinrich Schletter's of 1853. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Leipzig's city art museum, founded as the Städtisches Museum in 1848 and since 4 December 2004 in a new building decided by the city council in 1996. It houses the Maximilian Speck von Sternburg Stiftung's collection and the Evelyn Richter and Ursula Arnold archives of the Ostdeutsche Sparkassenstiftung.

f: A museum of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin within the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, whose 2025 operating budget of about 275.3 million euros is met by about 196.4 million euros from the federal government, about 38.6 million euros from the State of Berlin and about 20 million euros from the other Länder. The Kaiser Friedrich Museumsverein is the friends' association.
w: Berlin's state gallery of European painting from the 13th to the 18th century, a public institution since 1830 and at the Kulturforum since 1998 in a building by Hilmer & Sattler. Its money comes through the federal and state funded Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation, with no separate figure for the gallery.

f: A museum of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin within the Stiftung Preußischer Kulturbesitz, whose 2025 operating budget of about 275.3 million euros is met by about 196.4 million euros from the federal government, about 38.6 million euros from the State of Berlin and about 20 million euros from the other Länder. The pages read did not state a figure for the museum itself.
w: Museum on Berlin's Museum Island showing the Egyptian Museum and Papyrus Collection and the Museum of Prehistory and Early History, including the bust of Nefertiti. Egypt's former antiquities chief Zahi Hawass asked for the bust in 2011 and started a petition for its return in 2024; the foundation's position is that it came to Berlin through an agreed division of finds from an excavation Egypt had authorised.

f: Privately funded: the Hasso Plattner Foundation, set up in 2015 by SAP co-founder Hasso Plattner, is the museum's operator and shareholder and pays for its running, its exhibition programme and additions to the collection. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Art museum on Potsdam's Alter Markt in the rebuilt Palais Barberini, opened in 2017 and founded by the SAP co-founder Hasso Plattner to show his collection of Impressionist painting. In October 2022 climate activists threw mashed potato at Monet's 'Getreideschober'; the museum put the damage at a five-figure sum.

f: A municipal museum of the City of Lyon, whose human resources budget carries the museum's payroll of 6.8 M€; the museum's own 2025 operating account shows 1,783,562 euros of spending and 1,800,158 euros of income, of which 1,071,068 euros from tickets to the permanent collection (activity report 2025). Acquisitions are backed by the Club du musée Saint-Pierre, an endowment fund of regional companies each giving 50,000 euros a year.
w: Lyon's fine arts museum, in a 17th century abbey on place des Terreaux, created under a decree of 1801 and run by the city. Its purchases lean on a club of companies, among them bioMérieux, Seb and three banks, and it took part in a state-funded provenance survey of works acquired since 1933 (museum website; activity report 2025).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Paid mainly by the Métropole de Lyon: 13 M€ of grant in 2025 against 5.3 M€ of own income, of which 3,583,022 euros from tickets and 764,408 euros from room hire and patronage (activity report 2025). In 2022 the operating budget was 19.9 M€, of which 14.4 M€ came from the Métropole (regional audit chamber, 4 October 2024).
w: Museum of natural history and human societies at the meeting of the Rhône and the Saône, in a building by Coop Himmelb(l)au opened in December 2014 and run as a public cultural establishment of the Métropole de Lyon, the City of Lyon and the ENS de Lyon. The regional audit chamber found the building cost 314 M€, 'more than five times the initial estimated value', and that almost all funding comes from the Métropole alone (CRC Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes, 4 October 2024).
nodes: Paid mainly by the Métropole de Lyon

f: A municipal museum run directly by the City of Lille (régie municipale), which collects its income. In 2021 that income was 75 % operating receipts, with 526,395 euros from tickets, and 25 % grants and patronage; named patrons were the Fondation Crédit Mutuel Nord Europe, Engie, M comme Mutuelle and Crédit du Nord (activity review 2021). The pages read did not state the city's total spend.
w: Lille's fine arts museum, in a palace on place de la République inaugurated on 6 March 1892 and paid for in part by a city lottery, extended in 1997 by Ibos and Vitart. It is a city service with about 103 permanent staff, and its company patrons are led by a mutual bank's foundation (museum website; scientific and cultural project).

f: A public museum of Montpellier: its site gives Montpellier Méditerranée Métropole as the body handling its data and a montpellier.fr address, and the city announced the appointment of its director (France 3 Occitanie, January 2025). A company foundation created in 2008 gathers about thirty regional firms giving 10,000 euros a year each and has bought more than seventy works for over 3 million euros (museum website). The pages read did not state the authority's budget for the museum.
w: Montpellier's fine arts museum, founded by the painter François-Xavier Fabre in 1825 and open to the public since 1828, built on the gifts of local collectors, above all Alfred Bruyas, patron of Courbet. Juliette Trey was named to take over as director in May 2025, the first woman in the post (France 3 Occitanie, January 2025).

f: The museum says it runs 'with the support of the State, the City of Avignon, the Region, Department and private patrons'; the city lends the two 18th century mansions it occupies (museum website). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Contemporary art museum in Avignon born of the dealer Yvon Lambert, who signed over to the French state a collection of more than 550 works, valued at more than 90 million euros, to be kept permanently in Avignon (franceinfo). On 17 April 2011 four visitors with a hammer destroyed Andres Serrano's Piss Christ and a second photograph there after a campaign by Catholic groups (franceinfo).
why: Catholic movements including the Institut Civitas petitioned and demonstrated against Andres Serrano's 'Immersion Piss Christ' at the Collection Lambert, and on 17 April 2011, the day after the rally, four visitors destroyed it and another Serrano photograph with a hammer (franceinfo, archive articl
nodes: Catholic movements including the Institut Civitas petitioned and demonstrated against Andres Serrano's 'Immersion Piss Christ' at the Collection Lambert, and on 17 April 2011, the day after the rally, four visitors destroyed it and another Serrano photograph with a hammer (franceinfo, archive article).

f: A budget of eight million euros, 70 % of it own income 'thanks to a good number of patrons', according to its president Françoise de Panafieu (Objectif Gard, July 2026). Its partners page shows the French state, the Région Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, the Département des Bouches-du-Rhône and the City of Arles as institutional partners, and Fondation LUMA, BMW, Kering and SNCF as main partners.
w: Annual summer photography festival founded in 1970, with more than forty exhibitions in heritage sites across Arles, chaired by Françoise de Panafieu. Most of its money is private: its main partners are Maja Hoffmann's Fondation LUMA, which runs its own art centre in the town, the carmaker BMW and the luxury group Kering (festival website; Objectif Gard, July 2026).
nodes: La Friche la Belle de Mai

f: A budget of 17.6 million euros, of which nearly 45 % is own income from tickets, tours, patronage and partnerships; the rest comes from the Ministry of Culture, the City of Avignon, the Grand Avignon, the Région Sud and the Département de Vaucluse under a multi-year agreement (festival document for 2026-2030; Avignon city council, 26 April 2025). The Fondation Crédit Coopératif has been its main patron since 2011.
w: Theatre festival founded by Jean Vilar in 1947, run by an association and directed since 2023 by Tiago Rodrigues, reappointed for the 2027 to 2030 editions. In July 2023 the festival said the eight Black performers of Rébecca Chaillon's 'Carte noire nommée désir' had been verbally and physically attacked with racist remarks, and on 16 December 2025 a Paris court gave six people suspended prison terms for harassing Chaillon online (France 3).
nodes: Département de Vaucluse under a multi-year agreement
Fondation Crédit Coopératif has been its main patron
La Friche la Belle de Mai

f: A national museum paid mainly by the French state: in the 2023 accounts its income was 11,036 thousand euros, of which 5,608 thousand euros was the Ministry of Culture's operating grant and 2,432 thousand euros its own income from tickets, room hire and concessions (annual performance report for the Culture budget, 2023). Patronage brought 226,706 euros over 2020 and 2021, from the Fondation d'Entreprise Michelin, Maison Perrier-Jouët, The Japan Foundation and Priti Paul with Apeejay Trust (activity report 2020-2021).
w: France's national museum of Asian arts, founded by the industrialist Émile Guimet and opened in Paris in 1889, a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture chaired by Yannick Lintz since November 2022. Since 2024 Tibet scholars and Tibetan associations have accused it of replacing 'Tibet' with 'Monde himalayen' to please Beijing, and four associations took it to the Paris administrative court on 2 July 2025 (franceinfo).
why: Tibetan associations demonstrated in Paris on 5 January 2025 against the removal of the word 'Tibet' and four of them filed a case against the museum at the Paris administrative court on 2 July 2025 (franceinfo, 2 July 2025).
nodes: Tibetan associations demonstrated in Paris on 5 January 2025 against the removal of the word 'Tibet' and four of them filed a case against the museum at the Paris administrative court on 2 July 2025 (franceinfo, 2 July 2025).

f: Part of the public establishment it has shared with the Musée d'Orsay since 2010. In the 2025 accounts the establishment's income was 104,199,245 euros: 30,684,508 euros of Ministry of Culture operating grant and 61,602,681 euros of own income (EPMO activity report 2025). The pages read did not give figures for the Orangerie alone.
w: National museum in the Tuileries garden holding Monet's Nymphéas, installed in 1927, and the Jean Walter and Paul Guillaume collection, which the state bought in 1959 and 1963 from Domenica Walter, who kept the pictures until her death in 1977. It had 1,129,211 visitors in 2025 (EPMO activity report 2025).

f: Run by the private association Les Arts Décoratifs under a state concession. In 2023 the association's consolidated accounts showed 40.02 M€ of income against 42.89 M€ of charges, a deficit of 2.87 M€; the Ministry of Culture's operating grant was 15.2 M€ and own income 19.8 M€, of which gifts, sponsorship and partnerships were 5,151,000 euros (activity report 2023).
w: Museum of decorative arts, design and fashion in the Rohan and Marsan wings of the Louvre, managed with a library, the Musée Nissim de Camondo and two schools by an association founded in 1882 and chaired since December 2021 by Johannes Huth. Its director Christine Macel left the post in October 2024 after two years, citing an audit that described a 'crisis of governance and organisation' (The Art Newspaper, 11 October 2024).

f: A public establishment paid by the state and the City of Paris. In the 2023 accounts its income was 117,296 thousand euros: 43,208 thousand euros of Ministry of Culture operating grant, 16,785 thousand euros of other earmarked public money and 35,463 thousand euros of own income (annual performance report for the Culture budget, 2023). Founding patrons listed are the Fondation d'entreprise Société Générale and the Fondation Bettencourt Schueller.
w: Concert hall, music museum and education complex at La Villette, in a building by Jean Nouvel inaugurated in 2015, home of the Orchestre de Paris. The regional audit chamber put the full cost of the building at 534.7 M€ against a first envelope of 276 M€, and the hall claimed 170 million euros from Nouvel before both sides settled in October 2021 (CRC Île-de-France, 2016; franceinfo, 21 October 2021).

f: A national theatre paid mainly by the state: in the 2023 accounts its income was 44,257 thousand euros, of which 25,056 thousand euros was the Ministry of Culture's operating grant and 11,617 thousand euros its own unearmarked income (annual performance report for the Culture budget, 2023). Company patrons listed on its site include AG2R La Mondiale, the Banque de France, Fondation Covéa, Danone and Fondation Lazard Frères Gestion.
w: State theatre founded by Louis XIV in 1680, a public establishment tied to its troupe's own society of actors, led since August 2025 by Clément Hervieu-Léger. Its Salle Richelieu closed on 16 January 2026 until the end of July for works of nearly 22 million euros, 'very largely' paid by the Ministry of Culture, with plays moved to nine partner theatres (franceinfo, 15 January 2026).

f: Founded and funded by the Groupe Galeries Lafayette, the department store group; admission to exhibitions is free. Its collection belongs to the Fonds de dotation Famille Moulin, born in 2013 of a gift by Guillaume Houzé and his grandmother Ginette Moulin (foundation website). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Contemporary art foundation in the Marais, in a building by Rem Koolhaas with moving floors, founded by the Groupe Galeries Lafayette and opened on 10 March 2018. The money and the collection both come from the family that owns the department stores (foundation website).

f: A departmental museum of the Val-de-Marne, which has backed contemporary art since 1982 and built the collection. The state and the region paid half of the 37 million euro construction budget, and the state has also supported purchases through the regional museum acquisition fund (InventCulture case study, 2023). The pages read did not state the yearly budget.
w: Contemporary art museum opened in November 2005 in Vitry-sur-Seine by the Val-de-Marne department, then run by communists, as the first contemporary art museum in the Paris suburbs; Alexia Fabre led it until 2022 and Nicolas Surlapierre took over on 3 October 2022 (InventCulture case study, 2023; Le Quotidien de l'Art).

f: The foundation states that all the money for its 2025 activities came from its own resources; its annual report for 2025 puts the total cost of activities at 14,923,536 euros, of which 8,580,812 euros went to art and museums. It describes itself as a family foundation living on its endowment, created in 1955 by the financier Juan March Ordinas, founder of Banca March. Entry is free.
w: A family foundation in Madrid with exhibitions, concerts, lectures and a research library, chaired since 18 March 2026 by Catalina March Juan, great-granddaughter of the founder. Público (10 November 2013), reporting on José Ángel Sánchez Asiain's history of the financing of the civil war, names Juan March as one of the three first sources of money for the military coup of 18 July 1936.

f: The foundation lives on dividends from the insurer Mapfre S.A., of which it holds an indirect 69.6% through Cartera Mapfre S.L.: its audited accounts for 2025 record 53,000 thousand euros of dividends received (62,000 thousand in 2024), and its site gives total income of 63.8 million euros in 2025. The culture area, which runs the Recoletos halls in Madrid and the KBr photography centre in Barcelona, cost 14,125 thousand euros in 2025.
w: The exhibition halls of the foundation that controls the listed insurer Mapfre, set up on 5 November 1975; the halls show painting and photography in three seasons a year and charge 5 euros. The foundation is the majority owner of the company whose dividends fund it, under the supervision of the Protectorate of Foundations of the Ministry of Culture.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Fundación Telefónica is paid for by its founder, the telecoms company Telefónica, S.A., which gave it 39,000,000 euros for general activities in 2024 and 45,797,000 euros in 2023, according to the foundation's accounts for 2024. Entry to the Espacio and all its activities is free.
w: The exhibition and events space of Telefónica's corporate foundation, opened in 2012 on four floors of the company's 1930 headquarters on Gran Vía. The foundation, set up by Telefónica, S.A. on 25 June 1998, also keeps the company's art and technology collection.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Four public bodies sit in its consortium and foundation: the Ministry of Culture, the Generalitat de Catalunya, Barcelona City Council and Barcelona Provincial Council. Ara reported on 27 July 2026 a 2025/26 budget of 55.8 million euros, 49% from public contributions and 51% from its own resources; the Liceu's accounts for 2022/23 show ordinary income of 52.4 million euros, 28 million euros of it from the public administrations and 7.9 million euros from sponsorship.
w: Barcelona's opera house, opened on 4 April 1847 and built by private shareholders, whose Society handed ownership to the public administrations when the foundation was created on 5 September 1994, after the fire of 31 January that year. In February 2012 it announced a two-month halt and a redundancy procedure for 395 staff over a 3.7 million euro deficit (betevé).
nodes: Four public bodies sit in its consortium

f: A state museum of the Ministry of Culture: staff, investment and general contracts are paid centrally by the ministry, and the museum itself controls only a petty-cash budget, 964,568 euros in 2025, which its annual report puts at about 5% of its real budget. Named sponsors on its patronage page include ASISA, Samsung, Fundación Mutua Madrileña, Bolsas y Mercados Españoles, Fundación Palarq, Fundación ADEY, Redeia and Fundación Ibercaja.
w: Spain's national archaeology museum, founded in 1867 by Isabel II, with an estimated 1,266,592 museum objects, the Dama de Elche among them. Elche's city council has asked for years for a temporary loan of the bust and the Ministry of Culture refused again in September 2023 on a technical report (Alicante Plaza); the museum has also published online the objects it holds from Civil War seizures and received three restitution requests in 2025 (annual report 2025).
nodes: Museo de Arte Moderno de Buenos Aires

f: Málaga City Council pays for it: under the contract approved in July 2024 the city pays the Centre Pompidou in Paris 2,694,900 euros a year from 2025 to 2029 and 3,151,915 euros a year from 2030 to 2034, split between a fee for the brand and a fee for the collections, and provides the building (Málaga City Council, 11 July 2024; The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2024, gives 2.7 million and 3.1 million euros). A municipal agency manages the centre.
w: A branch of the Paris museum in a city-owned building in Málaga's port, opened in March 2015 and run by the municipal agency that also manages Picasso's birthplace. The city buys the name and the loans: 1,300,000 euros a year for the use of the brand and 1,394,900 euros for the collections in the first five years of the 2025 to 2035 contract (Málaga City Council, 11 July 2024).

f: The foundation's own table gives its 2025 grants as 10,000,000 euros from the state's Fundo de Fomento Cultural and 350,000 euros from the Municipality of Porto, with 1,840,690 euros of patronage and sponsorship. The state grant rose from 7,000,000 euros in 2016 to 10,000,000 euros in 2021 and has stayed there.
w: Porto's concert hall by Rem Koolhaas and OMA, opened on 15 April 2005 and run by a foundation set up by the Portuguese State and the Municipality of Porto under Decree-Law 18/2006, with private founders that hold four of seven board seats. In September 2020 the labour inspectorate ACT sent 34 cases of service-contract workers to the public prosecutor (Diário de Notícias); the board said in January 2022 that the labour court had ruled for it in 15 cases (Renascença).

f: A national museum managed by the state company Museus e Monumentos de Portugal, E.P.E. The roof and facade restoration begun in 2025 is paid with 1.3 million euros from the EU-funded Recovery and Resilience Plan (PRR), and named patrons in 2025 were Super Bock Group, Fundação BPI 'la Caixa', Fundação Millennium bcp, Câmara Municipal do Porto and Fundação Manuel António da Mota. The pages read did not state the museum's running budget.
w: Portugal's first public art museum, founded in Porto in 1833 from church and convent property confiscated during the Liberal Wars, and housed in the Palácio dos Carrancas. Its friends' association, the Círculo Dr. José de Figueiredo, founded in 1940, handles the patronage money the museum raises and buys works for it (activity report 2025).

f: The VriendenLoterij gives 350,000 euros a year and added 106,073 euros from its 2024 proceeds; projects are paid by Dutch ministries, the European Commission and charitable funds.
w: The house on the Prinsengracht where Anne Frank hid, run by an organisation founded on 3 May 1957 with Otto Frank among its founders; it had 1,208,327 visitors in 2024. Its dependence on ticket income is the thing to follow: the 2024 report lists diversifying income to reduce dependence on museum income among its aims.

f: Mainly the Dutch state: Eye's accounts for 2025 show total income of 24,304,157 euros, of which 14,700,415 euros was structural subsidy from the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OCW) and 197,339 euros from the municipality of Amsterdam (AFK). Tickets and other audience income brought 4,221,742 euros, sponsors 497,538 euros and the VriendenLoterij 450,026 euros; the year closed with an operating result of minus 3,218,988 euros.
w: The national museum for film, on the IJ in Amsterdam, which grew out of the Nederlands Historisch Film Archief set up in 1946. It ran deficits in 2024 and 2025 and its director confirmed in November 2025 that jobs would go after the in-house restaurant lost money (NH Nieuws, 25 November 2025).

f: Almost wholly the Dutch state: its annual report for 2024 gives total income of 15.7 million euros, of which 13.4 million euros was structural subsidy from the Ministry of Education, Culture and Science (OCW), and puts public subsidies at 91.07% of income. Ticket income was 529,639 euros and the VriendenLoterij gave 106,211 euros; the year's operating result was minus 505,796 euros.
w: The national museum for architecture, design and digital culture in Rotterdam's Museumpark, which started on 1 January 2013 from the merger of the Netherlands Architecture Institute, Premsela and Virtueel Platform, and keeps the state's architecture collection. Its 2024 report says Rotterdam's culture-plan committee made critical remarks about its role in the city and that the city contribution it was advised to receive ended up 'buiten budget'.

f: Its balance sheet at 31 December 2025 carries tangible fixed assets of 260,411,174 euros.
w: A museum of modern and contemporary art on an estate in Wassenaar, opened in 2016 by Joop van Caldenborgh, founder of the chemicals company Caldic, who gave the collection, the museum and the estate to the Voorlinden Foundation and chairs its board (Ara, 11 September 2026; ANBI page). Two of the five board seats are held by members of the Van Caldenborgh family.

n: Royal Museum of Fine Arts Antwerp (KMSKA)
f: The Flemish government paid for the whole eleven-year renovation, which VRT put at more than 100 million euros against an original budget of 44 million euros, and gives the museum its operating money. The museum also raises private money: named partners are Ackermans & van Haaren, Astrea, Bank Van Breda, Kolmont, Mercier Van Lanschot, Soudal, Vivium and Alken-Maes, with project support from the National Lottery, the King Baudouin Foundation and the Baillet Latour Fund. The pages read did not state amounts for the operating grant or the sponsors.
w: Flanders' fine arts museum in Antwerp, founded by Napoleon's decree of 5 May 1810, closed from 2011 and reopened on 24 September 2022 after a renovation whose cost more than doubled under five successive culture ministers (VRT, 15 September 2022). It had more than 570,000 visitors in 2025 (VRT, 2 March 2026).

f: The museum says it receives annual structural subsidies from the Flemish Government. Umicore, KBC Bank and Insurance, Port of Antwerp and SD Worx were its four founding sponsors, each with a structural contribution over five years, and Port of Antwerp still sponsors the care and accessibility of the collections. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Antwerp's museum of the city, the port and world cultures, in a 60-metre tower by Neutelings Riedijk Architecten, with a collection of 500,000 pieces that includes Congolese objects acquired by Antwerp's Museum Vleeshuis in 1920. From 2022 to 2025 it researched how three of those objects left Congo, among them a power statue confiscated after Chief Nkolomonyi's arrest in 1923 (Restitution Matters).

f: Established and funded by the Brussels-Capital Region since 2017: a Kanal spokesperson told The Art Newspaper the region fully funds the 230 million euro conversion of the former Citroën garage. The region's yearly budget for it, first promised at 35 million euros, is 28 million euros in 2026 and is expected to fall to 10 million euros by 2029; Kanal pays the Centre Pompidou 2 million euros a year until 2031.
w: A museum of modern and contemporary art and architecture in a 40,000 square metre former Citroën garage by the Brussels canal, due to open on 28 November 2026. Its director general Yves Goldstein leaves on 30 November after what the regional government calls 'a difference of opinion regarding the future of Kanal', and the Inspectorate of Finance called the foundation's multi-year budget 'unrealistic and disproportionate' in 2023 (The Art Newspaper, 23 September 2026; The Brussels Times, 13 August 2023).

f: An autonomous municipal company of the City of Leuven, which guarantees affordable entry through a 'price subsidy' set in a management agreement: 2,577,888 euros in the 2020 accounts, which also show operating subsidies of 4,315,778 euros in 2020 against 1,512,443 euros in 2019. The Flemish government supports it under the Heritage Decree and the Arts Decree; Delen Private Bank pays for restoration and Cera has lent its art collection.
w: Leuven's city museum of old and contemporary art, with more than 58,000 objects, set up by the city as an autonomous municipal company. Company sponsorship is sold in tiers from 5,000 euros to 45,000 euros a year for an Official Sponsor (museum website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A state museum of the Italian Ministry of Culture with special autonomy since 2015, including financial and accounting autonomy (museum website). The ministry's statistics office records 265,893 visitors and gross ticket takings of €2,057,926.00 for 2023 (Ministry of Culture, Tavola 8, 3 July 2024). The pages read did not state amounts for the state grant or name sponsors.
w: The state gallery of Venetian painting, in the former church, monastery and Scuola Grande of Santa Maria della Carità; it holds Leonardo's Vitruvian Man. With the ministry it has pursued the puzzle maker Ravensburger since 2019 over fees for reproducing the drawing; a Venice court ruled for the museum in November 2022 and German courts ruled for Ravensburger in March 2024 and June 2025 (Harvard International Law Journal, 1 April 2025; AFP via eNCA, 12 June 2025).

f: Its statute says it pays for its work from the income of an endowment first made up of gifts of the family of Count Vittorio Cini, from the contributions of its Sostenitori and from other public and private income (statute). The Sostenitori with seats on its General Council are Intesa Sanpaolo, Fondazione Cariplo, Eni and Assicurazioni Generali (governance list, 13 July 2026). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: A private foundation for humanities research on the island of San Giorgio Maggiore, created in 1951 by Vittorio Cini in memory of his son Giorgio; it holds the island on a concession in use from the state (foundation profile; statute). The four corporate and banking funders name a vice president and board members, and the heads of Intesa Sanpaolo and Eni sit on its General Council (governance list, 13 July 2026).

f: Run by the Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia (MUVE), whose founding member is the Comune di Venezia; the foundation's 2024 accounts show a value of production of €40,580,726, of which €36,284,529 from ticketing across its museums, €1,034,482 from bookshop and cafe concession fees, €330,713 in operating contributions and €77,500 in sponsorships (MUVE accounts 2024). The palace had 1.24 million visitors in 2024 (MUVE press release). Donors named in the accounts include Fondazione Al Thani, Coop Italia, Gruppo PAM, Dolce & Gabbana, Generali Italia, Chanel and Bulgari.
w: The former seat of the Doge and the government of the Venetian Republic; the Italian state owns it and has entrusted it to the city since 1923, and since 2008 the city's museum foundation runs it, with the mayor of Venice as vice president (museum website; MUVE website). In 2022 the city left the director's post unfilled after Gabriella Belli's term and hundreds signed a petition for a public selection (Artribune, 9 August 2022).

f: Its 2025 budget forecasts a value of production of €33,264,149, of which €23,804,149 in operating contributions: €18,587,500 from the state (FUS and other measures), €640,000 from the Veneto Region, €1,750,000 from the Comune di Venezia plus €326,649 for a mortgage, and €2,450,000 from private donors, the largest being Intesa Sanpaolo (€760,000) and Fondazione di Venezia (€600,000); subscriptions and tickets are forecast at €7,200,000 (Budget 2025).
w: Venice's opera house, opened in 1792 and rebuilt after fires in 1836 and 1996, run by a foundation whose president is the mayor of Venice (theatre website). The appointment of Beatrice Venezi as music director in September 2025 brought a letter from the orchestra asking for its withdrawal and a strike that cancelled the season opening on 17 October 2025; the foundation cancelled all future work with her on 26 April 2026 and she has challenged that (Artribune, 26 September 2025 and 26 April 2026; ANSA, 17 October 2025 and 10 June 2026).
why: The orchestra and staff struck on 17 October 2025 against the way Beatrice Venezi was appointed music director, the premiere of Wozzeck was cancelled and about a thousand people gathered in Campo Sant'Angelo (ANSA, 17 October 2025).
nodes: The orchestra and staff struck on 17 October 2025 against the way Beatrice Venezi was appointed music director, the premiere of Wozzeck was cancelled and about a thousand people gathered in Campo Sant'Angelo (ANSA, 17 October 2025).

f: A civic museum of the Comune di Milano, run by the city's culture department (museum website). Fondazione Pasquinelli gave €5 million toward its expansion into the second Arengario tower (Artribune, 26 July 2021). The pages read did not state amounts for the city's yearly spending.
w: Milan's museum of Italian 20th century art, in the Palazzo dell'Arengario on Piazza del Duomo since 6 December 2010, part of the city's Civiche Raccolte d'Arte (museum website). Its planned doubling into the second Arengario drew an objection from the heritage Soprintendenza in March 2021 to the footbridge the city's competition brief asked for (Artribune, 11 March 2021).

f: A public and private arrangement: the Comune di Milano owns the building and the civic collection, and since the opening in 2015 the company 24 Ore Cultura has held the concession for exhibitions and cultural activities (Artribune, 27 June 2026). In June 2026 the city put out a European tender for an eight-year concession of exhibitions, cafe, restaurant, bookshop and parking, estimated at €84.36 million in total, with a base fee to the city of €100,000 a year (Artribune, 27 June 2026).
w: Milan's museum of world cultures, in the former Ansaldo factory in the Tortona district, built to a design by David Chipperfield, who refused to attend the opening on 27 October 2015 in a dispute with the city over the stone floor that went to the Court of Milan (Dezeen, 28 October 2015). The city keeps the civic ethnographic collection while the concession holder runs the exhibitions and services; bids for the next concession were due on 28 September 2026 (Artribune, 27 June 2026).

n: GAM - Galleria Civica d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino
f: Part of the Fondazione Torino Musei since 2003; the foundation cashed €7,701,670.64 from public bodies in 2025, of which €5,894,766.34 from the Città di Torino, €960,000 from the Regione Piemonte, €500,000 from the Città Metropolitana, €150,000 from the Chamber of Commerce and €196,904.30 from the Ministry of Culture (Fondazione Torino Musei, public contributions paid 2025). The pages read did not state private funders' amounts.
w: Turin's civic gallery of modern and contemporary art, which traces its collection to the Civic Museum opened in 1863, in a building of 1959 on Via Magenta (museum website). In 2017 the city cut the civic museums' resources by 20%, 28 staff were made redundant and the foundation's visitors fell from 816,113 to 616,960 (Artribune, 5 January 2018).
nodes: Castello di Rivoli Museo d Arte Contemporanea

f: Owned and paid for by Fondazione CRT, the Turin banking foundation, through the company OGR-CRT, which the site calls an 'ente strumentale di Fondazione CRT'; the foundation says it invested 100 million euros in the conversion (OGR website). The pages read did not state yearly running costs.
w: A 19th century railway repair works in Turin, bought by Fondazione CRT in 2013 and opened on 30 September 2017 as a venue for contemporary art, music and technology business (OGR website; Artribune, 30 October 2017). In April 2024 the foundation's board named a new head of OGR, Davide Canavesio, in a session that led its president Fabrizio Palenzona to resign, saying board members had sought 'patti occulti'; Turin prosecutors later placed Palenzona under investigation (Open, 23 April 2024; Teleborsa, 22 July 2024).
nodes: Castello di Rivoli Museo d Arte Contemporanea

f: A functional body ('ente funzionale') of the Autonomous Province of Trento, which appoints its president and selects its director (museum website; Finestre sull'Arte, 15 February 2019; Artribune, 12 September 2025). It posts yearly final accounts for 2014 to 2025 on its transparency pages. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The museum of modern and contemporary art of Trento and Rovereto, founded in 1987, in a building by Mario Botta opened in Rovereto on 15 December 2002 (museum website). The province's council named the art critic and politician Vittorio Sgarbi president in February 2019, unpaid; from 2020 the administrative director acted as director, and a director chosen by public selection, Micol Forti, took office only on 1 December 2025 (Finestre sull'Arte, 15 February 2019; Artribune, 12 September 2025).

n: Museo e Real Bosco di Capodimonte
f: A state museum of the Italian Ministry of Culture, whose director general is chosen in a ministry competition (museum website; Artribune, 24 June 2024). Two support groups raise private money: Amici di Capodimonte, founded in 2005, and American Friends of Capodimonte, founded in 2016 for donors who pay tax in the United States (museum website). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The Bourbon royal palace on the hill of Capodimonte in Naples, begun in 1738 and opened as a national museum in 1957, with the Farnese collection and a park of 134 hectares (museum website). Eike Schmidt took up the directorship in January 2024, then took leave within months to run for mayor of Florence for the centre-right and lost the runoff of 23 and 24 June 2024 (Artribune, 24 June 2024).
nodes: Two support groups raise private money

f: A body of the Italian Ministry of Culture with special autonomy; its ticket takings were €55,291,542 from 4,267,233 visitors in 2024 and €52,201,160.47 in 2023 (Ministry of Culture, 13 May 2025; Tavola 8, 3 July 2024). The Great Pompeii Project spent €105 million from the European Regional Development Fund and national funds, of which €78 million were EU cohesion funds (park website; Artribune, 21 June 2023).
w: The excavated Roman city of Pompeii and the nearby sites of Oplontis, Stabiae and Boscoreale, run by a ministry park under a director general, Gabriel Zuchtriegel (park website). Since 15 November 2024 tickets carry the visitor's name and entries are capped at 20,000 a day, after a summer of over four million visitors (Euronews, 9 November 2024).
nodes: MICAS Malta International Contemporary Art Space

f: A civic museum of Roma Capitale under the Sovrintendenza Capitolina; museum services are run by Zètema Progetto Cultura s.r.l., a company wholly owned by the city (museum website; Rome city government resolution 81 of 20 March 2026). For Zètema's service contract from March to 31 December 2026 the city's budget sets aside €32,498,179.15, and ticket takings are collected by Zètema for the city and paid over monthly (Rome city government resolution 81 of 20 March 2026).
w: Rome's civic museum of antiquities and paintings on the Capitoline Hill, which traces its origin to Pope Sixtus IV's gift of bronze statues to the People of Rome in 1471 (museum website). Its front-of-house staff work for the city's in-house company Zètema, which in December 2022 opened its first public hiring call in over eight years, 67 room assistants at €1,495.20 gross a month (Artribune, 16 December 2022).

f: A park of the Italian Ministry of Culture with special autonomy, whose ticket takings were €101,902,884 from 14,733,395 visitors in 2024 and €79,340,891.50 in 2023 (Ministry of Culture, 13 May 2025; Tavola 8, 3 July 2024). The restoration of the Colosseum was sponsored by the shoe company Tod's, of Diego Della Valle, with about €25 million (Blitz Quotidiano, 31 July 2013 and 8 August 2016).
w: The ministry park for the Colosseum, the Roman Forum, the Palatine and the Domus Aurea, set up by decree on 12 January 2017 (park website). In April 2025 the competition authority fined the former ticket seller CoopCulture €7 million and six tour operators, almost €20 million in all, over tickets bought up by bots and bundled with tours (Artribune, 8 April 2025); the audit court had earlier questioned the length of the rights given to Tod's in return for its €25 million (Blitz Quotidiano, 8 August 2016).

f: A private-law opera foundation whose founding members are the Italian state, the Veneto Region, the Municipality of Verona, the Chamber of Commerce of Verona and Cattolica Assicurazioni (foundation website). The Ministry of Culture records a charge on its budget of €11,472,255 for part of 2025 (Ministry of Culture sheet, August 2025). The fundraising scheme 67 Colonne raised over €2.1 million in 2024 and sponsors led by UniCredit a further €2.75 million (foundation website, 29 May 2024).
w: The summer opera festival in Verona's Roman amphitheatre, held since 1913, and the Teatro Filarmonico, run by a foundation chaired by the mayor of Verona (foundation website; Ministry of Culture sheet). The culture minister put it under a commissioner in April 2016 for management and cash problems, and in 2023 the centre-right majority of its council reappointed the superintendent Cecilia Gasdia against the vote of mayor Damiano Tommasi, who took a related appointment to court (ANSA, 15 April 2016; Il Fatto Quotidiano, 4 March and 24 June 2023).

f: A self-governing institution funded mainly by the Danish state: the Agency for Culture and Palaces lists its operating grant at DKK 34,071,985 for 2025 and DKK 32,519,350 for 2026. Its 2024 annual report gives turnover of DKK 83,819 thousand, foundation support of DKK 23,946 thousand (including a Ny Carlsbergfondet purchase grant of DKK 9,800 thousand in total) and entrance income of DKK 7,341 thousand.
w: A state-recognised museum of contemporary art on the coast west of Copenhagen, inaugurated in 1996 in a building by Søren Robert Lund and run by a board whose chair is appointed by Dansk Industri and deputy chair by Ishøj Kommune. Under the 2025 museum reform it loses at least 19% of its state subsidy, DKK 600,000 in 2025 and DKK 1.6m a year for the next three years (The Art Newspaper, 31 March 2026).

f: Owned and run by the City of Copenhagen, which is its main funder: the municipal grant was DKK 8.9m in 2022. The state grant to Copenhagen's two recognised museums together (Museum of Copenhagen and Thorvaldsens Museum) rose from DKK 2.1m in 2024 to DKK 6.5m in 2025 and is listed at DKK 7,050,227 for 2026; foundations named in 2024 include Augustinus Fonden, Villum Fonden, Novo Nordisk Fonden and Aage og Johanne Louis-Hansens Fond.
w: Denmark's first publicly owned art museum, opened in 1848 to show the sculptor Bertel Thorvaldsen's works and the collections he gave to Copenhagen in 1838; it sits in the city's Kunst & Historie unit with the Museum of Copenhagen and Nikolaj Kunsthal. The state agency noted in 2014 that the city owns and runs the museum while three of the seven board members, the chair among them, represent the city, an arrangement it said could cause unclear lines of management.

f: A state enterprise under the Ministry of Culture: its state appropriation was DKK 612.3m in 2025, 67.7% of ordinary operating income of DKK 905.0m, with DKK 292.7m from sales of tickets and services. The City of Copenhagen gave DKK 53.6m in 2025; A.P. Møller og Hustru Chastine Mc-Kinney Møllers Fond gave the Opera House and supports its upkeep, and Realdania is paying for a children's venue in Stærekassen with an approved total of DKK 155.5m.
w: Denmark's national stage for ballet, opera, drama and orchestra, on Kongens Nytorv since 1748 and run by a board of eight, six appointed by the culture minister. After Politiken's 2023 reporting on its ballet school, a lawyers' inquiry received 97 reports covering the 1970s to today, found grounds for employment-law action against three staff and criticised the 2020 to 2023 board; the inquiry cost about DKK 10.7m. Scandinavian Tobacco Group is listed among its sponsors.
why: The theatre's partners page, read on 15 November 2026, lists Scandinavian Tobacco Group as a sponsor that has supported the theatre for many years; the company's own website describes it as a global leader in cigars.

f: A foundation funded mainly by public grants: NOK 139,749,848 in public operating grants in 2025 out of operating income of NOK 177,259,768, from the Ministry of Culture, Bergen kommune and Vestland fylkeskommune, with ticket and sales income of NOK 21,883,139. Main partners are Sparebankstiftelsen DNB, BAHR and De Bergenske, and sponsors include Bara Eiendom AS, EGD Holding AS and Santos AS.
w: Four art museums in central Bergen and the homes of Edvard Grieg, Ole Bull and Harald Sæverud, merged in 2007 and named Kode in 2013, holding about 60,000 objects. Its China collection was burgled in 2010 and January 2013, and in October 2023 seven of its 20 marble half-columns from the Yuanmingyuan summer palace were handed back under a 2013 agreement with Zhongkun Investment Group and Peking University.

f: A limited company wholly owned by the Norwegian state. Its accounts in the Brønnøysund register show operating income of NOK 976,709,525 in 2025, of which sales income was NOK 117,599,844, and a result of NOK 2,630,282; equity was negative at NOK -118,280,731. The pages read did not state the amount of the state grant.
w: Norway's largest music and performing arts institution, which gave its first performance in 1958 under Kirsten Flagstad and moved into the Snøhetta opera house in Bjørvika in 2008. In 2015 the opera director Per Boye Hansen's contract was not renewed, the culture minister replaced almost the whole board, and management warned of cuts to cover rising pension costs (News in English, May and June 2015); equity has been negative in every year from 2023 to 2025.

f: A department of Museum Stavanger AS (MUST), owned by Stavanger kommune (53%) and Rogaland fylkeskommune (47%); MUST's turnover in 2025 was NOK 114.3 million, with own earnings of 30%, and its public funders are Stavanger kommune, Rogaland fylkeskommune and the Ministry of Culture. The pages read did not state amounts for the art museum alone.
w: The art museum by Mosvannet, with roots in the Stavanger art society's permanent gallery begun on 11 February 1865; it holds Norway's largest Lars Hertervig collection. MUST names Lærdal Medical and Sparebankstiftelsen SR-Bank among its largest private contributors, and in 2025 Christen Sveaas' art foundation bought a Frida Hansen work and deposited it with the museum.

f: Part of the City of Gothenburg's cultural administration and co-financed by Västra Götalandsregionen; the pages read did not state amounts for its running costs. The city property company Higab is rebuilding and extending the museum for SEK 1,050 to 1,120 million at 2025 prices, up from SEK 800 million when the city council decided the investment in 2021.
w: A municipal art museum on Götaplatsen, in a building put up for the 1923 Jubilee Exhibition, whose collection was built on merchants' gifts, among them the Fürstenberg gallery and an 1876 bequest of SEK 250,000 that still funds purchases. The extension's cost has risen by about a third and would raise the museum's rent to SEK 61 to 66 million a year; a Sweden Democrat councillor reserved against the increase.

f: A museum of the City of Malmö, which says municipal financing is the base; the pages read did not state amounts. For the planned new museum in Kungsparken the city is seeking gifts from companies, foundations and individuals through Stiftelsen för Malmö Konstmuseum.
w: A municipal art museum founded in 1841 as the art department of Malmö museum and its own museum since 2000, housed in Malmöhus castle where about 2% of its more than 40,000 works can be shown. The city council took a direction decision on 11 September 2025 to move it to the restaurant pavilion in Kungsparken, the former Casino Cosmopol, with building planned to start in 2027; the final decision waits on the financing.

f: Belongs to the City of Stockholm, with ticket income (standard admission SEK 165) beside it. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: A municipal art hall on Djurgården, opened in 1916 as Sweden's first independent public hall for contemporary art and known for the juried Vårsalongen; it is led by Joanna Sandell Wright. Its concrete extension Liljevalchs+, planned from 2013 and opened in August 2021, leaked rainwater in its first month and had its cracked facade repaired three years later (SVT, 27 August 2021 and 8 November 2024).

f: A limited company wholly owned by the Swedish state: the state grant was SEK 259.7 million in 2025 (SEK 255.2 million in 2024) out of turnover of SEK 323.1 million, with ticket income of SEK 46.5 million and other operating income of SEK 16.9 million.
w: Sweden's national stage for theatre, founded by Gustav III in 1788 and in its house on Nybroplan since 1908, led by Mattias Andersson as theatre director and Kitte Wagner as chief executive. In April 2019 the chief executive Eirik Stubø left after public protest that followed an SVT documentary on the singer Josefin Nilsson, in which a man tied to the theatre had been convicted of assaulting her; the board chair said the decision was not about one event.

f: A limited company wholly owned by the Swedish state: the state appropriation was SEK 518.1 million in 2025, of which the base grant was SEK 506.8 million, out of operating income of SEK 658.8 million; ticket income was SEK 111.8 million and sponsorship and donations SEK 8.0 million.
w: Sweden's national stage for opera and ballet, founded in 1773, in the opera house on Gustav Adolfs torg inaugurated in 1898. The National Property Board puts the total renovation and extension of the house at SEK 3.25 billion at 2032 prices, partly paid by private donors the pages read do not name; the house is due to close during 2026, with a move to Gasometer in Norra Djurgårdsstaden from 1 February 2027 and a return in 2032.

f: A foundation in the City of Helsinki group since 2023. Its 2025 accounts show income from ordinary activities of EUR 12,307,993.09, of which grants and subsidies received were EUR 9,957,623.72 (EUR 5,978,744.98 in 2024); the accounts do not name the grant givers.
w: Helsinki's city art museum in Tennis Palace, which looks after the city's collection of more than 10,000 works including its public art and organises the Helsinki Biennial; the city council moved its operations and staff to the HAM Helsinki Art Museum Foundation from 1 January 2023. A city working group proposed on 8 October 2025 to move it from rented Tennis Palace to the Olympia Terminal and the Port of Helsinki head office in Makasiiniranta.

f: A foundation funded mainly by the Finnish state: statutory state funding of EUR 40.4 million in 2025 (52% of its financing), a state rent subsidy of EUR 13.6 million (17%), and EUR 5.4 million (7%) from Helsinki, Espoo, Vantaa and Kauniainen; own financing was 22.6%. Main partners are the pension insurer Varma and Stockmann, with the Jane and Aatos Erkko Foundation paying for the ballet's youth company.
w: Finland's only professional opera company, established in 1911, with the Finnish National Ballet from 1922, in the Opera House by Töölönlahti since 1993; the Ministry of Education and Culture is the foundation's founder. Parliament sets its funding each year while its productions are contracted three to five years ahead, a gap the board lists as a risk; the 2025 report saw no immediate risk of a cut.

f: A state museum, one of Iceland's three head museums: its state appropriation for 2024 was ISK 722 million, with a special allocation of ISK 45 million in 2023 and ISK 20 million in 2021 under a government drive for the head museums. Its own income is mainly admission fees, with some from the shop and the hire of works.
w: Iceland's national art museum, founded in 1884 on the initiative of Björn Bjarnarson, in a former ice house on Fríkirkjuvegur since 1987 and also in Safnahúsið. An expert report of April 2024 found its storage and exhibition space inadequate and its purchase budget too small to collect Icelandic art history; the culture minister told the cabinet on 10 January 2025 the situation was unacceptable, and a new building has been costed at ISK 15 billion (The Art Newspaper, 16 October 2024).

f: A public limited company owned by the Icelandic state (54%) and the City of Reykjavík (46%). The owners' operating contribution was ISK 601 million in 2024 and ISK 600 million in 2025, beside income from operations of ISK 1,858.9 million in 2024; the two owners also pay monthly on the bonds that financed the building, until 2046.
w: Reykjavík's concert hall and conference centre, opened in May 2011 after building stopped in October 2008 and resumed in March 2009 on a decision of the state and the city; it is home to the Iceland Symphony Orchestra and the Icelandic Opera. In May 2018, 20 service workers quit over pay cuts after the director received a 20% rise, the union VR vowed a boycott, and the director then asked for her rise to be rescinded (The Reykjavík Grapevine, 8 and 9 May 2018).
why: Twenty service workers quit in May 2018 over pay cuts imposed while the director received a 20% pay rise; the singer Ellen Kristjánsdóttir and the labour union VR vowed to boycott the hall (The Reykjavík Grapevine, 8 and 9 May 2018).

f: A public-law corporation carried by the Federal Republic of Germany under the law of 1 May 2005; its site carries the line 'Gefördert durch Der Beauftragte der Bundesregierung für Kultur und Medien'. A friends' society, the Gesellschaft der Freunde der Akademie der Künste, pays for exhibitions, purchases, publications and young artists. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: An artists' society founded in 1696, with six sections, a president elected by the members (Manos Tsangaris since May 2024) and an archive of more than 1,400 artists' estates. On 29 August 2024 it asked the Bundestag to suspend its planned antisemitism resolution, saying the text put artistic freedom at risk; the Bundestag adopted the resolution on 7 November 2024.

Named project funders are the Kulturstiftung des Bundes (Theatertreffen, MaerzMusik), the Hauptstadtkulturfonds (MaerzMusik), a federal youth ministry (Treffen junge Szene), Berliner Sparkasse and Van Cleef & Arpels. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The federal government's festival house in Berlin: Theatertreffen, Musikfest Berlin, MaerzMusik, Jazzfest Berlin and the Gropius Bau, directed by Matthias Pees. The Minister of State for Culture chairs the supervisory board of its parent company, which also runs the Berlinale and the Haus der Kulturen der Welt.

f: Funded by the state of Berlin as an institutionally funded stage in the culture budget (chapter 0810, title 68246); a Senate answer of 26 March 2025 lists EUR 508,938 for it in the 2025 distribution of funds for pay settlements. The pages read did not state the yearly grant.
w: A Berlin state theatre at Am Festungsgraben, led by artistic director Çağla Ilk with managing director Torben Schumacher. In 2021 staff complaints of abuse of power against the then artistic director Shermin Langhoff reached the press and a dramaturge's case ended in a settlement with EUR 15,000 severance.

f: Part of the Stiftung Oper in Berlin, funded by the state of Berlin; a Senate answer of 26 March 2025 lists EUR 4,945,748 for the foundation as a whole in the 2025 distribution of funds for pay settlements. The renovation of the house was planned at EUR 239 million (federal government 200, friends' association 30, Berlin 9) and stood at about EUR 400 million by May 2015. The pages read did not state the yearly grant.
w: An opera house on Unter den Linden opened in 1742, home of the Staatskapelle Berlin, led by Elisabeth Sobotka with Christian Thielemann as general music director. A parliamentary inquiry reported in June 2016 on the cost and time overruns of its renovation; Daniel Barenboim, music director from 1992, resigned at the end of January 2023.

f: Carried by the Free State of Bavaria, which the German Music Information Centre names as its 'Träger' under public sponsorship. The pages read did not state amounts or name corporate sponsors.
w: Bavaria's state opera in the Nationaltheater in Munich (2,101 seats), led by Staatsintendant Serge Dorny with Vladimir Jurowski as music director. It ended Anna Netrebko's engagement in March 2022 over her closeness to Vladimir Putin and in March 2026 announced her return for a recital on 23 July 2027.

f: A municipal enterprise of the City of Munich: the city's operating grant for the 2024/25 business year was EUR 40,246 thousand, against EUR 3,260 thousand in sales and EUR 714 thousand in donations and other grants; the year closed with a deficit of EUR 830 thousand (annual accounts 2024/25). The city cut the grant by EUR 2,100 thousand during the year as part of its budget consolidation.
w: Munich's city theatre on Maximilianstraße, led by Barbara Mundel, run in one municipal enterprise with the Schauburg children's theatre and the Otto-Falckenberg-Schule. The accounts report 159,524 spectators at 1,012 performances and events in 2024/25 and occupancy up from 60.5 % to 65.5 %.

f: The annual report for 2024/25 lists a public base grant (Basisabgeltung) of EUR 56,144,000 against sales of EUR 13,784,510, of which ticket income was EUR 10.6 million. The main sponsors named on its site are JP Immobilien, Wiener Städtische and Casinos Austria.
w: A spoken theatre on the Ring in Vienna, part of the Austrian federal theatres group, with the Akademietheater as second stage. The Rechnungshof reported in May 2016 that debt rose from EUR 11.83 million to EUR 30.56 million between 2007/08 and 2012/13 and that no receipts existed for EUR 14.62 million of advances; director Matthias Hartmann was dismissed in 2014.
why: Casinos Austria, named as a main sponsor on the Burgtheater's support page (opened 15 November 2026), describes itself on its own site as one of the leading gambling companies, with twelve casino locations.

f: Part of the KHM-Museumsverband; the Kunsthistorisches Museum has administered it since 2001 and handles its sponsoring and fundraising. The pages read did not state who funds the group, amounts or sponsors.
w: Vienna's ethnological museum in the Neue Burg, with about 200,000 objects, directed by Claudia Banz since the start of 2025. It holds the Aztec feather headdress known as the penacho, which Mexico has sought to show at home since 1991; the museum says the object cannot be transported.

f: A private museum run as a private foundation and, by its own statement, 'zur Gänze eigenfinanziert': the money is the fortune of Heidi Goëss-Horten (1941 to 2022), partial heir of the department store owner Helmut Horten, plus ticket income (EUR 18 full price). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Opened in June 2022 in the Hanuschhof in Vienna to show the collection Heidi Goëss-Horten built from 1987. The museum states that Helmut Horten bought department stores from Jewish owners between 1936 and 1939, held stakes in two armaments companies and approved the use of forced labourers, and that the fortune behind the collection rests on those foundations; Christie's called off further sales of her jewellery in August 2023 after criticism.

f: A limited company whose sole shareholder is the state of Salzburg. Its 2025 accounts show sales of EUR 1,676,050.14 and other operating income of EUR 6,070,105.55, with a surplus of EUR 648,177.71; the accounts do not break the other income down by payer. Named sponsors and patrons are fürst developments, Salzburg AG and the gallerist Thaddaeus Ropac.
w: Salzburg's state museum of modern and contemporary art on the Mönchsberg and in the Rupertinum, founded in 1983 with the 'Schenkung Welz' and directed by Harald Krejci. It has held the Generali Foundation collection, about 2,100 works, on permanent loan since 2014; the president of the state parliament chairs its supervisory board.

The cantonal parliament approved CHF 7 million for repairs on 9 June 2022. The pages read did not state the canton's yearly amount.
w: A museum and research centre for Paul Klee in a Renzo Piano building in Bern, opened on 20 June 2005 at a cost of about CHF 110 million, founded by Maurice E. Müller and Martha Müller-Lüthi with Klee's heirs. In June 2022 the cantonal parliament dropped a proposed CHF 600,000 cut to its yearly contribution but tied future contributions to energy savings.

f: A public-law foundation (FONDAMCO, since 1 January 2005) that brings together the private Fondation MAMCO, the Canton of Geneva and the City of Geneva; multi-year partners are also the Fondation Leenaards, the Fondation genevoise de bienfaisance Valeria Rossi di Montelera and JTI. The renovation of its building costs CHF 66 million: CHF 44 million in city credits approved in October 2024 and CHF 22 million in private gifts raised by the Fondation MAMCO.
w: Geneva's museum of modern and contemporary art, opened in 1994 by eight founders gathered in the Fondation MAMCO, with a collection of nearly 6,000 works, directed by Lionel Bovier since 2016. Its building has been closed for works since early 2025, with projects held off site; the tobacco company JTI is among its six multi-year partners.

f: Grant-in-Aid from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport was £3.347m in 2024-25 (£4.353m in 2023-24), 40% of income; total income was £8.315m, with donations and legacies £1.883m, other trading activities £2.019m and exhibition and other charitable income £0.657m. A permanent endowment fund stood at £10.927m at 31 March 2025.
w: A national museum in Hertford House holding 5,637 works bequeathed under Lady Wallace's will of 1897, run by trustees as a non-departmental public body of DCMS. A Charity Commission order in 2019 ended the long-standing reading of the will as a ban on loans, and in 2021 a plan to close the library and archive to the public was dropped after a petition of almost 30,000 signatures.

f: IWM, the five-site group that includes IWM London, had total income of £79.010m in 2025-26: Grant-in-Aid from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport £35.564m (44%), admissions at its charging sites £18.261m, commercial income £11.681m, fees £6.553m and external grants, donations and sponsorship £4.518m. Corporate supporters named for the year include BAE Systems and Bloomberg Philanthropies.
w: The national museum of war and conflict since 1914, founded in 1917 and run by trustees as a non-departmental public body of DCMS. In 2025 it closed the Lord Ashcroft Gallery, built with a £5m gift from Michael Ashcroft in 2010, to make room for post-1945 galleries, and it says the cost of caring for its collections is £8 million a year above its Grant-in-Aid.
