f: The city museum runs the PolArt residency and holds about 80,000 objects. Nornickel funds its new Arctic Museum of Modern Art in full, RUB 3B of RUB 150B it put into Norilsk.
w: Nornickel also backs its exhibitions and courses; AMMA, in a former shopping centre, was due to open in 2026.
tn: Nornickel, which pays for its new museum building, was ordered to pay 146 billion rubles for the 2020 Norilsk diesel spill.

f: The Altes Museum is one of the Staatliche Museen zu Berlin. The pages read did not state who funds it or give amounts.
w: Karl Friedrich Schinkel's building of 1823 to 1830 on the Lustgarten shows the Antikensammlung and part of the Münzkabinett. The collection grew from the art holdings of the Brandenburg electors and Prussian kings (museum website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the Bauhaus-Archiv or give amounts. The Gropius building is being renovated and extended by Staab Architekten; a Berlin development site reported on 9 February 2026 that completion had moved from autumn 2025 to the end of 2026, with public opening in 2027.
w: The main building on Klingelhöferstraße is closed; the museum shows its work at the Temporary Bauhaus-Archiv and calls itself the owner of the world's largest Bauhaus collection. Brigitte Franzen became director in April 2026 (Entwicklungsstadt, 9 February 2026).

f: The collection began as a gift to the State of Berlin by Karl Schmidt-Rottluff. taz reported on 5 March 2021 that the Berlin Senate had confirmed funding for the museum's plan to decolonise its work. The pages read did not state budget figures.
w: The museum opened on 15 September 1967. Schmidt-Rottluff's estate holds about 100 objects from colonial contexts, which the museum has been reappraising and digitising since January 2021.

f: The Deutsches Theater is one of Berlin's state-owned stages.
w: Iris Laufenberg has led the house since summer 2023. In 2025 the staff representations of the Berlin state theatres opened a letter against a planned change of their legal form.

f: Public: Berlin pays through the Stiftung Oper in Berlin, whose state grant is listed at EUR 174,357,000 for 2026 and EUR 180,798,000 for 2027 in a Berlin parliament committee document. The Komische Oper's co-directors said in November 2024 that a 9% cut to 2025 operations applied; renovation of the Behrenstraße house is estimated at around EUR 500 million (Tagesspiegel, 19 December 2024).
w: The company has played at the Schillertheater in Charlottenburg since 2023 while its main house is renovated. Berlin's 2025 culture cut of about EUR 130 million led it to cancel a planned tent production in January 2025.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the Deutsche Oper or give amounts for it. A Berlin parliament committee document lists the state grant to the Stiftung Oper in Berlin, Berlin's opera foundation, at EUR 174,357,000 for 2026.
w: Aviel Cahn is named as Intendant on the opera's site, which also names Maxime Pascal, Michele Spotti and Titus Engel as its conductors.

f: A Friends association and a foundation founded in 1977 support it (theatre website).
w: Joachim Lux was Intendant from 2009 to 2025; Sonja Anders has led it since the 2025/26 season, with Tom Till as managing director, whose contract the supervisory board extended to 2031 on 4 July 2025.

f: The Bayerisches Staatsschauspiel is a Bavarian state theatre; the Free State of Bavaria is funding a new rehearsal and workshop centre for it with a total budget of roughly EUR 196 million (Bavarian building ministry, 2024).
w: The Staatsschauspiel plays at the Residenztheater, the Marstall and the Cuvilliéstheater. Its new production centre in Bogenhausen was topped out in December 2024, with completion planned for December 2026.

f: Mainly public: the City of Zurich paid CHF 39,607,500 in 2023/24 out of total operating revenue of CHF 48,214,123, with CHF 1,540,140 from sponsors and supporters, CHF 3,242,919 from ticket sales and CHF 515,000 from the Gemeinnütziger Fonds of the Canton of Zurich (annual report 2023/24).
w: A stock company in which the City of Zurich holds 37.7% and the Canton of Zurich 13.3%. The board did not renew the contracts of co-directors Nicolas Stemann and Benjamin von Blomberg, who say the city withheld Covid-era funds (The Art Newspaper, 11 June 2024).
nodes: Gemeinnütziger Fonds of the Canton of Zurich

f: Annual budget of EUR 27 million (five-season average), of which EUR 6.94 million subsidies (40% Republic of Austria, 35% Land Vorarlberg, 25% Stadt Bregenz) and EUR 1.3 million sponsors and donations (festival facts and figures, 2025). Main sponsors: Casinos Austria, Hypo Vorarlberg, illwerke vkw AG and Mercedes-Benz Österreich.
w: A non-profit GmbH owned by the Bregenzer Festspiele Privatstiftung. Tiroler Tageszeitung reported that the federal government, the state and the town cut its subsidies by 30% for 2025 and 2026, EUR 2.1 million a year.

f: Run by UniCredit Bank Austria, which said on 9 December 2024 it would end the operation; Signa was both the landlord of the Freyung building and the long-standing main sponsor (Salzburg24, 9 December 2024). On 2 February 2025 a transition period was reported as financially secured while new financing with the advisory board and the new owner of the building was developed (LEADERSnet).
w: Bank Austria ended its engagement at the end of 2025, as previously announced, and said it would support cultural and social initiatives instead of operating a museum. The house reported about 230,000 visitors a year and about 20 permanent staff.

f: A private foundation of Francesca Thyssen-Bornemisza (named by The Art Newspaper in 2020 as Francesca von Habsburg); the pages read give no budget or donor list. Ocean Space in Venice is funded by TBA21-Academy, which the foundation set up, and its restoration was led through the foundation as part of her philanthropic work.
w: Headquarters are in Madrid, with an office in Vienna, Ocean Space in the church of San Lorenzo in Venice and the Alligator Head Foundation in Jamaica.

f: The museum's site links to a City of Zurich culture page for it; the pages read did not state who funds it or give amounts.
w: On 20 March 2026 the city transferred ownership of 11 Benin objects held at the museum to Nigeria; the museum led the Benin Initiative Schweiz, which examined 96 artefacts in Swiss collections.

f: A private foundation created by the engineer Léonard Gianadda after his brother Pierre died in 1976. The pages read did not state its budget or funders; its site lists three bodies, the Fondation Pierre Gianadda, the Fondation Annette et Léonard Gianadda and the Fondation Léonard Gianadda Mécénat, and an Amis de la Fondation membership.
w: Léonard Gianadda died on 3 December 2023 aged 88; the pages read did not say who runs the foundation now.

f: The Canton of Vaud's information office put the project's cost at about CHF 186 million, of which CHF 75 million was raised from the private sector, and called it a public-private partnership with the City of Lausanne, the CFF and patrons (press release, 19 June 2022).
w: A district of three cantonal museums, the MCBA, mudac and Photo Elysée, opened in stages: the MCBA building in 2019 and the other two in 2022.
nodes: Canton of Vaud's information office put the project

f: The City of Lausanne is paying CHF 7,250,000 of the renovation of the Hermitage house, and the Fondation de l'Hermitage CHF 5,200,000, which it is to raise from patron foundations and sponsors (Préavis 2026/46, 9 July 2026).
w: The museum has been closed since 10 November 2025 for renovation, with works planned from March 2026 to January 2028.

f: The pages read do not state the museum's budget or operating foundation. Its predecessor company Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance bought Van Gogh's Sunflowers at Christie's London in 1987 for $39.9m including fees (The Art Newspaper, 16 December 2022). Sompo Holdings is the defendant in the Sunflowers restitution suit.
w: A Tokyo museum run in the Sompo insurance group's name; its Van Gogh Sunflowers has been the subject of a US restitution suit by heirs of the Berlin banker Paul von Mendelssohn-Bartholdy since December 2022, dismissed for lack of jurisdiction in June 2024 and upheld on appeal in November 2025.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum.
w: A museum and Japanese garden founded by Zenko Adachi, with Yokoyama Taikan listed first among its artists; the site cites a garden ranking and a Michelin Green Guide three-star rating.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The page read names Special Corporate Sponsors for 2026/2027, including Onward, Toyota, TBS and Nippon Life, and a Patronage and Support section; it does not give amounts or the public subsidy.
w: Japan's national theatre for opera, ballet and dance, and drama, run by the New National Theatre Foundation (president Zeniya Masami); it opened in autumn 1997.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The Korea War Memorial Organization, a state-affiliated agency, runs the memorial; the Korea Times article read did not say how it is funded.
w: A state-affiliated agency's war museum in Yongsan; in June 2026 it removed a poster and a Dandong memorial hall stop that gave China's account of the Korean War, and the Defense Ministry opened an inspection on 15 June 2026.
nodes: Korea Times article read did not say how it

f: The page read says the museum was founded through a donation from the businessman Sato Keitaro, known as the coal god; it did not state the current operator or funding.
w: Opened in 1926 as Japan's first public art museum, with a founding gift from Sato Keitaro (museum website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: In 2003 the Guangdong provincial authorities committed 884.2 million yuan (about $129.39 million) to build the new facility (China Daily). The page read did not state operating funding.
w: The provincial museum of Guangdong; the older museum opened in 1959 and a new 67,000 square metre building was funded by the provincial government.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. The Jiangsu provincial government and its culture bodies supervise it, per the 2026 probe reporting.
w: In February 2026 a probe into the 1959 donation of 137 paintings by the Pang family found works sold off in the 1990s; the museum apologised, 29 people were implicated and the National Cultural Heritage Administration ordered a nationwide museum audit.

n: Sejong Center for the Performing Arts
f: The Asia Economy interview read did not give the total budget or funding sources; it says the six resident arts groups account for 42% of the budget.
w: A performing arts centre in Gwanghwamun run with six resident groups (traditional orchestra, dance, choir, musical, theatre, opera); Ahn Hosang became president in 2021.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: National Centre for the Performing Arts (NCPA)
f: The page read did not state funding.
w: Beijing's national performing arts complex, designed by the French architect Paul Andreu, opened at the end of 2007 with its own chorus, orchestra and opera singers.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The four-year renovation that ended with the reopening on 29 May 2021 is given as a budget of 58,327,000 euros in the museum's press kit and 58.3 million euros by The Art Newspaper France; another page of the same kit gives about 52 million euros, financed by a City of Paris subsidy of more than 46 million euros plus subsidies from the Ministry of Culture and the Région Île-de-France. Named major patrons were the Caisse d'Épargne Île-de-France, the Fondation ENGIE and Free (museum press kit).
w: A City of Paris museum (one of the Paris Musées network) in two Marais mansions, closed in 2016 and reopened on 29 May 2021; permanent collections are free. The money is mostly municipal, with named bank, foundation and telecom patrons for the renovation.

f: The six-year renovation that ended with the October 2015 reopening was budgeted at 92 million euros and paid by the French Ministry of Higher Education and Research (The Art Newspaper, 19 October 2015). The pages read do not state the museum's current annual funding.
w: An anthropology museum in the Palais de Chaillot, part of the Muséum national d'histoire naturelle. It holds about 23,000 human remains (National Assembly report, 10 June 2026); 24 skulls were handed to Algeria in July 2020 and a bill passed by the Senate would release six Kali'na and Arawak people exhibited in 1892.
nodes: Museo Nazionale della Scienza e della Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci

n: Cité de l'architecture et du patrimoine
f: In 2021 State subsidies were 18,182,843 euros, of which 17,297,276 euros was the Ministry of Culture's public service grant; own resources were 3,716,561 euros (16.7 percent), including 455,440 euros of patronage and partnerships (2021 activity report).
w: A national institution under the Ministry of Culture in the Palais de Chaillot, home to the Musée des Monuments français casts, a contemporary architecture gallery, the École de Chaillot and an architecture archive centre. Own income fell sharply in the 2020 closure and the Ministry added an exceptional 500,000 euros at the end of 2021.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A not-for-profit association (loi 1901) that receives subsidies from the City of Paris (legal notice); in 2022 the Paris Council voted 185,000 euros to it (35,000 under Art pour Grandir, 150,000 for the Bureau du Spectacle). Partners named in the 2026-27 brochure include Van Cleef & Arpels (Dance Reflections), the Fondation d'entreprise Hermès, the Gulbenkian Foundation's French delegation and the Caisse des Dépôts.
w: A Paris theatre and dance house on the Place du Châtelet and at Les Abbesses, run by director Emmanuel Demarcy-Mota, who also leads its resident troupe. It worked from the Espace Cardin while the Châtelet theatre was renovated from 2016.
nodes: Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki

f: A public cultural cooperation body (EPCC) of the City of Paris and, since 2019, the commune of Pantin. Its 2026 budget as approved on 16 January 2026 has 17,751,780 euros of operating income, including 9,416,153 euros of operating subsidies (10,096,738 euros the year before) and 4,741,753 euros of sales and services.
w: An artistic establishment of the City of Paris with artist residencies and a programme of shows and exhibitions. Its board attached the 2026 budget to a possible extra City subsidy to be voted by the Paris Council; director Valérie Senghor was appointed in 2025.

f: In 2025 operating revenue was 45.5 million euros against 47.4 million euros of spending: a public service subsidy of 22.28 million euros (48.9 percent), other subsidies 1.9 million euros (4.2 percent) and own resources 21.3 million euros (46.9 percent), a balance of minus 1.9 million euros (2025 activity report).
w: The public body running the Parc de la Villette and the Grande Halle; its 2025 report states 2025 was the last year of its 2020-2025 performance contract, that the previous governance left that year and that a new president, Claire Landais, was named in January 2026. It also records provisions for disputes arising from hosting the Paris 2024 Games.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The museum belongs to the Institut de France, which received it by bequest in 1912, and is run by the private operator Culturespaces under a concession, renewed in 2023 for five years (The Art Newspaper France, 15 June 2023). The pages read do not state fees, accounts or sponsors' amounts.
w: A private mansion museum on Boulevard Haussmann bequeathed to the Institut de France by Nélie Jacquemart in 1912 and open since 8 December 1913. Culturespaces has managed it since 1996; it closed from 1 August 2023 to 1 September 2024 for works led by the Institut de France.

f: The museum is one of the foundations of the Académie des Beaux-Arts, to which Paul Marmottan left his house and collections in 1932; its holdings grew by gifts and bequests from the Monet, Rouart, Donop de Monchy and other families (museum website).
w: A Paris museum in a former townhouse with the largest Monet holding, owned and governed by the Académie des Beaux-Arts, which elected Pierre-Antoine Gatier director on 15 October 2025 to succeed Erik Desmazières. A portrait long held as a Monet self-portrait was reattributed to Charles Giron in 2020.

f: Owned by the Institut de France; a foundation chaired by the Aga Khan financed restoration under a 2006 partnership with a commitment of 30 million euros over 2006 to 2025 (Ministry of Culture reply to the Senate, 10 September 2020), and the Ministry committed 0.8 million euros a year for ten years, 40 percent of planned works. The State gave an exceptional 4.5 million euros in 2021 (The Art Newspaper France, 25 March 2021).
w: A château and art museum bequeathed by the duc d'Aumale to the Institut de France, with a condition that the collection not be loaned. It lost about 5 million euros in 2020 (Public Sénat, 6 January 2021) and Time Out reported on 29 January 2026 a fundraising campaign for a 68 million euro renovation, noting that Aga Khan funding ended in 2020.

f: A public establishment under the Ministry of Culture. The Abu Dhabi Authority for Tourism and Culture committed 10 million euros from 2007 to restore the Imperial Theatre, about 5 million euros of it spent by 2014 (Carenews, 2017); Rolex has funded clock restoration since 2008, 110,000 euros then and 50,000 euros in 2015 (Carenews, 17 February 2017). The works master plan running since 2015 is supported by the Ministry, which validated its phase 3 programme in October 2025 (Ministry reply, 9 June 2026).
w: A royal and imperial château in Seine-et-Marne, run as a State establishment. The Imperial Theatre was restored with Abu Dhabi money and renamed after Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan; the Chinese Museum was burgled in 2015, a theft Napoleon.org described in 2020 as unsolved, and a further attempt was foiled in late 2019.
why: The Abu Dhabi Authority for Tourism and Culture, a government body of the United Arab Emirates, committed a 10 million euro sponsorship in 2007 to restore the Imperial Theatre, which was renamed after the UAE leader Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan (Carenews, 2017).
nodes: The Abu Dhabi Authority for Tourism and Culture, a government body of the United Arab Emirates, committed a 10 million euro sponsorship in 2007 to restore the Imperial Theatre, which was renamed after the UAE leader Sheikh Khalifa bin Zayed Al Nahyan (Carenews, 2017).

f: The extension was estimated at 24.5 million euros, financed by the State 4.9 million, the Alsace regional council 4.2 million, the Haut-Rhin departmental council 3.3 million, the City of Colmar (agglomeration) 6.852 million, the Société Schongauer 1.75 million and patronage 3.5 million euros (Ministry of Culture written answer, 13th legislature). The Société Schongauer, an association, has managed the museum since 1853 (2025 press kit).
w: A museum in a thirteenth-century Dominican convent in Colmar holding the Isenheim Altarpiece, run since 1853 by the Société Schongauer; the City of Colmar was owner of the works for the extension by Herzog & de Meuron opened on 12 December 2015.

f: The six-year renovation and extension by Stanton Williams, reopened on 23 June 2017, cost 48.8 million euros according to The Spaces; the pages read do not name its funders.
w: A fine arts museum founded in 1800, in a nineteenth-century palace and a seventeenth-century chapel, with a 4,000 square metre Cube for contemporary art added in 2017. The only cost figure is 48.8 million euros for the 2017 works.

f: One of 11 museums run by the City of Nice (museum website).
w: A city museum of modern and contemporary art, closed since 7 January 2024 for renovation; the first architect's contract was ended and a new consultation launched in early 2025, with a reopening target of 2029. Céline Kopp became director on 1 January 2026.

f: Works from 2018 to 2025 totalled 25 million euros, financed by the City of Toulouse with 587,630 euros from the DRAC and 581,899 euros from the Occitanie regional council (press kit, December 2025). The cloister restoration is also funded by a crowdfunding campaign (press kit).
w: A municipal fine arts museum in a fourteenth-century Augustinian convent, partly reopened on 19 December 2025 after works that began in 2018; the church reopens in autumn 2027 and the grand cloister is being restored with a public appeal.

f: State-owned and managed directly by the Ministry of Culture since 1993; the Fundación Museo Sorolla works with it. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: The house of the painter Joaquín Sorolla, left to the Spanish State by the will of his widow Clotilde García del Castillo (1925, accepted 1931). The Casa Museo is closed for rehabilitation work and visits are limited to the extension building at Calle Zurbano 68.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Run by the Fundación Lázaro Galdiano, F.S.P., a public-sector foundation with the Ministerio de Cultura y Deporte logo on its site; its budgets and audited accounts for 2021 to 2024 are published. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: A public collection of private origin in the Palacio de Parque Florido, Calle Serrano, opened to the public on 27 January 1951. Its transparency page states that the Tribunal de Cuentas has never audited the foundation.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Ministerio de Cultura y Deporte logo on its site

f: Run by the Fundació Orfeó Català - Palau de la Música Catalana. Its 2021 budget shows 2,715,000 euros from sales and services, 1,272,000 euros from promotions, sponsors and collaborations, 1,688,778 euros from official subsidies and donations (2,368,156 in 2020) and 300,000 euros from the Orfeó Català; the site shows Fundació Banc Sabadell, Fundació Damm, Fundació la Caixa, Fundació Salvat, the Ministerio de Cultura (INAEM) and UNESCO logos.
w: A concert hall in Barcelona whose former president Fèlix Millet and treasurer Jordi Montull were convicted for taking more than 23 million euros from its accounts between 2000 and 2009; the court also found 6.6 million euros in commissions went to the party CDC through the Palau.
nodes: Fundació Orfeó Català - Palau de la Música Catalana

f: Municipal: since September 2024 it is managed by the Málaga city agency that also runs Casa Natal Picasso, Centre Pompidou Málaga and the Museo Ruso, whose 2026 budget is 16,813,500 euros, of which the Ayuntamiento de Málaga transfers 13,794,013.28 euros and private sponsors 300,000 euros.
w: Málaga's municipal contemporary art centre, merged with the MUPAM into MUCAC under the city's public agency; the memorandum for 2026 states the former CAC building, MUCAC Mayoristas, stays closed in 2026 for a full refurbishment by the city's urban planning office.

f: Run by the Fundación Palacio de Villalón. The 2026 plan budgets 5,253,251 euros of income: 2,292,531 euros from the Ayuntamiento de Málaga under a 2011 agreement, 1,200,000 euros from tickets, 690,000 euros from the shop, 255,000 euros from sponsors and 140,000 euros from Friends.
w: Shows the Colección Carmen Thyssen Bornemisza, lent free of charge to the foundation under a loan contract, in municipal buildings granted to it; the city guarantees the museum's budget balance by a 9 June 2011 agreement.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: TEA Tenerife Espacio de las Artes
f: The pages read did not state who funds TEA or in what amounts.
w: An arts centre in a building by the Swiss architects Jacques Herzog and Pierre de Meuron with the Canarian architect Virgilio Gutiérrez, holding a main collection, the Óscar Domínguez collection and the Isla de Tenerife photography centre collection.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A state museum; the pages read did not state its budget or funders, and its site links an annual report and a support-us page.
w: Home of the Farnese, Egyptian, Pompeii, epigraphic and numismatic collections. In July 2025 Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli named Francesco Sirano its director in a late-night announcement of five directors; Paolo Giulierini had been reconfirmed director in July 2019.

f: A state site on a cultura.gov.it domain; the pages read did not state its budget or funders.
w: The Bourbon royal palace begun in 1752 to a design by Luigi Vanvitelli and a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1997. Its first director under the 2016 reform, Mauro Felicori, was at the centre of a union row in March 2016 and left on 31 October 2018 at the retirement age.

n: Gallerie Nazionali di Arte Antica (Palazzo Barberini and Galleria Corsini)
f: A Ministry of Culture museum: funded by Ministry transfers plus own income from tickets (1,200,000 euros budgeted for 2023), shop, concessions, loan fees, Art Bonus donations and sponsorships.
w: Two state galleries in Rome run as one institute. Its director Flaminia Gennari Santori was in her eighth and last year in 2023 and Luigi Gallo, director of the Galleria Nazionale delle Marche, was named acting director in November 2023.
nodes: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia

f: A private-law foundation whose founders are the Italian State, Roma Capitale and Regione Lazio, with Acea and the Rome Chamber of Commerce as private members; the Ministry of Culture sheet gives the burden on its budget as 24,702,197 euros for 2025. Ticket income was above 14.3 million euros in 2024 (estimate).
w: Rome's opera house, whose board decided on 2 October 2014 to outsource its orchestra and chorus and start collective dismissals of 182 workers; an agreement with unions on 18 and 19 November 2014 avoided them.

f: A private-law foundation; the Ministry of Culture sheet gives the burden on its budget as 15,645,729 euros for 2025, and its board is chaired by the Mayor of Naples with seats for the Città metropolitana, Regione Campania and the Ministry.
w: Naples' opera house. In 2023 a Naples court annulled the government decree ending superintendent Stéphane Lissner's term early; in 2025 the foundation, without a permanent superintendent since March, saw the Ministry-backed choice of Fulvio Macciardi contested by Mayor Gaetano Manfredi.

f: A foundation with the Comune di Milano and Regione Lombardia as founding members; the Ministry of Culture assigned it 5,895,000 euros for 2024 under a rule giving it at least 6.5 percent of the theatre share of the performing arts fund. Its site lists Intesa Sanpaolo, Eni, A2A, Allianz and Fondazione Monte di Lombardia among patrons.
w: Milan's city theatre, directed by Claudio Longhi and run by CEO Lanfranco Li Cauli; Sergio Escobar led it from 1998 to July 2020.
nodes: Fondazione Monte di Lombardia among patrons
Museo Nazionale della Scienza e della Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci

f: In 2024 State contributions were 17,136,793 euros, Comune di Firenze 4,500,000 euros, Regione Toscana 2,900,000 euros, Città Metropolitana 1,550,000 euros, and private contributions 2,932,865 euros including Fondazione CR Firenze 1,000,000 euros and Intesa Sanpaolo 980,443 euros.

A private institution that states it is self-financed with a network of donors, and receives funding from Regione Piemonte and Compagnia di San Paolo, with some projects supported by Fondazione CRT; the building is owned by the City of Turin and granted in concession.
w: A centre for contemporary art named after Mario Merz, established in 2005 and led by Beatrice Merz as president, in the former Officine Lancia power station.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

GAM - Galleria Civica d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino

f: The pages read did not state who funds it.
w: A museum on the roof of the Lingotto, the former Fiat factory, housing 25 works collected by Giovanni Agnelli and Marella Caracciolo and donated in 2002; Sarah Cosulich became director with the programme that opened on 27 May 2022.

f: Part of the Fondazione Torino Musei with GAM and MAO. The foundation's 2022 to 2024 forecast budgets 5,540,000 euros from the Comune di Torino, 1,291,000 euros from Fondazione CRT, 1,500,000 euros from Compagnia di San Paolo and 825,000 euros from Regione Piemonte, of 12,991,000 euros total income for 2022.
w: The old fortress and palace in Piazza Castello, a UNESCO World Heritage site, that houses the Museo Civico d'Arte Antica; the foundation's figures cover its three museums together.
nodes: Castello di Rivoli Museo d Arte Contemporanea
GAM - Galleria Civica d'Arte Moderna e Contemporanea di Torino

f: The state paid most of the costs: La Nación, in an article of 2 November 2003 updated on 5 June 2020, gave the state 82% of total costs, ticket sales 16% and donations and other income about 2%. The Fundación Teatro Colón raises member and patron money, and the theatre's site names Banco Ciudad as its main sponsor ally.
w: Opera house in Buenos Aires with its own orchestra, choir and ballet and a training institute. In 2024 its director Jorge Telerman presented an austerity season with fewer costly international contracts (La Nación, 15 February 2024).

f: The state of Amazonas, through its Culture and Creative Economy Secretariat, runs it. In July 2024 Iphan agreed to transfer R$ 1.35 million under the PAC Seleções programme for design work, R$ 750 thousand of it for the theatre's restoration design (Portal Amazônia, 31 July 2024).
w: Opera house in Manaus tied to the rubber boom, listed by Iphan since 1966. Brazil put it forward with Belém's Theatro da Paz for UNESCO World Heritage in a candidacy made official on 31 January 2025 (CNN Brasil, 2 February 2025).
nodes: PAC Seleções programme for design work

f: The Fundação Osesp, an Organização Social de Cultura, runs the hall and the orchestra under a management contract with the São Paulo State Culture Secretariat (Tribunal de Contas do Estado de São Paulo, 12 March 2020). The pages read did not state the contract's amount.
w: Concert hall of the Orquestra Sinfônica do Estado de São Paulo, run since 2005 by the Fundação Osesp, which also runs the Campos do Jordão winter festival and a music documentation centre.

n: Theatro Municipal do Rio de Janeiro
f: A state house: the Fundação Theatro Municipal is tied to the Rio de Janeiro state culture secretariat, and its pay depends on state transfers. In 2017 the state finance secretariat said salary delays reflected a shortage of funds; a union leader said in July 2018 that R$ 53 million meant for programming and upkeep had not been transferred.
w: Opera house in central Rio with its own orchestra, chorus and ballet. A state fiscal crisis left staff unpaid for months in 2017 and cancelled a Swan Lake season (Agência Brasil, 1 November 2017).

f: The 2022 restoration cost R$ 235 million from public and private sources, of which R$ 187 million was raised through the Lei Rouanet (CartaCapital, 8 September 2022); Agência Brasil gives R$ 34 million from São Paulo state, R$ 25 million from BNDES and R$ 183 million authorised under the Lei Rouanet. Today Shell and Vale are named as maintainers and Itaú as master sponsor.
w: University of São Paulo museum in the Independence monument building, closed in 2013 and reopened in September 2022. The reopening became a fight between the São Paulo state government and the federal culture secretariat over permission and branding (CartaCapital, 8 September 2022).

f: Run by the Associação Museu Afro Brasil as an Organização Social of the São Paulo state under a management contract with the State Culture Secretariat since 2009 (museum's own museological plan). In 2020 the state cut transfers to the Organizações Sociais by 14%, R$ 68 million, and the museum dismissed 23 of its 80 staff (Alma Preta, 20 May 2020).
w: Museum of Afro-Brazilian art and history in Ibirapuera Park, founded by the artist Emanoel Araujo and opened on 23 October 2004. In June 2025 its director Hélio Menezes was removed after just over a year, and two board members resigned (ArtReview, 30 June 2025).

f: Paraná's State Secretariat of Culture allocated R$ 3,129,379.00 to the museum in 2024 (Arte Brasileiros, 15 October 2024). The Friends of MON Association (AAMON) rents spaces for private events and the museum says that income funds its activities.
w: State museum in Curitiba in a building designed by Oscar Niemeyer, opened in 2002. In October 2024 a private wedding for the daughter of a state audit court member drew conflict-of-interest criticism (Arte Brasileiros, 15 October 2024).

f: A private family-run trust owns and runs it; the trust documents name a fund originally contributed by Mexico's Ministry of Finance and Public Credit (The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2025). The Art Newspaper says journalist Adriana Malvido states the museum receives a US$450,000 fee for Kahlo and Rivera loans.
w: Museum in the La Noria hacienda in Xochimilco, opened in 1994 by the collector Dolores Olmedo, with more than 140 Rivera and 25 Kahlo works. Closed in 2020, it faced an open letter and a protest in July 2025 over changes made in 2020 to the trust and a planned move of the collection (The Art Newspaper, 16 July 2025).

f: A non-profit cultural trust administered by Banco de México with a Patronato set up by the collector Franz Mayer; it takes donations through a 'Conservar para el futuro' campaign and memberships (museum website). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Applied arts and design museum in a 16th-century former hospital of the Order of San Juan de Dios, run as a trust administered by the central bank.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: Museo Nacional de Historia, Castillo de Chapultepec
f: Federal: the museum's site is hosted by the Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH) and carries the federal government logo. The pages read did not state a budget or sponsors.
w: National history museum in the castle built in 1785 to 1787 as a viceroy's retreat, later a military academy and Maximilian and Carlota's residence; it opened as a museum in September 1944 (INAH).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The state pays most of it: of M$ 3,341,309 in 2025 revenue (thousand pesos), M$ 2,404,654 came from the budget law through the Ministry of Cultures (MINCAP). The rest was event rental M$ 572,550, concessions M$ 188,907, shop M$ 107,796 and donations M$ 28,000 (financial statements for 2025).
w: Culture centre under the Plaza de la Ciudadanía, run by the Fundación Centro Cultural Palacio de La Moneda, with exhibition halls and a shop and restaurants.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: Museo Nacional de Arqueología, Antropología e Historia del Perú
f: The pages read did not state its funding. It belongs to the Ministry of Culture; in November 2015 Congressman Ramón Kobashigawa said the ministry told him the funds for a new national museum at Pachacámac had been redirected to the El Niño response (Congress of Peru, 10 November 2015).
w: National archaeology and history museum in Pueblo Libre, Lima. In November 2015 a residents' defence front told Congress the Ministry of Culture planned to move the collection to a new museum at Pachacámac and deactivate it (Congress of Peru, 10 November 2015).
nodes: It belongs to the Ministry of Culture

f: The federal government paid for the redevelopment, listed by the ABC at A$550 million in March 2025.
w: National war museum and memorial in Canberra. ABC's Four Corners reported on 10 March 2025 that its chair Kim Beazley holds roles with Luerssen Australia and Lockheed Martin that were not on his disclosure forms; the regulator ACMA later found the programme breached impartiality rules (ABC Media Watch, 2026).
why: ABC News reported on 10 March 2025 that the Memorial has accepted sponsorship from the weapons manufacturers Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Thales, BAE Systems and Northrop Grumman, and that its director said it would keep doing so.

f: The Victorian Government pays more than two fifths: in 2023 to 2024 grants were A$49.710 million of A$112.908 million total revenue and income, with sales of goods and services A$52.724 million and fundraising A$4.939 million (Annual Report 2023 to 2024). In March 2024 The Ian Potter Foundation gave A$15 million to the State Theatre redevelopment.
w: Performing arts centre in Melbourne, home to the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, The Australian Ballet, Melbourne Theatre Company and Opera Australia, run by the Victorian Arts Centre Trust. The State Theatre closed in March 2024 for redevelopment as part of a A$1.7 billion arts precinct project.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Box office was A$50.7 million of A$106 million total revenue in 2024 (48%); the rest came from Creative Australia, the NSW and Victorian governments, sponsors such as BMW and Qantas, donors and the Opera Australia Capital Fund, which gave A$1.1 million in 2024. It lost A$10.1 million in 2024 (A$6.1 million with the Capital Fund) and returned to break-even in 2025 (annual report 2024; media release on 2025).
w: Australia's largest performing arts company, with more than 1,300 employees, performing at the Sydney Opera House and Arts Centre Melbourne. In 2024 its CEO Fiona Allan and artistic director Jo Davies left and it recorded a A$10.1 million deficit (annual report 2024).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Governments pay more than a third: in 2023 government funding was A$17.0 million of A$45.4 million revenue (Creative Australia A$12,453,495 and Create NSW A$3,872,878), ticket sales A$21.1 million, and sponsorship and donations A$5.6 million (Annual Financial Report 2023).
w: Orchestra based at the Sydney Opera House, with Simone Young as chief conductor; it ran an operating deficit of A$1.75 million in 2023 (A$2.86 million in 2022).

f: A state agency's branch: the Moderna museet agency received SEK 165.1 million in appropriation and SEK 71.4 million in other income (entry fees, sales) in 2023 across Stockholm and Malmö, and the Malmö venue is a three-party arrangement between the City of Malmö, Region Skåne and the Swedish state. The City of Malmö lets the premises rent-free, a value the report puts at about SEK 5.7 million (annual report 2023).
w: Moderna Museet's Malmö branch, opened in December 2009 as a joint project of the state, Region Skåne and the City of Malmö (annual report 2023). Its accounts are the national museum agency's, so Malmö figures are not published separately in the report read.

f: Founded on private money from Björn and Lillemor Jakobson, founders of the baby products firm BabyBjörn; Jakobson declined to give the cost in 2012 and said Artipelag would not go bankrupt even with no visitors (The Art Newspaper, 1 March 2012). Since 2022 the Artipelag Foundation owns it and its statutes tell it to seek donations, sponsorships and other funding; the pages read gave no amounts or donors.
w: Private art venue on Värmdö opened in 2012 by Björn Jakobson and his wife Lillemor, now owned by a foundation.

f: Run by AD-museo Oy, owned by the Finnish Architecture and Design Museum Foundation. In 2025 the foundation received capital calls of EUR 58,000,000 each from the City of Helsinki and the Finnish state, EUR 10,000,000 from the Jane and Aatos Erkko Foundation, and smaller sums from other foundations; donations received in 2025 totalled EUR 129,400,000 (foundation annual report 2025). The report read did not state the museum's operating grants.
w: The former Design Museum and Museum of Finnish Architecture were combined; the old Design Museum site now redirects to admuseo.fi. The foundation is being capitalised for a new museum building on the Makasiinirata site, with a base capital target of EUR 150 million (foundation annual report 2025).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: Museum of Applied Arts Budapest (Iparművészeti Múzeum)
f: State museum. A 2021 contract for the first renovation phase was signed at about HUF 40.208 billion net with Fejér-B.Á.L. and Swietelsky (economx, 13 August 2021); government resolution 1350/2026 of 27 October 2026 sets HUF 827,486,958 of support for preparatory work and a value-preserving demolition (Hungarian Gazette, 27 October 2026).
w: Lechner's building has been closed to the public since 2017 and its renovation stalled; staff protested in July 2025 (444, 22 September 2025). A 2026 government resolution restarts it with a new wing on Hőgyes Endre utca.

f: An institution of the Hungarian Academy of Arts (MMA), to which Parliament transferred the building free of charge on 7 October 2013 (Infostart, 7 October 2013). The pages read did not state its budget or grants.
w: Budapest's exhibition hall since 1896, handed to the state-backed Hungarian Academy of Arts in 2013 to 2014; director Gábor Gulyás resigned in 2012 citing loss of independence and left on 31 August 2013.

n: MMSU, Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art Rijeka
f: Mainly the City of Rijeka and Croatia's Ministry of Culture: in January to June 2024 the City of Rijeka paid EUR 145,266.18 of staff costs for 14 employees and the exhibition programme of EUR 23,804.95 was split EUR 14,471.09 City of Rijeka and EUR 9,333.86 Ministry of Culture (MMSU half-year report 2024).
w: Rijeka's public museum of modern and contemporary art. Its half-year report shows other income was small: the lines for tickets, publications and sponsors were zero or not filled.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A state museum. Its 2018 reopening after 15 years of reconstruction cost EUR 12 million according to N1 (27 June 2018); the page did not say who paid. The pages read gave no current budget.
w: Reopened on 28 June 2018. An earlier reconstruction design was dropped in 2010 after more than EUR 1 million was spent on work that never began (Vreme, 28 April 2010).

f: Public: the Ministry of Culture and National Heritage is its operator and in 2019 to 2023 grants from the Ministry were by far the largest source of income; sponsors gave PLN 9.638 million in 2019 to 2022, 81.4% of it from companies with State Treasury shareholding (NIK, Kontrola Państwowa 4/2024). The museum names PGE and ORLEN as patrons.
w: Poland's Supreme Audit Office (NIK) found irregularities in the museum and in the Ministry's oversight in an audit covering 2019 to 2023; director Łukasz Gaweł was dismissed on 2 February 2024 after the minister cited staff reports of 'managing through conflict' (Rzeczpospolita, 2 February 2024).
nodes: Museum of the Second World War

f: The pages read did not state its funders or budget. The President of Wrocław appoints its acting director, which indicates municipal control (City of Wrocław, 16 January 2020).
w: Museum at pl. Strzegomski 2. Its first director Andrzej Jarosz died on 10 December 2019 and Piotr Lisowski became acting director on 16 January 2020 (City of Wrocław, 16 January 2020).
nodes: President of Wrocław appoints its acting director

f: Funded through the Romanian Ministry of Culture. In 2013 the ministry cut the 2013 budget by 22% and director Sabin Luca said March goods-and-services funding of 21,000 lei covered only electricity (Mediafax, 2 April 2013); in April 2025 interim manager Alexandru Chituță called the approved 2025 budget an insult, with salaries over 9 million of it (G4Media, 2 April 2025).
w: Repeated budget rows with the Ministry: in 2013 the ministry demanded the director's resignation and he refused; in 2025 the interim manager asked to move the museum under Sibiu city hall.

n: National Museum of Art of Romania
f: A public museum under the Ministry of Culture; its site names the Friends of MNAR Association, Banca Transilvania (official partner of the Brâncuși exhibition) and the National Cultural Fund Administration (AFCN, co-funder of a textile exhibition) as partners. The pages read gave no budget figures.
w: Housed in the former Royal Palace. Ex-manager Călin Stegerean won a Bucharest Court of Appeal ruling in June 2026 annulling the ministry's evaluation that ended his term; in 2021 a union accused him of poor management.

f: The pages read did not give its subsidy. Its 2024 cleaning and security contracts were about RUB 235.9 million, up 30% from RUB 163.5 million (Delovoy Peterburg, 25 March 2024). Funds tied to its director Valery Gergiev received almost RUB 2 billion from the federal budget during the war, including RUB 535 million for Russian Seasons in 2024 (Novaya Gazeta Europe, 15 July 2025).
w: Opera, ballet and orchestra house led by Valery Gergiev, who also heads the Bolshoi. After the 2022 invasion Western bodies cut ties with Gergiev, and Italy's Caserta palace cancelled his concert on 21 July 2025.

f: The pages read did not state its funders. A volunteer operation at the museum in March 2022 took donated goods from Europe and the US through a logistics centre in Poland (CIMAM, 7 March 2022).
w: Ukraine's largest art museum with 18 sites; in March 2022 its masterpieces were hidden in the Potocki Palace branch or behind sandbags and the building became a volunteer hub.

f: The Esplanade Co Ltd is a not-for-profit registered charity. In the year to 31 March 2020 it received operating grants of S$37.8 million and a government rental subvention of S$18.4 million, from the Singapore Totalisator Board and the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth, against company income of S$26.6 million (annual report FY2019/20). Singtel gave S$10 million in 2018 and DBS S$3.5 million in 2023 (Esplanade website).
w: Singapore's performing arts centre, opened on 12 October 2002 and run by The Esplanade Co Ltd. Most of its cost is met by government grants; the report states a cost recovery rate of 48% in FY2019/20.

f: Total income was RM20.2 million in 2024, excluding donations, of which RM9.2 million was ticket sales; other lines were hall hire, corporate suite subscribers Mitsubishi Corporation and Mitsui & Co., and a CIMB sponsorship of the youth orchestra.
w: Malaysia's first concert hall for classical music, opened on 17 August 1998 in the Petronas Twin Towers and home of the Malaysian Philharmonic Orchestra. PETRONAS, which calls itself Malaysia's national oil and gas company, is its principal donor.
why: PETRONAS describes itself as Malaysia's national oil and gas company (petronas.com, opened 2026-11-18) and the DFP/MPO Annual Report 2024 names it principal donor and main benefactor of the hall and orchestra.

f: The pages read name the Indonesia Heritage Agency as the body restoring the museum after the fire of 16 September 2023 and give no budget, cost or funder amounts.
w: Indonesia's national museum in Jakarta, reopened on 15 October 2024 after a fire on 16 September 2023 damaged Building A. Its reopening show presents more than 2,500 repatriated objects, about 300 returned from the Netherlands between 1978 and 2023.

f: The page read does not name the funder; it says more than 10 crores a year in allocated funds went unused, per a CAG report of August 2022 as reported by Live History India.
w: A museum in Kolkata with the highest footfall of any museum in India. A CAG audit report of August 2022 found 53.7% of posts vacant, no soft copy of the accession register and storerooms without smoke detectors or sprinklers.

f: Run by the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi; The Art Newspaper (2 Dec 2025) gives no cost or funding figures.
w: A Norman Foster building on Saadiyat Island that opened in December 2025, originally due in 2013; the British Museum ended its 2009 loan deal in October 2017 because construction had not started.

f: Run by the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi; the pages read state no funder, cost or collection value, and its chairman said acquisition prices will likely never be revealed (The Art Newspaper, 2 Dec 2025).
w: A 35,000 sq m museum by Mecanoo on Saadiyat Island, opened in November 2025. Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, chairman of the Department of Culture and Tourism, said acquisition prices will likely never be revealed.

f: The page read names Emaar as master developer and does not state who funds or owns the opera.
w: A 2,000-seat venue in the Opera District, Downtown Dubai, built by master developer Emaar; Emaar chairman Mohammad Alabbar called it a tribute to the city, and Jasper Hope is its chief executive.

f: Saudipedia says the museum is supervised by the Ministry of Culture and that a curators' council headed by the Minister of Culture oversees its development; the pages read give no budget.
w: Saudi Arabia's official museum, opened in 1999 in the King Abdulaziz Historical Center; its director general is Laila Alfaddagh. It hosted Van Cleef & Arpels: Time, Nature, Love, which ran until 15 April 2023.
why: Saudipedia states the museum is supervised by the Ministry of Culture, with a curators' council headed by the Minister of Culture.

f: The page read does not state how the Cairo Opera House is funded.
w: Home of the Egyptian ballet and opera company. In June 2013 its staff went on strike after the head of the opera house was dismissed by the culture minister.

f: Daily Maverick (18 May 2021) describes Robben Island Museum as government-funded, in contrast to the Apartheid Museum; the pages read give no grant amounts. It was established in 1997 by the Department of Arts and Culture.
w: The museum on the island where Nelson Mandela was held, which also manages the Mayibuye Archives. Since 2018 former prisoners and a 2026 complainant have raised ferry procurement and governance, and a 2021 forensic probe recommended discipline against the then CEO, which the council dropped.

f: Gold Reef City paid for construction, about 80 million rand, and leases the building to the museum's Public Benefit Company for the duration of the casino licence; the museum relies on donations, contributions and sponsorships (museum website).
w: A museum on a seven-hectare site beside the Gold Reef City casino complex, opened in 2001 as part of the Akani Egoli (Gold Reef City) casino licence bid; chairman is Dr John Kani. In April 2021 it closed temporarily and journalist Max du Preez said it was running into bankruptcy.

f: The Market Theatre Foundation received about R10 million a year from 28 donors, including Bloomberg Philanthropies, the Goethe-Institut, the US embassy and the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture, plus R8 to 12 million from sponsors and about R5 million from its own goods (Mail & Guardian, 22 Apr 2023).
w: A Johannesburg theatre in the Newtown precinct, part of a foundation that also runs the Market Laboratory and the Market Photo Workshop, in its 50th year in 2026. The minister dissolved its council in October 2025.

f: Mostly earned income: £28,846k total income in the year to 31 October 2024, of which £22,574k came from theatre, education and tours (annual report 2024). Deutsche Bank sponsors the Playing Shakespeare schools programme; Garfield Weston Foundation and Wolfson Foundation are named capital funders.
w: A charity set up to run the reconstructed Elizabethan playhouse on Bankside, founded by Sam Wanamaker. In 2020 it cut about 40 staff in a restructure after losing 90% of summer income, the 2020 annual report says.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Arts Council England National Portfolio funding, trusts and foundations (Jerwood named), individual and corporate donors, box office and trading. Public funding was £2,238,843 and donations and legacies £4,749,947 in the year to 31 March 2025 (accounts 2025). In 2023 the Court won NPO funding for 2023 to 2026 with a 5% reduction (accounts 2023).
w: The English Stage Company runs the theatre in Sloane Square as a charity. Its accounts for the year to 31 March 2023 record the departure of artistic director Vicky Featherstone and executive producer Lucy Davies, an interim executive director on secondment from Arts Council England, and a deficit of £752,674.

f: Arts Council England paid £1,417,530 in the year to 31 March 2025 (2023-24: £2,542,530, including a £750,000 advance), and fundraising brought in £1,192,502, with Jerwood Foundation, Genesis Foundation and Charlotte Aitken Trust each giving £50,000 or more (accounts 2025). Box office was £2,443,561 and a board member gave an unrestricted £500k.
w: A charity theatre founded in 1970 in Waterloo. The 2025 accounts record a deficit of £580,234, the end of Kwame Kwei-Armah's tenure in September 2024, a fundamental review of main-house producing, and a planned reduction in permanent headcount for 2025-26.

f: In the year to 31 March 2025 the Trust reported sponsorship and donations of £8,624k, Arts Council funding of £5,745k, theatre presentations income of £23,110k and trading income of £3,861k (accounts 2025). Arts Council England and Barclays appear as funders and supporters on its site; the Mayor of London's press release says East Bank, which includes Sadler's Wells East, received more than £600m of investment from the Mayor.
w: A charity running dance theatres at Angel, the Peacock Theatre and, since February 2025, Sadler's Wells East in Stratford. Its sponsorship and donations rose from £3,698k to £8,624k in 2024-25 and Arts Council funding from £4,617k to £5,745k (accounts 2025).

f: A mixed model: total income £82.0 million in 2024/25, of which box office £46.4 million, Arts Council England's National Portfolio grant £15.3 million a year (18.6% of income) plus a £320,367 touring grant, and fundraising £6.7 million (annual report 2025). Named funders include Garfield Weston Foundation, Paul Hamlyn Foundation, Foyle Foundation, Gatsby Charitable Foundation and Esmée Fairbairn Foundation.
w: The company runs the Royal Shakespeare Theatre, Swan Theatre and The Other Place in Stratford. It ended its BP sponsorship of £5 tickets for 16 to 25-year-olds on 2 October 2019, early, after Mark Rylance quit as an associate artist and school climate strikers threatened a boycott.
why: BP sponsored the RSC's £5 tickets for 16 to 25-year-olds from 2013; on 2 October 2019 the RSC said it would end the partnership at the end of 2019, three years early, after Mark Rylance resigned in June 2019 and young people objected (France 24, 2 October 2019).
