f: Mostly earned income: total income £60.5m in 2024 (rental and ticket commission £41.2m, other event income £7.3m, philanthropy £3.3m including gift aid, Members' seat rate and other items £2.1m), with a £20.7m DCMS and Arts Council England loan taken in March 2021 (annual report 2024). A £300m capital project is to be funded from surplus, a Capital Appeal for about £50m of voluntary income, and Seatholders.
w: A Royal Charter body and registered charity that opened in 1871 and is held in trust for the nation. Seats are held as private property rights by Seatholders, who make up most of its Council and pay a seat rate; in 2024 that rate was £1,690 per seat plus VAT, raising £2,142,920.

f: Public grants of £5,306k in the year to 31 October 2025 (Creative Scotland £3,250k, City of Edinburgh Council £1,926k, Festivals Expo Fund £80k, EventScotland £50k), donations and legacies of £4,209k and sponsorship of £155k (2024: £758k), with ticket sales 22% of income (annual report 2025). 65% of income was earned and 35% from public sector grants.
w: A charity founded in 1947 that runs the August festival and owns the Hub; Nicola Benedetti directed her third festival in 2025. Creative Scotland raised its three-year grant in January 2025 after real-terms decline since 2008, yet the 2025 festival was cut back; sponsorship income fell from £758k to £155k.

f: Grants and donations £14,100k in the year to 31 March 2025, led by Arts Council England (£10,007k) and Manchester City Council (£3,596k), with trusts and foundations £325k from three organisations; income from Aviva's naming-rights partnership and 23 other brand partnerships runs through a trading subsidiary (annual report 2025). The £241m building cost was met by Manchester City Council £93.3m, UK Treasury £78.1m, Arts Council England £21m, Arts Lottery £7m and £39.3m of fundraising (Place North West, 5 September 2023).
w: A charity that runs the biennial Manchester International Festival and, since October 2023, Aviva Studios, a venue whose budget rose from £110m in 2017 to about £241m by September 2023. The council expects about £80m from naming rights and sponsorship over the 30-year lease.

f: Government funding of €9.4m, 75% of income in 2024 (2023: €8.4m, 67%), made up of an Arts Council grant of €8.5m (2023: €8m) and a restricted capital grant of €750k from the Department of Tourism, Culture, Arts, Gaeltacht, Sport and Media; box office €2,059,808 and fundraising and other income €465k (financial statements 2024).
w: Ireland's national theatre, opened on 27 December 1904. An Arts Council-commissioned Mazars report on 2019 to 2021 led to a condition of funding that the Abbey commission the Crowe Ireland governance review, completed in August 2024; the Board adopted a code of governance in December 2024.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A provincial Crown corporation: total revenues of $36,113,931 in 2023-24, of which provincial operating contributions were $12,940,000 (about 45% of core operating budget) and provincial contributions for other purposes $11,807,896; museum admissions and memberships $5,223,245, IMAX $2,498,804, and grants and sponsorships only $12,500 (statements of financial information 2023-24). The separate Royal BC Museum Foundation paid the museum $147,614.
w: The province owns the corporation and the downtown site, which includes BC Archives; Premier John Horgan stopped a $789 million rebuild on 22 June 2022, and the CEO stepped down in July 2023. The Auditor General's report qualified the 2023-24 statements over deferred revenue and over the museum's Foundation.

f: A federal Crown corporation that also runs the Canadian War Museum: its 2025-26 budget is $114.20 million, made up of $80.36 million of parliamentary appropriations (including $2.3 million of capital), $19.44 million of revenues, $5.70 million from restricted equity and $8.70 million from deferred appropriations (corporate plan 2025-26 to 2029-30).
w: Established under the Museums Act of 1990, amended on 12 December 2013, when the Canadian Museum of Civilization became the Canadian Museum of History. In October 2012 Heritage Minister James Moore announced the change with a non-renewable $25 million for a new Canadian History Hall, and historians' groups and a 2015 journal article questioned the government's role.

f: The pages read gave few figures: the Canada Council for the Arts listed it among the Quebec organisations receiving the most funding, at $688.8K in 2024-2025 (Canada Council, Quebec funding overview). The CCA runs a donation campaign with a campaign cabinet of volunteers and is a registered charity (118830009 RR0001); the pages read did not state its endowment or other grants.
w: Founded by Phyllis Lambert in 1979 as a museum and research centre, directed by Giovanna Borasi.

f: Total operating revenue of $38,975,908 in 2024: ticket sales $18,428,252, ancillary $4,067,796, donations, memberships and fundraising $11,930,612, the Shaw Festival Theatre Endowment Foundation $2,387,105, and grants of $2,162,143 including Ontario Arts Council $1,130,633 and Canada Council $780,000 (audited statements 2024). Heritage Canada was named in the March 2024 federal budget for a $15 million grant to its All.Together.Now campaign.
w: Founded in 1962 by Brian Doherty and Calvin G. Rand. The 2023 statements show a deficiency of revenues over expenses of $6,492,228 and 2024 one of $491,717 after an operating surplus of $767,788, leaving net assets at minus $6,726,227.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: For 2024 the Festival reported revenue of almost $75.4 million against expenses of $76.5 million, a deficit of more than $1.1 million (My Stratford Now, 7 April 2025). Its Endowment Foundation, with fund balances of $144.9 million at 31 October 2024, granted the Festival $13,085,682 that year (Endowment Foundation statements 2024).
w: A charity theatre company in Stratford, Ontario, supported by a separate Endowment Foundation and a US body, Stratford Shakespearean Festival of America. It ran a deficit of more than $1.1 million in 2024 after a surplus of more than $400,000 in 2023, with about 430,000 attending.

f: Parliamentary appropriations of $73.1 million in 2024-2025 (2023-2024: $86.7 million, including one-time compensation funding and drawdown timing), programming ticket sales of $12.1 million, and a $7.1 million grant from the National Arts Centre Foundation, whose donors gave more than $8.9 million (annual report 2024-2025). Earned revenues are 41% of the budget.
w: A federal Crown corporation that began operating the centre in 1969, with an Orchestra, Dance, English Theatre, French Theatre, Indigenous Theatre and Popular Music streams. It posted a planned deficit of $4.1 million in 2024-2025 and its President and CEO Christopher Deacon wrote that he would retire in December 2025.

f: Federal appropriations of $209,240,000 in each of FY2024 and FY2025 (Salaries and Expenses $174,760,000 plus Repair, Restoration and Renovation $34,480,000); the FY2026 request was $186,000,000. The buildings and Sculpture Garden are private gifts (Andrew W. Mellon, Paul Mellon, Ailsa Mellon Bruce, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, the Morris and Gwendolyn Caffritz Foundation), the collection was assembled by donation or purchase from private funds, and special exhibitions draw on private funds as well as federal money.
w: A museum on the National Mall run by a nine-member Board of Trustees (five private members and four ex-officio federal office-holders). Congress pays operating costs, while the Mellon family and foundation gave the buildings and the collection came from private gifts and purchases. The Washington Examiner reported on 22 April 2026 a $116 million gift from Mitchell Rales for its Across the Nation loan programme.

n: Freer Gallery of Art and Arthur M. Sackler Gallery (National Museum of Asian Art)
f: Part of the Smithsonian, which received about $1.09bn in government appropriations in fiscal year 2024 and is about 62 percent federally funded. The Sackler Gallery carries the name of Arthur M. Sackler, whose 1982 gift was $4 million and more than one thousand objects; the museum says it no longer accepts donations from the Sackler family.
w: Two galleries under one board, staff and budget; the Freer opened in 1923. The Smithsonian kept the Sackler name after the family's Purdue Pharma OxyContin litigation, saying the 1982 gift agreement requires it in perpetuity, and added a wall text acknowledging the opioid crisis.
why: The museum's own acknowledgement text says the Sackler family owns Purdue Pharma, which made billions from OxyContin, and that the 1982 Sackler gift agreement requires the gallery to keep Arthur M. Sackler's name; the Smithsonian declined a senator's request to drop it in July 2019 (museum acknowled
nodes: Sackler Gallery carries the name of Arthur M

The museum's own acknowledgement text says the Sackler family owns Purdue Pharma, which made billions from OxyContin, and that the 1982 Sackler gift agreement requires the gallery to keep Arthur M. Sackler's name; the Smithsonian declined a senator's request to drop it in July 2019 (museum acknowledgement text, 2022; art-critique.com, July 2019; Antiques and the Arts Weekly, 10 December 2019).

f: Part of the Smithsonian, which received about $1.09bn in government appropriations in fiscal year 2024 and is about 62 percent federally funded; the museum's own page lists named gifts by Harriet Lane Johnston, John Gellatly, William T. Evans and Andrew Mellon to its collection. The pages read did not state the museum's own budget or donors.
w: The Smithsonian's museum of American art, with the Renwick Gallery for craft. It is one of eight Smithsonian museums named in the White House content review launched on 12 August 2025, and the White House threatened in December 2025 to withhold federal funds if documents were not handed over.

f: The pages read named no amounts for the museum's operating budget. Its trustees include Peter L. Bain, Guy E. Flynn and Harry Gruner, who are also the officers of the separate Walters Art Museum Foundation, which reported net assets of $2,430,680 for the year to June 2025.
w: A Baltimore museum whose director of 11 years, Julia Marciari-Alexander, left in 2024 to become president of the Samuel H. Kress Foundation, after which two staff members ran it as interim co-directors.

f: The pages read did not state the Library's funders or amounts; its site says its Board of Governors operates under the auspices of Amherst College and invites donations, memberships and planned giving.
w: A research library and theatre on Capitol Hill founded by Henry Clay Folger and Emily Folger, opened in 1932 and governed by a Board of Governors under Amherst College's auspices. Its site says it holds more than 300,000 objects.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Robert Woods Bliss gave the Dumbarton Oaks estate to Harvard in 1940 and left Harvard an estimated $10 million in his will, for developing the estate, according to a Harvard Crimson report on his estate. The pages read did not state current funding.
w: A Georgetown estate, garden and research library given to Harvard by Robert Woods Bliss, a former ambassador to Argentina, in 1940. It houses Harvard's programmes in Byzantine studies and pre-Columbian art.

f: In the year to August 2025 it reported revenue of $101,338,288: contributions $61,602,734, programme service revenue $32,265,163 and investment income $5,653,928, against expenses of $99,029,073 and net assets of $522,735,301. David Geffen gave $100 million toward the $550 million rebuild of David Geffen Hall, which reopened on 8 October 2022.
w: The orchestra of Lincoln Center, resident in David Geffen Hall, which was renamed for Geffen after his $100 million gift in 2015. Gustavo Dudamel starts as music and artistic director in the 2026-27 season; the Form 990 for 2024 shows Deborah Borda's pay at $1,728,420.

f: In the year to September 2025 the Los Angeles Philharmonic Association reported revenue of $244,631,714: contributions $67,996,857, programme service revenue $152,439,141 and investment income $14,965,981, against expenses of $221,639,070 and net assets of $590,579,111. It also operates the Hollywood Bowl, which the County of Los Angeles owns.
w: The association behind the orchestra, Walt Disney Concert Hall and the Hollywood Bowl. Its Form 990 shows Gustavo Dudamel paid $3,775,000 in 2025; he starts at the New York Philharmonic in 2026-27.

f: Owned by the County of Los Angeles and run by the Los Angeles Philharmonic under a long-term lease, with ticket pricing approved by the county. In 2024 over 1.3 million people attended, and access programmes are 14 percent of tickets (50,000 $1 tickets and 70,000 free tickets). The pages read did not state the Bowl's own revenue.
w: An amphitheatre in the Hollywood Hills owned by the county and operated by the LA Phil, which employs close to 1,000 staff there. Its shuttle service costs the LA Phil more than $5 million net a year even with a county subsidy.
nodes: Los Angeles Philharmonic under a long-term lease

n: Autry Museum of the American West
f: Philanthropy is its primary revenue source (individuals, foundations, corporations and government agencies); it reported 2024 revenue of $11,958,406 against expenses of $21,652,677 and net assets of $176,858,533. It pays the City of Los Angeles $1 a year for its Griffith Park land under a lease to January 2037.
w: Formed in 2003 by the merger of the Autry Museum of Western Heritage (founded 1984, opened 1988), the Southwest Museum of the American Indian (1907) and the Women of the West Museum. The merger was contentious, and the Autry put the Southwest Museum site on the market in 2019.

f: In the year to June 2025 it reported revenue of $27,491,131 (contributions $12,845,145, programme services $12,930,540, investment income $1,255,239) against expenses of $39,657,290 and net assets of $436,875,878. Jack and Audrey Skirball provided initial funding in 1983.
w: A Jewish cultural centre in Brentwood designed by Moshe Safdie and led from 1996 to 2020 by its founder Uri D. Herscher, whose pay was $2,366,225 in the year to June 2019. Expenses have exceeded revenue in each of the last five years shown.

f: In the year to June 2025 it reported revenue of $80,826,148 (contributions $47,048,673, programme services $15,070,068, investment income $3,776,640) against expenses of $76,783,278 and net assets of $199,850,185. Revenue was $57,126,433 against expenses of $77,300,001 in 2024 and $59,745,832 against $85,822,656 in 2023.
w: Chicago's opera company, owner of the 1929 Civic Opera House and permanent home of the Joffrey Ballet since 2017. General director Anthony Freud announced his exit in September 2023, two years before his contract ended, and left at the end of July 2024.

f: In the year to June 2024 it reported revenue of $78.8 million against expenses of $80.2 million: ticket sales $23 million, direct operational support $23.8 million and an annual 5 percent endowment draw. The SEMPRE ALWAYS campaign, launched in 2020 with a leadership gift and challenge from the Zell Family Foundation, reached $159.9 million of a $175 million goal by 30 June 2024.
w: The orchestra and its owner-operator body, which is renaming itself Chicago Symphony from 24 September 2026. Klaus Makela becomes music director in 2027/28; Riccardo Muti has been Music Director Emeritus for Life since 2023/24.

f: In the year to August 2025 it reported revenue of $71.87 million, with contributions about 68.9 percent ($49.5 million) and royalties 13.7 percent, against expenses of $54.54 million and net assets of $149.50 million. Royalty income fell from $24 million in 2018-19 to $7 million in 2023-24, mainly from reduced Hamilton revenue.
w: The New York theatre behind Shakespeare in the Park, led since 2005 by Oskar Eustis, who will step down on 31 July 2028; it cut about 50 staff (19 percent) in 2023 and Broadway Journal reported a further round in December 2025.

f: It is a private operating foundation founded by Donald and Shelley Rubin. In 2024 it reported revenue of $15.56 million (sales of assets 43.3 percent, investment income 32.0 percent, contributions 11.9 percent) against expenses of $17.44 million and net assets of $198.61 million.
w: Closed its Chelsea building on 6 October 2024 after 20 years, laying off about 40 percent of staff, to become a museum without walls; it denied that the closure was linked to claims it had shown stolen works.

f: The City of Tulsa owns the museum and the University of Tulsa manages it. The $140.9 million new building is paid for with $91.5 million of public money, including $65 million from the 2016 Vision Tulsa sales tax package and $8.6 million from the city's Improve Our Tulsa package, and $49 million of private gifts, including $10 million from the A.R. and Marylouise Tandy Foundation (Tulsa Flyer, 2 April 2026). The city approved $5 million for the museum in its fiscal year 2027 budget (Tulsa Flyer, 16 October 2026).
w: Founded by the Tulsa oilman Thomas Gilcrease, who opened it in 1949; the city bought the collection with a 1954 bond issue and the University of Tulsa has run it since 2008 (museum website). The rebuild came in about 70% over the original city estimate of $83.6 million and the reopening has moved to March 2027 (Tulsa Flyer).

f: A private nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $19,380,360, of which contributions were $15,039,282, against $4,889,377 in 2022 (ProPublica). Its supporters page lists the George Kaiser Family Foundation, the Oklahoma Arts Council, the National Endowment for the Arts, the Zink Family Foundation, the Anne and Henry Zarrow Foundation and the Andy Warhol Foundation among funders at $10,000 and above, without amounts (museum website).
w: Founded when Waite and Genevieve Phillips gave their Tulsa villa to the community; it opened on 25 October 1939 (Oklahoma Historical Society). The supporters page also lists the Waite and Genevieve Phillips Foundation and the Eugene B. Adkins Trust.
nodes: Andy Warhol Foundation among funders at

f: Founded and repeatedly funded by The Meadows Foundation, which Algur H. Meadows, an oilman who founded General American Oil Company in 1936, created in 1948. The foundation gave $18.5 million for the current building in 1998 (the SMU release of 2015 says $20 million), $25 million of a $33 million gift in 2006, and $25 million of a $45 million gift in 2015, of which $13 million is for exhibitions and education and $12 million for acquisitions (museum website; SMU news release, 23 March 2015). Admission is $12 for adults (museum website).
w: A museum of Spanish art on the Southern Methodist University campus, which opened on 3 April 1965 with Meadows's own collection (museum website). Its budget and accounts are not published separately from the university in the pages read.

f: A unit of The University of Texas at Austin. In 2020 to 2021 its funding sources were $7,026,909: the university's state support 61%, endowment earnings 27%, gifts and grants 11% ($679,510) and earned revenue 1%. Its endowment stood at $52,184,672 market value, and a campaign with a $70,000,000 goal had raised $41,797,685 by 31 August 2021 (annual report 2020 to 2021).
w: Founded in 1957 by Harry Huntt Ransom, a UT English professor who later became chancellor; the building opened in 1972 (HRC website). It holds a complete Gutenberg Bible and the Gabriel Garcia Marquez papers (HRC website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A nonprofit that relies mainly on gifts: its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $30,422,659, of which contributions were $24,668,406 and program service revenue $5,400,329, against expenses of $30,729,991 (ProPublica). In 2022 expenses of $30,094,011 exceeded revenue of $27,493,921 (ProPublica). The pages read did not name its major donors.
w: One of the larger US opera companies, which says it has produced 91 premieres, 76 of them world-premiere operas (HGO website). In April 2020 it furloughed 25 of its 120 employees and estimated losses of up to $15 million over the longer term (OperaWire, 22 April 2020).

f: A nonprofit theatre funded mostly by gifts: its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $26,118,373, of which contributions were $15,399,469 and program service revenue $9,301,807 (ProPublica). In July 2022 an anonymous donor pledged a $25 million matching grant to an $80 million campaign, the largest grant in its history (Houston Arts Journal, 20 July 2022).
w: Houston's resident theatre company, led by artistic director Rob Melrose; its budget fell from $19 million to $11 million in 2020 to 2021 during the pandemic (Houston Arts Journal, 20 July 2022). The Edgerton Foundation gave it a New Play Award for Dear Alien in December 2025 (BroadwayWorld).

f: A nonprofit funded by foundations and individuals. In the year to 2025 its revenue was $4,229,733: capital campaign $1,482,050, contributions $1,279,092, endowment $875,000 and earned income $593,591; expenses were $3,252,421 (annual report FY25). The Opening Spaces campus campaign lists The Brown Foundation, Houston Endowment, the Cullen Foundation, the Stavros Niarchos Foundation, the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation, LVMH and the Texas Commission on the Arts among donors, without amounts (annual report FY25).
w: Commissioned by John and Dominique de Menil, who engaged Mark Rothko in 1964; it opened in 1971 with Rothko's 14 paintings (Rothko Chapel website). Hurricane Beryl in July 2024 damaged several paintings and closed the building for five months (annual report FY25).
nodes: Texas Commission on the Arts among donors

f: A nonprofit funded mainly by gifts: its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $23,202,519, of which contributions were $17,054,895 and program service revenue $5,802,959, against expenses of $24,071,168 (ProPublica). The pages read did not name its donors or public grants.
w: Formed in 1963 and known for its annual Wagner Ring cycle from 1975; it performs in McCaw Hall (HistoryLink). In February 2021 it laid off the remaining 24 furloughed employees (Seattle Opera blog, 5 February 2021).

n: Denver Center for the Performing Arts
f: A nonprofit that earns most of its income: its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $66,757,028, of which program service revenue was $49,167,982 and contributions $15,662,096 (ProPublica). A Colorado cultural sales tax, the Scientific and Cultural Facilities District, brings in more than $8 million a year for DCPA programmes, and the Bonfils Foundation has supported its operating budget (DCPA, obituary of Daniel L. Ritchie).
w: Runs eight theatres including the Buell Theatre and the Ellie Caulkins Opera House, a Broadway touring series and the DCPA Theatre Company; its chief executive is Janice Sinden (DCPA website). In October 2025 it ended its Off-Center immersive programming after two financial losses and a July layoff of 12 staff (Denver Gazette, 8 October 2025).

f: Run by The Musical Arts Association, a nonprofit. Its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $76,819,625, of which contributions were $50,110,758, program service revenue $19,381,712 and investment income $6,783,072, with net assets of $291,683,678 (ProPublica). Cuyahoga Arts & Culture, funded by a county tax, gave it $863,659 in 2025 and $1,000,000 in 2026 (CAC grant lists).
w: The orchestra performs at Severance Music Center and Blossom Music Center; Franz Welser-Moest is in his 25th and final season as music director (orchestra website). Its county grant comes from a tax on cigarettes that has been falling: it was the largest of the 2014 awards at over $3 million across two years (Ideastream, 25 November 2014).

n: The Philadelphia Orchestra and Ensemble Arts
f: In 2023 to 2024 the combined organisation had $132.6 million of revenue: ticket sales 38%, ancillary income such as parking and rentals 24%, and contributions and endowment 38% (NBC Philadelphia, 23 April 2025). The Philadelphia Orchestra Association's Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $55,220,839, of which contributions were $31,511,726, and net assets of $190,051,709 (ProPublica).
w: The orchestra merged with the Kimmel Center under a new parent company in 2021; the Kimmel inherited about $30 million of debt that a package from board members and area philanthropies erased (Philadelphia Inquirer, 22 October 2021). Ryan Fleur became president and chief executive in April 2025 and the orchestra's contract with Local 77 expires in September 2026 (NBC Philadelphia, 23 April 2025).

f: Part of the University of Pennsylvania; the pages read did not name its funders or give its budget. It asks for gifts through a University Museum Annual Giving Fund (museum website).
w: Founded in 1887, it holds over a million artifacts and the Morton Cranial Collection (museum website). In April 2021 it apologised for holding remains of children killed in the 1985 MOVE bombing, and a university-commissioned report of August 2021 found 'extremely poor judgment' by two anthropologists (WHYY, 28 April 2021; Billy Penn, 26 August 2021).
why: More than 100 people rallied outside the Penn Museum on 28 April 2021 over its handling of the remains of two children killed in the 1985 MOVE bombing, and called for the firing of curator Janet Monge (WHYY, 28 April 2021).
nodes: More than 100 people rallied outside the Penn Museum on 28 April 2021 over its handling of the remains of two children killed in the 1985 MOVE bombing, and called for the firing of curator Janet Monge (WHYY, 28 April 2021).

f: Owned by The College of Physicians of Philadelphia, whose Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $10,033,293, of which contributions were $5,334,937, program service revenue $2,719,611 and investment income $1,016,738, with net assets of $46,743,502 (ProPublica). The pages read did not name its donors.
w: Holds about 6,500 human remains and more than 35,000 objects (Fortune, 22 August 2025). In May 2023 it took down its online exhibits and YouTube videos while it reviewed how to show human remains, and in August 2025 it adopted a policy to 'sharply limit' new acquisitions of remains (WHYY, 10 May 2023; Fortune, 22 August 2025).

f: A nonprofit funded mainly by gifts: its Form 990 for the tax period ending in 2023 shows revenue of $22,814,015, of which contributions were $16,170,567 (ProPublica). Milwaukee County has invested nearly $19 million in it since 2015, according to county supervisor Steve Taylor (press release, 18 February 2025). The director's pay was $549,000 in 2022 to 2023 (same release).
w: Director Marcelle Polednik stepped down on 31 July 2025 after nine years, announced on 14 May 2025 (Urban Milwaukee; museum release). A union and a former board member criticised the board and the museum's finances (Urban Milwaukee, 15 July 2025).
nodes: Milwaukee County has invested nearly in it

f: Run by the Buffalo Fine Arts Academy. The expansion was led by $65 million of support from the investor Jeffrey E. Gundlach, whose matching challenges drew private donors and government at every level; 2,767 donors raised about $230 million overall (annual report, year to 30 June 2023). In that year government grants were $705,000, corporate and foundation support $3,121,768 and restricted contributions $54,159,215 (annual report, year to 30 June 2023).
w: Founded in 1862 as the Buffalo Fine Arts Academy; the Albright building opened in 1905, the Knox wing in 1962, and the OMA-designed expansion on 12 June 2023 as the Buffalo AKG Art Museum (museum website). The name honours John J. Albright, Seymour H. Knox Jr. and Jeffrey E. Gundlach (museum website).

f: Kolumba is run by the Archdiocese of Cologne (Erzbistum Köln). The pages read did not state its budget or any sponsor; admission is EUR 8 for adults, EUR 5 reduced, EUR 30 for an annual pass, and under 18s enter free (museen.koeln).
w: The art museum of the Archdiocese of Cologne, founded in 1853 as the Diocesan Museum and renamed Kolumba in 2004; Peter Zumthor's building opened on 15 September 2007 (museen.koeln).

f: The museum has been run since 2000 by the Stiftung Wilhelm Lehmbruck Museum. The Land North Rhine-Westphalia gave acquisition support for Alicja Kwade's sculpture Superheavy Skies (press release of 16 April 2024, part of about EUR 740,000 for 13 municipal museums) and exhibition support for the 2026 Anish Kapoor show (press release of 24 May 2026).
w: A sculpture museum in the Kantpark, opened in 1964 on the Lehmbruck collection that the Kunstverein began in 1912 with a gift from the Böninger family; about 100 works were lost in the 1937 'Degenerate Art' campaign (museum website).

f: The museum calls itself a public institution without a permanent collection; the City of Düsseldorf decided on and will carry out the renovation of the building.
w: A temporary-exhibition hall on Grabbeplatz whose building opened in 1881, was replaced in the 1960s and reopened after renovation in 2002; in December 2016 more than 700 signers opposed a plan to place it under the Kunstpalast's directorship (ArtReview, 6 December 2016).

f: The museum is a city of Bonn institution: the Bonn city council appoints its Intendant, and its contact address is a bonn.de mailbox. The Land NRW funded the restoration of nearly 100 video tapes from its video art collection in 2026 (land.nrw, 24 May 2026). The pages read gave no budget.
w: A museum of contemporary art with about 9,000 works, centred on August Macke, the Rhenish Expressionists and German art after 1945; Stephan Berg's contract ends in November 2025 and Claudia Emmert, then director of the Zeppelin Museum, takes over on 1 December 2025 to the end of 2033 (bonn.de, September 2024).
nodes: Bonn city council appoints its Intendant

f: The museum is operated by the Stiftung für Kunst und Kultur e.V.; its website credits the 2021 extension to the private MKM Foundation of the collectors Sylvia and Ulrich Ströher. The pages read gave no other funders or amounts.
w: A museum in a converted grain mill in Duisburg's Inner Harbour, opened as a museum in 1999 and extended by Herzog & de Meuron in 2021; it shows the Ströher Collection of German art after 1945 and, from October 2026 for one year, the Haniel Collection.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The building belongs to the City of Bottrop. In 2016 the museum bought 28 Albers photographs and photomontages from the Josef and Anni Albers Foundation with money from several foundations the press release did not name and from the Land NRW (land.nrw, 21 September 2016).
w: A city museum in Bottrop's Stadtgarten, opened in 1976, named for Josef Albers, who was born in Bottrop in 1888; Anni Albers transferred more than 300 of his works in 1979, which led to the 1981 to 1983 extension.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts; its news is published on the City of Dortmund's site and a Friends of Museum Ostwall e.V. awards a prize (Revierpassagen, 10 November 2017).
w: A modern and contemporary art museum on the fourth and fifth floors of the Dortmunder U with a Fluxus focus, a large Jawlensky holding and Classical Modernism; its founder is given as Leonie Reygers (Ruhr Tourismus).

f: The City of Leverkusen is the main public funder; the Museumsverein Morsbroich e.V. raises money from private donors, nationwide foundations and the Land North Rhine-Westphalia (museum website). The pages read gave no amounts.
w: A museum of contemporary art in a baroque castle, opened on 27 January 1951; in February 2016 a KPMG report for the city recommended closing it to save about EUR 778,450 a year, and Gerhard Richter wrote an open letter against it (The Art Newspaper, 29 February 2016).

f: The museum belongs to the Würth Group, the company, and not to the Stiftung Würth; admission is free (Stuttgarter Zeitung, interview with Maria Würth; Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026). The pages read gave no budget.
w: The museum opened in 1991 in the Würth Group's administration building in Künzelsau-Gaisbach; Museum Würth 2 by David Chipperfield followed in 2020 (Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026).

f: The Kunsthalle belongs to the Würth Group, the company, and not to the Stiftung Würth; admission to all Würth museums is free (Stuttgarter Zeitung, interview with Maria Würth; Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026). The pages read gave no budget.
w: The Kunsthalle in Schwäbisch Hall opened in 2001, followed by the Johanniterkirche there in 2008, as part of the Würth Group's art venues (Schwäbische Zeitung, 17 June 2026).
nodes: Kunsthalle belongs to the Würth Group

f: The museum belongs to the Stiftung Frieder Burda, a civil-law foundation set up on 20 April 1998 that calls itself independent and charitable. The pages read did not state its income or any sponsor.
w: A museum of modern and contemporary art designed by Richard Meier, opened on 22 October 2004 on Lichtentaler Allee, linked by a glass bridge to the state-run Staatliche Kunsthalle Baden-Baden.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: It is one of 11 state museums of Baden-Württemberg; across them, the Land and the municipalities cover about 85 percent of running costs, third parties 6 percent, admission 6 percent and other income 3 percent (Rechnungshof Baden-Württemberg, Jahresbericht 2026). The Rechnungshof does not give a figure for this museum alone.
w: The state museum for archaeology, art and cultural history and popular culture in the Altes Schloss, Stuttgart; the state audit office recommended in its 2026 report that the state museums raise admission prices.

f: It is one of 11 state museums of Baden-Württemberg; across them the Land and the municipalities cover about 85 percent of running costs (Rechnungshof Baden-Württemberg, Jahresbericht 2026). The pages read gave no figure for this museum alone.
w: A state museum of cultural history in Karlsruhe Palace; its director Eckart Köhne called the palace a 'Bruchbude' in 2024, and the building closes for a general renovation by autumn 2025 at the latest (Stuttgarter Zeitung, 4 September 2024). In 2025 it showed 'Injustice & Profit' on its Nazi-era acquisitions.

f: The city paid EUR 8.62 per visitor in 2009, when the museum company closed with a loss of EUR 39,856 and business plans forecast deficits of EUR 1.8 million for 2010 and EUR 1.7 million for 2011 (Schwäbische Zeitung, 13 July 2010). The pages read gave no recent figures.
w: A museum in Friedrichshafen directed since 2014 by Claudia Emmert, who is also managing director and leaves for the Kunstmuseum Bonn on 1 December 2025 (bonn.de, September 2024).

f: The museum is an institution of the State of Baden-Württemberg (museum website). The Land is investing EUR 118.4 million in the renovation and restructuring of the building (Land Baden-Württemberg press release).
w: A state art museum whose main building is closed for several years; shows go on at the ZKM, the Orangerie and the Junge Kunsthalle; Staab Architekten won the renovation competition on 15 March 2018.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the Glyptothek or give amounts. Its own history page says King Ludwig I paid for both the building and the collection himself.
w: Munich's museum of Greek and Roman sculpture, built by Leo von Klenze between 1816 and 1830 for Ludwig I and part of the Antike am Königsplatz group of the State Collections of Antiquities (museum website). Reopened in 1972 after bomb damage in 1944.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts. Its history page says the Kingdom of Bavaria paid for collecting in the 19th century, and the home page links to a Preetorius-Stiftung without describing it.
w: Munich's ethnological museum, with a first curator hired in 1862 and a public opening in 1868. Its Africa collection holds about 50 objects assigned to the Benin Empire; the museum ran provenance research on them from December 2021 to May 2022, and Die Berliner Zeitung reported on 17 May 2023 that Bavaria and Saxony were the only German states without a return contract with Nigeria.

f: The museum's renovation site names the federal government and the Free State of Bavaria at 330 million euros each. Die Abendzeitung reported on 15 November 2019 that the budget went from 445 million to at least 745 million euros, with about 45 million euros from major donors and 40 million euros from the museum's own budget over ten years.
w: Munich's museum of science and technology, on the Museumsinsel, in a renovation begun in 2006 that opened its first renovated half in July 2022 (museum website). Costs rose from 445 million to at least 745 million euros by November 2019, and the architects' firm filed for insolvency in April 2019 (Die Abendzeitung).

f: A corporate museum: BMW's own pages place it inside BMW Group Classic, the division that preserves the company's history, and the BMW Welt page carries the notice BMW AG 2026. The pages read gave no budget.
w: BMW's company museum, opened on 18 May 1973, closed in 2004 and reopened in June 2008 with 5,000 square metres and seven themed houses (BMW newsroom). It is part of BMW Group Classic.
nodes: BMW's own pages place it inside BMW Group Classic

f: A public-law foundation (Music Information Centre entry). In 2010 the interview magazine of the city of Nuremberg gave a budget of 16.8 million euros, of which 15.3 million euros were public grants, from the Bund and the Länder, with sponsors the Nürnberger Versicherungsgruppe, Siemens and BMW.
w: Founded in 1852, with 1.3 million objects in 2010 (Nürnberg Heute, issue 88). Its director said then that delays and costs came from insufficient federal funding. Its music collection exhibition is closed until about 2030 because of construction (Music Information Centre).

f: A state museum run by the Free State of Bavaria and the city of Nuremberg (museum website). The pages read gave no amounts.
w: Nuremberg's museum of art and design, opened in April 2000 in a building by Volker Staab, run by the Free State of Bavaria and the city (museum website; Museen in Bayern). It shows a donation by René Block, Mein Balkan, from November 2026.

f: Funded by the federal government and the Free State of Thuringia at 15.09 million euros a year each, and the city of Weimar at 2.25 million euros, for 2027 to 2031, about 32.4 million euros a year (epd, 17 June 2026). Its 2026 plan totals 37.76 million euros (Bundestag committee paper, 8 June 2026).
w: The third largest cultural foundation in Germany after the Prussian Cultural Heritage Foundation and the Prussian Palaces and Gardens Foundation, with over 20 museums, palaces and writers' houses and twelve UNESCO World Heritage sites (Bundestag paper). It returned two books to the heirs of Julius Wahle in September 2022.

n: GRASSI Museum für Völkerkunde zu Leipzig
f: A museum of the Staatliche Kunstsammlungen Dresden, the Saxon state's art museums, under the Saxon ministry for culture (ministry release, 16 December 2022). The pages read gave no budget figures for the museum.
w: One of the Saxon ethnographic museums, directed with the museums in Dresden and Herrnhut by Léontine Meijer-van Mensch (ministry release, 16 December 2022). On 20 December 2022 a commemorative head of an Oba from the Grassi went to Nigeria; Saxony holds 262 Benin objects in all (ministry release).

f: The state of North Rhine-Westphalia gave 1 million euros a year, the city of Essen 2.5 to 2.7 million euros a year and the Landschaftsverband Rheinland 2 million euros a year (NRW Landtag answer, 6 August 2014, the latest figures read). The Stiftung Zollverein received 4.5 million euros a year in state institutional funding from 2011.
w: A dependent foundation within the Zollverein Foundation, in the former coal washing plant of the Zollverein colliery, existing since 1 January 2008 and built on the collections of the former Ruhrlandmuseum of Essen (museum website). The Zollverein site has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2001.

f: The festival's page lists funding by the state of North Rhine-Westphalia and Kultur Ruhr GmbH; Die Jüdische Allgemeine of 14 August 2018 states that the state is a shareholder of Kultur Ruhr GmbH. The pages read gave no amounts.
w: A festival of the arts in industrial halls across the Ruhr, organised by Kultur Ruhr GmbH in Bochum, with Lydia Steier as artistic director for 2027 to 2029 after Ivo van Hove (festival website). In June 2018 it disinvited and then reinvited the band Young Fathers over their BDS support, and in March 2020 a state MP demanded it disinvite Achille Mbembe.
why: In June 2018 Brian Eno, Ken Loach and others called for an international boycott of the festival after it disinvited Young Fathers over BDS (Die Jüdische Allgemeine, 21 June 2018).
nodes: In June 2018 Brian Eno, Ken Loach and others called for an international boycott of the festival after it disinvited Young Fathers over BDS (Die Jüdische Allgemeine, 21 June 2018).

f: The museums' website names partner foundations, among them the rem Curt-Engelhorn-Stiftung, the Bassermann-Kulturstiftung, the Brombeeren-Stiftung, the J.J. Achenbach-Stiftung and the Klaus Tschira Stiftung, and says the museums link to the city of Mannheim. Baden-Württemberg gave 61,600 euros in 2021 to record colonial-era holdings.
w: A group of museums in Mannheim with a friends' circle, over 200 volunteers and the Mannheimer Altertumsverein von 1859 (museum website). Its Weltkulturen collection holds about 40,000 objects, including the colonial-era Bumiller and Thorbecke collections from Africa (museum website; Die Rheinpfalz, 25 January 2021).

f: Run by the association Schinkel Pavillon e.V.; the pages read did not name its funders. In December 2024 ArtDog Istanbul reported the space said it could lose 50% of its funding under a proposed 13% cut to Berlin arts funding of about 130 million euros.
w: An octagonal building in Oberwallstraße designed by the East German architect Richard Paulick, hosting non-commercial exhibitions run by the Kunstverein Schinkel Pavillon e.V. since 2007 (Berliner Zeitung, 27 November 2024).

f: A private collection owned by Karen and Christian Boros, shown in a bunker they bought in 2003; visits are by guided tour at 20 euros, 12 euros reduced (Berlin.de). The pages read did not state who pays for the building or the programme.
w: A private contemporary art collection in a Second World War air-raid bunker in Berlin-Mitte, built in 1942 by forced labourers and bought by Karen and Christian Boros in 2003; shown since 2008 in four presentations (collection website).

f: A nonprofit whose revenue goes back into its exhibitions; its funders page names no funders and invites companies, foundations and individuals to become sponsors (KINDL website). The former brewery was bought in 2011 by Salome Grisard and Burkhard Varnholt and converted.
w: A centre for contemporary art in the Expressionist Kindl brewery buildings in Neukölln, shown since 2016 under founding director Andreas Fiedler and, since February 2020, artistic director Kathrin Becker (KINDL website).

f: Since 2004 a private sponsoring organisation has received grants from the district and city governments, and a friends' association founded in 1996 supports it (museum website, history). The supporters page names the Friends association and the federal environment ministry's climate protection initiative for 2018 lighting and gives no amounts.
w: A villa built in 1922 to 1923 for the textile entrepreneur Hermann Knobloch, later owned by Nazi-era officials and the Allgemeine Filmtreuhand GmbH, and a place for exhibitions since 1946 (museum website, history). Anna Gritz has directed it since 2022.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: GfZK, Galerie für Zeitgenössische Kunst Leipzig
f: In 2016 the Stiftung GfZK was funded by the city of Leipzig, the Saxon science and arts ministry and the Förderkreis of the gallery at 220,000 euros a year each (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016). In June 2025 the Greens' Claudia Maicher criticised Saxon budget draft cuts that include the GfZK (L-IZ, 1 June 2025).
w: A gallery of contemporary art in Leipzig, with Franciska Zólyom as director since 1 January 2012 and her contract extended from 2017 for five years (Saxon ministry release, 8 February 2016).

f: The building was funded by a donation of HK$3.5 billion from The Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust, which also covers part of the exhibitions and education projects over nine years (museum press release, 2022). Bank of China (Hong Kong) Limited is named as a strategic partner (museum press release, 2022).
w: A museum run with the Palace Museum in Beijing under a collaborative agreement with the West Kowloon Cultural District Authority, opened on 2 July 2022. Hong Kong Free Press reported that the agreement was signed in 2016 by Carrie Lam, then chief secretary, before any public consultation, and that the Hong Kong Alliance protested the project in early 2017.
nodes: Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust

f: A one-off government endowment of HK$21.6 billion in 2008, which the authority expects to be fully used by 2026/27 (The Standard, 6 October 2026). Operating income excluding interest was HK$768 million in the year to March, with ticket revenue and corporate sponsorship each up 30 percent (The Standard, 6 October 2026). In November 2022 a commercial site was sold to Sun Hung Kai Properties for HK$10.5 billion under a 47-year build-operate-transfer arrangement (ArtAsiaPacific, 23 August 2023).
w: Its chairman Henry Tang warned in August 2023 that programming could stop as money ran low, and in October 2026 it told the Legislative Council its endowment would run out in 2026/27.

f: The museum's pages are credited to the Leisure and Cultural Services Department of the Hong Kong government and admission to the permanent exhibitions is free (museum FAQ page). The pages read did not state a budget or any sponsor.
w: A Hong Kong government museum in Sha Tin with a Resource Centre on the fourth floor open by phone booking. The pages read did not state its funding or any dispute.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Cultural Services Department of the Hong Kong government

f: In the year to 31 March 2025 income was HK$201,414,000, of which government grants were HK$105,207,515, musical events HK$44,583,298 and donations and sponsors HK$49,704,160 (annual report 2024/25). Swire, the Principal Patron, renewed for three years from April 2024 with a grant above HK$50 million, about HK$16.7 million a year, and the Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust gave HK$30.3 million over three years for an education programme (annual report 2024/25).
w: A Hong Kong orchestra supported by the government and resident at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre, with a deficit of HK$9.79 million in 2024/25. The annual report says some podium sponsorship ended when music director Jaap van Zweden left.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Hong Kong Jockey Club Charities Trust

f: For 2026/27 the festival targets about HK$160 million of income: about 11 percent baseline government funding, about 24 percent box office, about 44 percent sponsorship and donations from corporations, individuals and charitable foundations, and about 21 percent other sources including the government's matching grant scheme (festival website). These are targets, not results.
w: A non-profit festival launched in 1973 whose income is mostly private sponsorship and donations. It launched the Hong Kong Arts Festival Foundation in 2022 for large projects the annual budget cannot cover.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. The page is on the hotel's site, with the copyright notice of Hotel Okura Tokyo Co., Ltd., and admission is free for hotel guests.
w: Japan's oldest existing privately operated museum, set up by industrialist Kihachiro Okura in 1917 and now on the fifth floor of The Okura Tokyo hotel. The page does not name the operating body.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The museum's site says it is a public interest incorporated foundation and does not state funders (museum website). A 2026 guide says it houses the private collection of Keita Gotoh, chairman of the Tokyu Group (Conde House Japan, 4 September 2026).
w: A foundation museum opened in 1960 for the collection of Tokyu Group chairman Keita Gotoh, holding part of the 12th-century Genji Monogatari Emaki, shown for about a week each Golden Week.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or name an operator.
w: A museum in a reconstruction of the red brick Mitsubishi Ichigokan, designed by Josiah Conder and first built in 1894, opened in 2010 with a focus on late 19th-century Western art.

f: The pages read did not name who funds the museum. It is part of Benesse Art Site Naoshima, which the Benesse site calls the collective name for all art-related activities conducted by Benesse Corporation and Fukutake Foundation (Benesse Art Site Naoshima). Admission is 1,800 yen online and 2,000 yen on site.
w: A single-installation museum on Teshima: Rei Naito's Matrix, dated 2010, in a concrete shell building by Ryue Nishizawa. It belongs to the Benesse Art Site Naoshima group, which already has its own record.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The Shumei Culture Foundation runs the museum; the pages read did not state how it is funded (museum website).
w: A museum in the mountains of Shigaraki, opened in November 1997 around the collection begun by Mihoko Koyama, run by the Shumei Culture Foundation. The museum's page title says I.M. Pei designed it.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state amounts or funders. The City of Yokohama took over organisation from the Japan Foundation in 2011, and partner logos on the site include the City of Yokohama, Yokohama Arts Foundation, NHK and Yokohama Museum of Art, not labelled as organisers (triennale website).
w: A contemporary art triennial first held in 2001 as Mega Wave, organised by an organising committee with the City of Yokohama since 2011. The 8th edition ran 15 March to 9 June 2024 and the 9th is announced for 23 April to 12 September 2027.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Korea's main international film festival, based at the Busan Cinema Center. In 2014 Busan mayor and festival chairman Seo Byung-soo asked the committee to cancel a screening of the Sewol documentary Diving Bell, and the committee screened it on 6 October 2014.

f: The Taipei Times reported on 16 January 2022 that the centre cost NT$6.75 billion (US$244.4 million) and took 10 years to complete, and that it was commissioned by the Taipei City Government. The pages read did not state its operating funders.
w: A Taipei City Government performing arts complex beside Shilin Night Market, with a trial phase from 11 March to 15 May 2022 and an official opening expected in August 2022. Construction began in 2012 and the building topped out in August 2014.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. Admission is free with a timed reservation (guide page).
w: A Beijing museum founded in 1981 inside the Confucius Temple and moved in 2006 to a new building in Xicheng designed by Ren Qing. The page does not name the operator.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or name its operator. The Wuhan Municipal Government is credited as sponsor of a website page about its treasures, and standard admission is free (Wuhan government page; guide page).
w: A provincial museum in Wuhan founded in 1953 that holds the chime bells of Marquis Yi of Zeng and the Sword of Goujian. It is distinct from the Hubei Museum of Art, which has its own record.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. Admission to the Solitary Hill and Wulin branches is free (guide page).
w: A Hangzhou museum that opened in 1929 as the Zhejiang Provincial West Lake Museum, with a Solitary Hill branch and a Wulin branch on West Lake Cultural Square. It holds more than 100,000 cultural relics and over 3,700 works by Huang Binhong.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or name its operator. Entry is free with a real-name timed reservation through the museum's WeChat channel (guide page).
w: A museum in a building by I.M. Pei beside the Humble Administrator's Garden, opened in 2006. The page does not name the operator.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: China Minsheng Bank established the museum in 2008 and operates it as part of its corporate responsibility platform; the page says it receives support from the bank and gives no figures (museum website).
w: Founded in 2008 by China Minsheng Bank, described by the museum as the first art museum dedicated to public welfare founded by a Chinese financial institution. A partner museum on the former French Pavilion at the Expo site opened in 2014 and the two merged in 2017.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum. It describes itself as the first non-profit, non-governmental art museum in China, founded by Zhang Baoquan in 2002 (Visit Beijing).
w: A Beijing museum of contemporary Chinese art founded by Zhang Baoquan in 2002 and, by its own account, the first non-profit and non-governmental art museum in China. The page says the transformation into a non-profit organisation was complete by 2006.
nodes: CRAC Valparaíso (Centro de Residencias de Arte Contemporáneo)

f: The page read did not state the academy's funding. It describes a collaboration of more than 30 years with the Getty Conservation Institute (Global Times, 27 December 2023).
w: The body that manages the Mogao Caves, with a daily visitor limit of 6,000 set after a 2002 study with the Getty Conservation Institute and the Australian Heritage Commission. Director Su Boming joined in 1992.
nodes: It describes a collaboration of more than 30 years

f: State museum under the Ministry of Culture. Takings of the merged GAMB system were above 21 million euros for January to August 2026.
w: State museum that merged with the Bargello Museums into GAMB after a 2024 ministerial decree. Director Cecilie Hollberg won a Florence court case in 2023 over a magazine's use of the David and in January 2024 apologised after Culture Minister Gennaro Sangiuliano called her remarks on tourism in Florence 'gravi e offensive' (Artribune).
nodes: Takings of the merged GAMB system

f: State museum under the Ministry of Culture, run since the 2024 merger with the Galleria dell'Accademia as the GAMB system. The museum site names Fondazione Il Bargello and Art Bonus donors for a tapestry restoration, Fondazione CR Firenze for its 2025 Welfare Culturale project and the Ministry's Piano Olivetti per la Cultura; the pages read gave no amounts.
w: Houses the Bargello, Cappelle Medicee, Orsanmichele, Palazzo Davanzati and Casa Martelli. The Galleria dell'Accademia returns part of its takings to the state, and the system's director-general wants more private partners (Il Sole 24 Ore, 6 October 2026).
nodes: Art Bonus donors for a tapestry restoration
Ministry's Piano Olivetti per la Cultura

n: Museo Nazionale Etrusco di Villa Giulia
f: State museum with special autonomy under the Ministry of Culture. A Ministry decree of 20 November 2023 transferred 950,000 euros to its budget from the Galleria dell'Accademia di Firenze to restore its financial balance. The museum site asks for museum subscriptions, the 5x1000 tax allocation and Art Bonus donations; full admission is 13 euros.
w: National museum of Etruscan art in Rome that also manages the Parco Archeologico di Veio; director Luana Toniolo has been in office since 16 May 2024 (museum website). Its budget was topped up from the Florence Accademia's takings in 2023.
nodes: Gallerie Nazionali di Arte Antica (Palazzo Barberini and Galleria Corsini)

f: State institute of the Ministry of Culture. Its own 2024 budget report says operating funds from the Directorate-General for Museums were 2,000,000 euros in 2021 and 2022, 600,000 euros for 2023 and 0 euros for 2024 against a need of about 15 million; ticket income passed 3,965,686 euros by 30 November 2023.
w: Runs the Vittoriano, the Museo Centrale del Risorgimento and Palazzo Venezia. Its director complained in the 2024 budget report of zero operating funds and a refused 1.5 million euro recovery-plan grant; the Lazio Corte dei conti criticised a Ministry plan to give services to the in-house company Ales in March 2022 (Finestre sull'Arte).
nodes: State institute of the Ministry of Culture

f: Self-financed non-profit (ONLUS) fabbriceria running Siena Cathedral and its museums. Its social report for 2025 shows revenue of 10,107,266.93 euros (2024: 10,015,097.20), of which 8,945,029 euros from services and sales to third parties, and a surplus after tax of 528,877.94 euros (2024: 1,595,705.15); its only public contribution was 30,000 euros for energy and gas.
w: Ecclesiastical lay board: two of seven councillors named by the diocesan Ordinary, five by the Ministry of the Interior, who must profess the Catholic faith. A first-instance labour ruling of 16 February 2026 ordered it to hire three outsourced workers; it intends to appeal (own social report).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Self-financed non-profit fabbriceria running Siena Cathedral

f: State body under the Ministry of Culture. Its 2025 budget forecast totals 9,094,257.96 euros: current Ministry transfers of 1,479,500 euros, ticket sales of 800,000 euros, private contributions of 80,000 euros and Ministry investment transfers of 5,816,207.96 euros.
w: Reorganised by a decree of 25 September 2024 into the Musei Nazionali di Bologna with 12 sites. Director Maria Luisa Pacelli's contract was not renewed and ended on 31 October 2024, which she told Open she learned three days before.

f: State museum institute under the Ministry of Culture. Finestre sull'Arte lists 18,827,658.61 euros of investment from 2015 to 2023 and private contributions of 177,500 euros in 2023; the pages read did not name the funders of the investment.
w: Autonomous state institute created in 2015 with four sites in Modena and Sassuolo; the Ferrara gallery passes to the Musei Nazionali di Ferrara from 1 January 2026. Martina Bagnoli directed it from 2015 to 2023.

f: Foundation funded by its members and public grants: in 2024 the Ministry of Culture gave 2,507,842 euros, Compagnia di San Paolo 910,790, Fondazione CRT 670,000 and the European Commission 1,030,000; contributions of the year totalled 9,562,986 euros, and the result was zero.
w: Runs the museum in the Mole Antonelliana, the Cinema Massimo, the Torino Film Festival, TorinoFilmLab and other festivals. Founding members are Regione Piemonte, Città di Torino, Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo, Fondazione CRT, GTT and the Associazione Museo Nazionale del Cinema (museum website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Run by the Consorzio delle Residenze Reali Sabaude, whose members pay yearly: Ministry of Culture 2,000,000 euros, Regione Piemonte 3,000,000, Città di Venaria Reale 50,000, Fondazione Compagnia di San Paolo 2,000,000 and Fondazione 1563 per l'Arte e la Cultura 1,000,000; the press kit puts public members at about 35% of the budget, private members 27% and own income 38%. The 2024 accounts balanced at zero on 15,640,647 euros of production value.
w: Former royal palace restored in a project of over 200 million euros promoted by the EU and funded through the Ministry and Regione Piemonte, and opened on 12 October 2007. A Piedmont Region resolution of 14 April 2025 reports an audited 2024 result of zero and net equity of 5,846,340 euros.
nodes: Fondazione 1563 per l'Arte e la Cultura 1

f: Civic museum operated by the Comune di Trieste, founded on the bequest of Baron Pasquale Revoltella, who left his palace, art collection and a substantial income to the city. The pages read gave no current budget or amounts.
w: Civic museum in three connected buildings. Finestre sull'Arte wrote on 8 July 2022 that Trieste's civic museums had been without a scientific director for at least five years, and il manifesto on 25 February 2023 called the Revoltella a museum 'oggi senza un direttore'.

f: Run by the Veneranda Biblioteca Ambrosiana under a Congregazione dei Conservatori. Artribune (31 January 2026) names Intesa Sanpaolo as financing the Sala dei Fiamminghi and Fondazione Monte di Lombardia as supporting a restoration, and reports a third consecutive surplus budget; no amounts were given.
w: Library and picture gallery founded under Cardinal Federico Borromeo; visitors rose from about 60,000 four years earlier to about 473,000 in 2025 according to its secretary general Antonello Grimaldi.

f: Municipal museums of the Comune di Milano. The Sala delle Asse restoration costs 1,625,000 euros, paid partly by the city and partly by Fondazione Cariplo; the Pala Trivulzio frame restoration of 2023 to 2025 was funded by a Renee Bormioli donation with Pilot Italia S.p.A. and Fondazione Cariplo, no amounts given.
w: The city's Culture Department runs it with Fondazione Cariplo support for the Sala delle Asse, the hall with wall paintings attributed to Leonardo da Vinci, which councillor Tommaso Sacchi said would be reopened for the 2026 Olympics.
nodes: Municipal museums of the Comune di Milano

n: Museo Nazionale della Scienza e della Tecnologia Leonardo da Vinci
f: Foundation under three ministries. In 2024 it received 781,338 euros from the Ministry of Education and Merit, 1,500,000 from the Ministry of University and Research, 335,998 from the Ministry of Culture, 250,000 from Regione Lombardia, 258,200 from the Comune di Milano and 250,000 from the Milan chamber of commerce, plus 1,885,317 euros from private firms, citizens and foundations; surplus 359,744 euros.
w: State-supervised foundation in a building owned by the Comune di Milano, inaugurated on 15 February 1953. The Corte dei conti report on 2024, sent to Parliament on 16 April 2026, is the source of these figures.

f: The pages read did not state a budget or funders for Msheireb Museums. The Art Newspaper (26 November 2015) said the $5.5bn Msheireb redevelopment that includes the museums is backed by Sheikha Mozah bint Nasser.
w: Four historic houses in Downtown Doha turned into museums in October 2015, one of them Bin Jelmood House, which covers the Indian Ocean slave trade and modern exploitation. The Art Newspaper described the complex as Qatar's latest bid to rebrand itself as a culture hub.

f: The pages read did not state a budget or the cost of the restoration. The National (25 October 2018) named the Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi as the body behind the reopening, with its chairman Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak speaking for it.
w: Abu Dhabi's oldest building, an inner fort from around 1795 with an outer palace of 1939, reopened on 7 December 2018 after about a decade closed, together with the Cultural Foundation established by Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan in 1981. The Department of Culture and Tourism Abu Dhabi leads it.
nodes: National named the Department of Culture

f: Privately owned by the Alserkal family: The National (16 June 2014) said one family owns the whole complex. The Alserkal Arts Foundation is supported by Abdelmonem Bin Eisa Alserkal, Ahmad Bin Eisa Alserkal and the family (Alserkal press release, November 2020). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: An arts district of warehouses in Dubai's Al Quoz industrial area, founded in 2007 by Abdelmonem Bin Eisa Alserkal, with over 70 galleries, arts organisations, designers and businesses across 90 warehouses and 500,000 sq ft.

f: Run by the Dubai Culture & Arts Authority, a Dubai government body (The National, 5 January 2017). The article did not state the cost or who funds it.
w: The museum of the founding of the UAE, beside the restored Union House where the 1971 declaration was signed, inaugurated by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid on 2 December 2016. Operated by Dubai Culture & Arts Authority.

f: The pages read did not state who funds it. Khaleej Times (9 June 2008) said it was opened by Sheikh Sultan bin Mohammed Al Qasimi, Ruler of Sharjah, as part of the Sharjah Museums Department's plan.
w: A museum of over 5,000 objects in seven galleries, in a converted early 20th-century souq on the Sharjah corniche, opened in June 2008 by the Ruler of Sharjah. It is part of the Sharjah Museums Department's plan.

f: The pages read did not state how the house is funded. Arab News said Sultan Qaboos bin Said Al Said ordered Oman's first opera house in 2001.
w: A 1,100-seat opera house designed by WATG, ordered by Sultan Qaboos in 2001 and opened in October 2011 with Puccini's Turandot. The pages read did not name its owner or funders.

f: The pages read did not name a funder or cost. The National (13 March 2023) said it was established under royal orders of the late Sultan Qaboos bin Said and inaugurated by Sultan Haitham bin Tarik.
w: A national history museum on a 300,000 square metre site in Manah, opened on 13 March 2023 by Sultan Haitham, its foundation stone laid by Sultan Qaboos on 14 July 2015. No funder was named in the pages read.

f: The pages read did not state who funds it. The National (13 March 2014) said some displays were on loan from the Department of Antiquities and did not name municipal, ministry or donor funding.
w: Jordan's largest museum, nearly 10,000 square metres, showing the 'Ain Ghazal plaster statues of about 7500 BC and Dead Sea Scrolls material. The pages read did not name its funders.

f: The pages read did not state Habima's budget. Jewish News (14 November 2016) reported that under Culture Minister Miri Regev, theatres that perform in settlements get a 10 percent bonus and those that refuse can face a one-third cut in government funding.
w: Israel's national theatre, in Tel Aviv. It performed in Kiryat Arba on 10 November 2016 to Regev's praise; the 2010 boycott row over the Ariel centre that the pages read describe concerned the Beersheva company, not Habima.

f: The pages read did not state the orchestra's funding. The New Arab (7 November 2025) did not mention funding.
w: An orchestra whose concert at the Paris Philharmonie on 6 November 2025 was interrupted by protesters with flares; four people were detained, and the musicians returned and finished the concert (The New Arab, 7 November 2025).
why: The New Arab, 7 November 2025, reported that protesters set off flares during the orchestra's Paris concert on 6 November 2025 and four people were detained.

n: Anu Museum of the Jewish People
f: The $100 million renewal reopened in March 2021: nearly a third came from the Nadav Foundation of Leonid Nevzlin, described as a former oil magnate, $52 million from other US philanthropists and foundations, and $18 million from the Israeli government (AP via KOMO, 10 March 2021). Its US arm, American Friends of Beth Hatefutsot, reported revenue of $42,843,588 in 2023 and $3,129,307 in 2024 (ProPublica).
w: Formerly Beit Hatfutsot, a museum of Jewish life that reopened in March 2021 after a $100 million rebuild. The largest donor group was the Nadav Foundation of Leonid Nevzlin, a former oil magnate per AP; the Israeli government gave $18 million.

f: The Jewish Chronicle (1 June 2023) said the refurbishment was supported in part by Dame Vivien Duffield and the Clore Israel Foundation, put the refurbishment at $50 million in its text, and said the museum is over 84 per cent self-funded (Jewish Chronicle, 1 June 2023).
w: Jerusalem's city museum in the Old City, reopened in June 2023 after a renewal backed by Dame Vivien Duffield and the Clore Israel Foundation. It is over 84 per cent self-funded per the Jewish Chronicle.

f: The pages read did not state cost or funders. Hürriyet Daily News (30 September 2019) said the renovation took nearly eight years and was announced by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism, with Deputy Minister Nadir Alpaslan opening the renovated building on 27 September 2019.
w: A Ministry of Culture and Tourism museum complex whose main building reopened on 27 September 2019 after nearly eight years of restoration, with seven exhibition halls and a store. The other two buildings were to open in 2020.

f: Authority over the building passed to the Directorate of Religious Affairs by decree on 10 July 2020 (Hürriyet Daily News, 10 July 2020). Since 15 January 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Tourism charges foreign visitors 25 euros; Turkish citizens visiting for religious reasons enter free (Orthodox Times, 15 January 2024).
w: Turned from museum to mosque on 10 July 2020 when President Erdoğan signed a decree minutes after the Council of State annulled the 1934 museum decision, over objections from UNESCO, Greece and others. The Ministry of Culture and Tourism has charged foreigners 25 euros since 15 January 2024.
nodes: Turkish citizens visiting for religious reasons enter free

f: The pages read did not state funders. Bianet said a 1948 restoration was sponsored by the Byzantine Institute of America and Dumbarton Oaks.
w: A Byzantine church made a mosque in 1511, a museum by a 1945 cabinet decree, and opened to worship again as a mosque on 21 August 2020 after the Council of State ruled on 11 November 2019 that its museum use was contrary to law (Bianet).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Run by the Rahmi M. Koç Museology and Cultural Foundation, which acquired and restored the buildings; Rahmi M. Koç chaired its trustees (Koç Holding page). The page did not state how the museums are funded.
w: A museum of industrial and transport history on the Golden Horn, opened in 1994 by a foundation chaired by Rahmi M. Koç, mostly from his private collection. The Koç Holding page lists further sites in Ankara and Ayvalık.

f: Run by the Ministry of Culture and Tourism; Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy inspected the renovation (Hürriyet Daily News, 23 July 2026). The article gave no cost or funding.
w: A Ministry museum in the 15th-century Mahmut Paşa Bedesteni and Kurşunlu Han, which unveiled a renewed display of 288 newly shown artifacts in July 2026 after works begun in May 2026.
nodes: Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy inspected the renovation

f: The page read did not state funders. Hürriyet Daily News (23 April 2023) did not mention the Packard Humanities Institute or any other funder.
w: A Ministry-run mosaic museum, closed 74 days after the 6 February 2023 earthquakes without damage and reopened in April 2023. Its display holds 2,500 square metres of mosaics, including the Gypsy Girl, and 12 pieces returned from the US in 2018.

f: Mainly public. The 2009-10 statement of revenues shows restricted grants from the Egyptian Ministry of Finance of EGP 110,080,500 out of total revenues of EGP 165,699,937 for the year ending 30 June 2010 (annual report overview 2009-10). Donors giving more than EGP 10 million since 2002 include USAID, the European Commission, the Qatar Emirate, the Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development and the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation.
w: A library, museums and research complex governed under Presidential Decree No. 76 of 2001 by a Council of Patrons and a Board of Trustees. In November 2011 staff protested to have its founding director Ismail Serageldin removed, over hiring rules and ties to the Mubarak regime (Intellectual Property Watch, 6 November 2011).
why: About 1,700 of roughly 2,300 staff took part in protests of more than a week in Alexandria demanding the removal of director Ismail Serageldin, Intellectual Property Watch reported on 6 November 2011.
