About 1,700 of roughly 2,300 staff took part in protests of more than a week in Alexandria demanding the removal of director Ismail Serageldin, Intellectual Property Watch reported on 6 November 2011.

f: Mainly public. Revenue of R203.7 million in 2024/25 included a Department of Sport, Arts and Culture subsidy of R102.1 million, conditional grants of R8.6 million, services in kind for property leases of R57.6 million, admission fees of R10.5 million and sponsorship of R4.1 million (Annual Report 2024/25).
w: The umbrella body for national museums in Cape Town, a Public Entity reporting to the Department of Sport, Arts and Culture. Its 2024/25 report records a deficit of R11.4 million, a qualified audit opinion on heritage asset management and a withdrawn plan to absorb two museums in Bloemfontein.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Donor funded. The site says it was established with Sweden (Sida), Belgium, the Clinton Foundation and the Wasserman Foundation, and names the Pears Foundation, the Annenberg Foundation, Canada, Japan, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and South Korea (KOICA) for later work. Corporate sponsors named include Airtel, Ecobank, I&M Bank, Vivo Energy, BK Group, Bralirwa and Rwanda Energy Group (memorial website).
w: The Kigali City Council owns the land and the Aegis Trust, a UK charity, manages the memorial for Rwanda's Ministry of National Unity and Civic Engagement. It is the burial place of 250,000 victims and hosts the Genocide Archive of Rwanda.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Public capital plus philanthropy. The Johannesburg Development Agency page lists Blue IQ, the Gauteng Provincial Government, the City of Johannesburg, the Department of Justice and philanthropic organisations as funders of the project. The Mellon Foundation gave the Trust $450,000 in 2021 and $129,000 in 2020, and the Mott Foundation $500,000 for 2017 to 2019 (grant pages).
w: A precinct containing the Constitutional Court and the Old Fort Prison Complex, where Gandhi and Mandela were held, delivered by the Johannesburg Development Agency. The Trust runs the site and plans a museum and archive.

f: The pages read did not state amounts or income sources. The Trust was founded in 1972 by Maharaja Gaj Singh of Jodhpur and is run by trustees headed by him as Managing Trustee (Trust website).
w: A private trust of the Jodhpur royal family that runs the museum in Mehrangarh Fort, the Maharaja Man Singh Pustak Prakash library and the Rao Jodha Desert Rock Park.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state funding. The site's copyright is credited to The James H. W. Thompson Foundation; admission is 250 baht for adults and 150 baht for ages 10 to 21 (museum website).
w: The former Bangkok home of James H.W. Thompson, known as the Thai Silk King, which holds his Asian art collection. A different body from the Jim Thompson Art Center.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state how the museum is funded. Returned objects came from a private collector, a UK dealer's estate and US museums, not from donors to the museum (AKP, 21 November 2025; The Star, 28 February 2026).
w: Cambodia's main museum of Khmer antiquities, run under the Ministry of Culture and Fine Arts. It has been the venue for returns of looted Khmer objects since 2024, including 296 objects from István Zelnik on 20 November 2025 and 74 objects from the Latchford estate in February 2026.

f: The Free State of Saxony is the Träger of the Sächsische Staatstheater, Staatsoper Dresden (miz). The Berliner Zeitung wrote on 3 March 2026 that the state grant for the Semperoper and the Staatsschauspiel Dresden was cut by 7.3 million euros in the previous year and by a further 5.9 million euros in 2026 (Berliner Zeitung, 3 March 2026). The pages read did not give the opera's budget or its sponsors' names.
w: Opera house on Theaterplatz that houses the Sächsische Staatskapelle Dresden, the Semperoper Ballett and the Staatsopernchor, run by the Free State of Saxony. Its funding is a state grant that was cut in 2025 and 2026 (Berliner Zeitung, 3 March 2026).

f: The Gewandhaus and its orchestra are financed mainly from public funds, with the City of Leipzig as sole sponsor since 1920; a sponsor network and the Freundeskreis cover what base funding does not (L-IZ, 24 May 2024). The Stiftung Zukunft Gewandhaus zu Leipzig, recognised on 7 December 2023, holds 1.5 million euros of capital. The Stadtrat approved the 2026 Wirtschaftsplan on 26 March 2026 and the city is to cover about 5.8 million euros of extra costs across its cultural institutions (L-IZ, 12 April 2026).
w: Leipzig's concert hall and orchestra, a municipal Eigenbetrieb, founded as a concert society in 1743 by sixteen citizens. Its newest funder is a foundation set up in 2023 by five private founders and the Stadt- und Kreissparkasse Leipzig.
nodes: Freundeskreis cover what base funding does not

f: The choir is an Einrichtung der Stadt Leipzig (choir website).
w: Boys' choir of Leipzig, a city institution led by the Thomaskantor, Andreas Reize since September 2021; his contract is proposed to run to 30 June 2034 (L-IZ, 26 May 2025). His appointment drew a protest from older choristers in 2021.

f: The opera belongs to the Städtische Bühnen Frankfurt GmbH, the client of the building (miz). A 2017 feasibility study put renovation of the Städtische Bühnen building at 840 to 880 million euros (miz).
w: Frankfurt's opera, part of the Städtische Bühnen with the Schauspiel, in a building from 1902 with later phases of 1951 and 1963 that has a renovation or replacement still under discussion. Generalmusikdirektor is Thomas Guggeis (opera website).

f: The Stadt Bochum's press office issued the announcement of the new Intendant, and the Verwaltungsrat of the house is chaired by Bochum's Kulturdezernent Dietmar Dieckmann (Stadt Bochum press release, 26 September 2024). as partners.
w: Municipal theatre of Bochum with several stages, led by Intendant Johan Simons, whose contract was due to end on 31 July 2026 and was extended by a year; Nicolas Stemann becomes Intendant in summer 2027 (Stadt Bochum, 26 September 2024).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The City of Cologne pays for the Bühnen Köln and for their renovation: the Rat approved a cost budget of 798.6 million euros on 1 October 2024 (Stadt Köln, 21 March 2025). dpa put the cost at well over one billion euros at the reopening on 24 September 2026 (infranken.de). The pages read gave no operating grant.
w: The Schauspiel reopened at the Offenbachplatz on 24 September 2026 after 14 years in interim venues, under Kay Voges (infranken.de). Its renovation, with the Oper, rose from 347.8 million euros in 2016 to a 798.6 million euro budget (Steuerzahlerbund; Stadt Köln).

f: The City of Cologne pays for the opera and for the renovation of the Bühnen: a cost budget of 798.6 million euros was approved by the Rat on 1 October 2024 (Stadt Köln, 21 March 2025), and dpa put the cost at well over one billion euros on 24 September 2026 (infranken.de). The opera's site shows the logos of Stadt Köln and REWE Group without stating their role.
w: Opera house by Wilhelm Riphahn, opened in 1957, reopened on 24 September 2026 under Intendant Hein Mulders after 14 years; the renovation cost rose from 347.8 million euros in 2016 to a budget of 798.6 million euros (infranken.de; Steuerzahlerbund; Stadt Köln).
nodes: REWE Group without stating their role

f: The concert programme is run by KölnMusik Betriebs- und Servicegesellschaft mbH, whose supervisory board has representatives of the City of Cologne and of WDR; its annual statements for 2020 to 2025 are linked on its site.
w: Concert hall opened in 1986 beneath the Heinrich-Böll-Platz, with the WDR Sinfonieorchester and the Gürzenich-Orchester Köln as house orchestras; Ewa Bogusz-Moore is artistic director and managing director of KölnMusik.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The City of Düsseldorf funds the renovation of the building: the Rat approved about 34.9 million euros for the facade on 24 September 2026, and federal funding is to be applied for part of the energy-related work (City of Düsseldorf press release). The hall is operated by Tonhalle Düsseldorf gGmbH; the pages read gave no operating grant.
w: Concert hall in the listed building at the Ehrenhof erected in 1926; a facade renovation of about 34.9 million euros is planned from the second quarter of 2027 for 38 months while concerts continue.

n: Deutsche Oper am Rhein (Düsseldorf und Duisburg)
f: The cities of Düsseldorf and Duisburg share the cost 70% and 30%, and their joint sponsorship runs to the end of 2034/35 (miz, 16 July 2025). The pages read gave no euro figures.
w: Opera and ballet company playing in Düsseldorf (180 performances a season) and Duisburg (78). Düsseldorf's council stopped plans for a new opera building, estimated at about 1.8 billion euros, on 5 June 2026 and will renovate the existing house.

f: The Land of Lower Saxony announced 28 million euros on 22 July 2025 for the building and technical development of the Staatstheater Hannover, from its draft 2026 budget; the city is not named as a funder in that release (Hannover.de). The supervisory board of the Niedersächsische Staatstheater Hannover GmbH is chaired by Culture Minister Falko Mohrs.
w: Opera of the Niedersächsische Staatstheater Hannover GmbH, owned by the state; Bodo Busse is opera Intendant from 2025/26. In February 2023 its ballet director Marco Goecke smeared dog excrement on a critic and was suspended.

f: The Stuttgarter Zeitung wrote on 30 November 2025 that the City of Stuttgart's double budget for 2026 and 2027 plans to cut more than 4 million euros of grants to the Staatstheater Stuttgart; ballet director Tamas Detrich publicly opposed it. The pages read did not give the Land's or the city's regular grant.
w: Three-branch house, with the Staatsoper, the Stuttgarter Ballett and the Schauspiel, owned by the state of Baden-Württemberg and the city. The opera building's renovation and a planned cut of city grants are the money issues on the pages read.

f: The cantons of Basel-Stadt and Basel-Landschaft, sponsors and Genossenschafter are thanked for their support in the 2024/25 annual report release, which gave no franc sums for them. The house recorded an operating result of CHF 510,000 and a loss of about CHF 181,000 for 2024/25; the bz Basel is media partner (Theater Basel media release, November 2025).
w: Three-branch theatre (opera, drama, ballet) led by Intendant Benedikt von Peter; in May 2024 it announced Marco Goecke, who had smeared a critic with dog excrement in Hannover in 2023, as ballet director from summer 2025 (SRF, 22 May 2024).

f: Public contributions were CHF 91.351 million in 2023/24 and CHF 88.472 million in 2022/23, against CHF 11.180 million and CHF 10.066 million from donations and sponsors and CHF 24.712 million from performances in 2023/24 (Opernhaus media release, 17 December 2024). In 2024/25 total revenue was CHF 135.9 million with a loss of CHF 0.54 million, and the canton's contribution rose by CHF 2.5 million while sponsor and donation income fell by CHF 1.4 million (Regierungsrat decision 440, 15 April 2026).
w: Opera and ballet house run by the Opernhaus Zürich AG under an ownership strategy of the Kanton Zürich, whose Regierungsrat names six of the eleven Verwaltungsrat members. The pages read did not name its sponsors.

f: The Regierungsrat of the Kanton Zürich granted the City of Zürich CHF 7,422,000 from the Kulturfonds on 24 June 2026 for the Kunstgesellschaft, the Schauspielhaus and the Tonhalle-Gesellschaft, of which CHF 1,872,000 are for the Tonhalle-Gesellschaft Zürich AG: Beethoven 2027 CHF 805,000, an app CHF 357,000 and infrastructure CHF 710,000, subject to approval by the Kantonsrat.
w: Orchestra and concert house run by the Tonhalle-Gesellschaft Zürich AG; Paavo Järvi is music director. The pages read give only the cantonal lottery-fund grant.

f: The main sponsors are the Kühne Foundation, Roche, UBS and Zurich Insurance, with Carl F. Bucherer a partner (Lucerne Festival website). Blick reported on 16 February 2025 that private main sponsors Sibylla and Christoph M. Müller did not renew a mid-six-figure sum over two former Credit Suisse chairmen sitting on the foundation board; the festival said it regrets this and that the Schwöbel family (owners of B. Braun) and the Jörg G. Bucherer Foundation add support.
w: Festival with the Lucerne Festival Orchestra and Academy whose artistic director is Michael Haefliger. Sponsors' money is large and contested in 2023 to 2025 over Credit Suisse's former chairmen on its board.
why: Blick reported on 16 February 2025 that private main sponsors Sibylla and Christoph M. Müller did not renew their support over two former Credit Suisse chairmen on the festival's foundation board.
nodes: Blick reported on 16 February 2025 that private main sponsors Sibylla and Christoph M. Müller did not renew their support over two former Credit Suisse chairmen on the festival's foundation board.

f: The pages read named no funders of the festival itself. Its archive is kept by the Claude Nobs Foundation, created in 2013, whose main donor is Audemars Piguet, with Millennium, Western Digital, Ernst Göhner Stiftung, Logitech, Loro, Memoriav and Fondation Casino Barrière Montreux also listed (Claude Nobs Foundation).
w: Festival founded in 1967 by Claude Nobs. Its concert archive of about 5,000 concerts since 1967 was inscribed in 2013 on the UNESCO Memory of the World Register and is digitised with EPFL; the Montreux Jazz Festival Foundation joined that partnership in 2024.
nodes: Fondation Casino Barrière Montreux also listed

f: The Ticino Grand Council approved CHF 17 million over the next five years for the festival on 12 June 2025, almost unanimously; many festival events are financed by sponsors or the City of Locarno (RSI, 12 June 2025). The Confederation is to end cultural partnerships from 2029, which affects the festival (RSI headline).
w: Film festival on the Piazza Grande with the Pardo awards. The canton's five-year grant of CHF 17 million was approved in June 2025 after amendments to cut it by 5% and to tie it to labour conditions were rejected.

f: Public bodies and five private founders. In 2024 public contributions were EUR 21,699,779 (State ordinary EUR 13,591,248, Regione Piemonte EUR 2,280,000, Città di Torino EUR 4,000,000); private founders paid EUR 3,617,000 and tickets brought EUR 6,203,517 (2024 accounts).
w: Opera foundation in Piazza Castello, Turin, chaired by the mayor. A EUR 25,000,000 loan from the Ministry of Culture and the Ministry of Economy, repayable over 30 years at 0.50%, followed the approval of its recovery plan (2024 accounts).

f: The home page lists the Ministry of Culture and the Comune di Parma among its partners, and as sponsors Chiesi (main partner), Fondazione Cariparma (major partner), Crédit Agricole (cultural partner), Iren (main sponsor of the season and the Festival Verdi) and Publitalia (media partner). The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Opera house on Strada Garibaldi in Parma that runs the Festival Verdi. The pages read did not state the foundation's accounts.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Public bodies and private partners. The Ministry of Culture lists a charge of EUR 10,880,696 on its budget for 2025; the Region, the Comune, and the private partners CRB, BolognaFiere, Hera and Pelliconi sit on the board (Ministry of Culture page). The 2024 result was a loss of EUR 1,616,288.
w: Opera foundation chaired by the mayor of Bologna; Elisabetta Riva became superintendent by ministerial decree of 23 April 2025.

f: Public bodies and Iren as private partner. The Ministry of Culture lists a charge of EUR 11,277,536 on its budget for 2025; the Comune, Region and Ministry sit on the board (Ministry of Culture page).
w: Genoa opera foundation chaired by the mayor, Silvia Salis, with Michele Galli as superintendent by ministerial decree of 23 April 2025.

f: Public bodies. In 2023 operating contributions were EUR 26,982,540 of EUR 33,754,943 total value of production (2023 accounts); the Ministry of Culture lists a charge of EUR 16,017,537 on its budget for 2025.
w: Palermo opera foundation chaired by the mayor, Roberto Lagalla; Marco Betta became superintendent by ministerial decree of 19 November 2024.

f: Four founders: the Ministry of Culture, Regione Puglia, Comune di Bari and Città Metropolitana di Bari (foundation website, Il Post). The Ministry of Culture lists a charge of EUR 10,231,766 on its budget for 2025. The pages read did not state the other founders' amounts.
w: Bari opera foundation chaired by the mayor; Nazzareno Carusi became superintendent by ministerial decree of 3 November 2025. Il Post reported in July 2025 on the regional president's own appointment to its board.

f: Wholly owned by public bodies: Regione Campania, Provincia di Salerno and Comune di Ravello. Il Post wrote in 2021 that the Campania Region is its principal member and finances the festival; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: Foundation that has run the Ravello Festival since 2003 and Villa Rufolo since 2007. In June 2021 its president Antonio Scurati resigned after a row over guests and the Region's role.

n: Museo Archeologico Nazionale di Reggio Calabria (MArRC)
f: The museum site sits on the Ministry of Culture's cultura.gov.it domain. The pages read did not state its budget or funders.
w: State archaeological museum in Piazza De Nava, Reggio Calabria, home of the Riace Bronzes.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: The pages read did not state who funds the museum or give amounts; the site has a Fondazione section and a foundation contact address.
w: Museum in Orani, Sardinia, devoted to the sculptor Costantino Nivola (Orani 1911 to Long Island 1988). The site says it is closed from 9 to 28 November 2026 for renovation.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A consortium of the Generalitat de Catalunya, the Ministerio de Cultura and the Ajuntament de Barcelona. In 2024 total income was EUR 20,023,314: EUR 14,238,425 from administrations, EUR 5,058,741 own income (tickets EUR 2,145,501, space rental and concessions EUR 2,215,488) and EUR 180,438 sponsorship (annual report 2024).
w: Barcelona's national art museum, run by a consortium of three administrations, director Pepe Serra. In December 2025 the lawyer for the Sijena monastery asked a court for Serra's resignation and EUR 90,000 over remarks about the Sijena murals (Ara, 24 December 2025).

f: The site identifies the museum as part of the Ministerio de Cultura of the Government of Spain. The pages read did not state a budget or amounts.
w: State museum of Spanish sculpture on three sites in Valladolid, including the Colegio de San Gregorio.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: Patronato de la Alhambra y Generalife
f: Mainly its own ticket income. The Andalusian budget for 2025 puts the Patronato's income at EUR 42,155,156, of which EUR 40,042,585 is public prices for visits and cultural activities and EUR 464,071 is an FEDER transfer (Junta de Andalucía budget 2025).
w: The body that protects and runs the Alhambra and Generalife, with a standard day ticket at EUR 22.27 (Patronato website). Groups of 11 to 30 count as group visits and authorised agents get 39% of annual ticket capacity.

f: The site carries the Ayuntamiento de Madrid logo and a Madrid Destino Cultura Turismo y Negocio, S.A. footer, and tickets link to a Madrid Destino store. The pages read did not state amounts.
w: Madrid municipal theatre on Calle del Príncipe, tied to the city council and its company Madrid Destino.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Donations and endowment carry the museum: the 2023 Form 990 shows $12,880,628 in contributions and $3,236,828 in investment income against $818,681 of program revenue. The C. Jean & Myles McDonough Charitable Foundation gave $10 million in 2019, the largest single gift in the museum's history, after $4 million in 2015. The capital campaign A Bold Step Forward seeks $125 million by 2028 (museum website).
w: Founded by the Worcester philanthropist Stephen Salisbury III, who gave land and $100,000, and opened on 10 May 1898 (museum website). Its Higgins Armory collection is the core of an arms and armor collection the museum calls the second largest of its kind in the Americas (museum press release, 22 April 2024).

n: Rhode Island School of Design Museum (RISD Museum)
f: The museum is run on behalf of the Rhode Island School of Design, whose own Form 990 for 2023 shows $228,805,896 in revenue, of which $187,784,480 is program service revenue and $16,002,179 contributions. Acquisitions are credited to named funds, among them the Helen M. Danforth Acquisition Fund, the Richard Brown Baker Fund for Contemporary British Art and the Mary B. Jackson Fund (museum website). The pages read did not give the museum's own budget.
w: Established in 1877 and overseen by a Museum Board of Governors and Fine Arts Committee on behalf of the RISD Board of Trustees (museum website). It is part of a school, so its finances are reported inside RISD's accounts.
nodes: Richard Brown Baker Fund for Contemporary British Art

f: Mainly donations and endowment: the 2023 Form 990 shows $2,430,613 in contributions, $775,347 in investment income and $438,225 in program revenue against expenses of $10,412,965. The museum rests on the estate of the former governor Moody Currier and his wife Hannah Slade Currier (museum website).
w: Chartered by the state legislature in 1919 as the Currier Gallery of Art; the building opened in October 1929 (museum website). Deputy director Karen Graham was interim executive director from April 2023 and resigned in September 2024, and Jordana Pomeroy is listed as Director and CEO (Manchester InkLink, 10 September 2024; museum website).

f: Donations carry the museums: the Form 990 for Springfield Museums Corporation shows $6,154,164 in contributions, $1,727,447 in investment income and $1,336,818 in program revenue for 2023. MassMutual is listed as Season Supporter, and the Massachusetts Cultural Council and the Art Bridges Foundation appear among partners (museum website). A National Endowment for the Humanities grant funded digitising the George Walter Vincent Smith archives from 2020 (museum website).
w: Five museums and the Dr. Seuss National Memorial Sculpture Garden around a quadrangle, tracing back to the City Library Association formed on 27 November 1857; the Seuss garden (2002) was authorized by Audrey Geisel and the Amazing World of Dr. Seuss Museum opened in 2017 (museum website). In October 2017 the museums and Dr. Seuss Enterprises dropped a mural of a Chinese man after three authors withdrew from a festival (New England Public Media, 9 October 2017).

On 9 October 2017 New England Public Media reported that the museum, after authors Mo Willems, Mike Curato and Lisa Yee withdrew from its children's literature festival over a mural showing a Chinese man, agreed with Dr. Seuss Enterprises to remove it; the festival was cancelled. The mural came from a Seuss book of 1937.

f: Donations and investments: the 2023 Form 990 shows $5,067,480 in contributions and $683,405 in investment income against $477,726 of program revenue. The museum is supported in part by the Delaware Division of the Arts, in partnership with the National Endowment for the Arts (museum website). In 2014 it sold works from its collection to pay debt and build an operating endowment (AAMD, 18 June 2014).
w: Formed in 1912 as the Wilmington Society of the Fine Arts around the work of Howard Pyle, it opened in June 1938 as the Delaware Art Center and holds the Samuel Bancroft Jr. Pre-Raphaelite collection (museum website). The Association of Art Museum Directors sanctioned it on 18 June 2014 for selling a work to pay debt (AAMD).

f: Endowment, gifts and earned income: the 2023 Form 990 for the Henry Francis Du Pont Winterthur Museum shows $5,685,503 in contributions, $4,143,918 in investment income and $2,381,515 in program revenue against expenses of $27,961,220, with assets of $420,321,549. Henry Francis du Pont secured its future through a gift in his will (museum website).
w: The house, collection and garden of Henry Francis du Pont, turned into a museum in 1951 and left to the institution by his will in 1969 (museum website). It holds more than 90,000 objects and a research library open to the public.
nodes: Henry Francis du Pont secured its future

f: Donations and investments: the 2023 Form 990 for the Eleutherian Mills-Hagley Foundation shows $4,406,808 in contributions, $3,428,477 in investment income and $360,399 in program revenue against expenses of $12,201,266. The museum site names no funders in the text read; it points to a Corporate Partners page (museum website).
w: The site of the gunpowder works founded by E. I. du Pont in 1802, with the du Pont family's ancestral home and gardens, plus a business-history library (museum website). It has been accredited by the American Alliance of Museums since 1972 and became Delaware's first Smithsonian Affiliate on 2 June 2014.

f: Mostly gifts: the 2023 Form 990 for the Brandywine Conservancy & Museum of Art shows $13,956,454 in contributions, $2,932,536 in investment income and $1,355,329 in program revenue, and in 2022 $17,604,874 in contributions. Corporate sponsors underwrite exhibitions and education, but the page read named none (museum website).
w: The museum is the arts arm of a land conservancy founded in 1967 by local residents and George A. 'Frolic' Weymouth; it opened in 1971 in a restored 1864 gristmill and centres on the art of the Brandywine region, especially the Wyeth family (museum website).

f: Mostly donations and investment income: the 2023 Form 990 shows $1,874,789 in contributions, $316,686 in investment income and $175,769 in program revenue against expenses of $3,042,000. The museum announced a $17 million fundraising campaign in 2018 and credits its Meighan and Abend Funds (museum website).
w: Grew from the Syracuse Museum of Fine Arts, founded in 1897 by George Fisk Comfort; Helen Everson's 1941 bequest led to the Everson Museum, chartered in 1949, and it opened in I.M. Pei's first museum design in 1968 (museum website).

f: Grants, contributions and donations were more than 60% of revenue in 2020 to 2022, and investments 8% to 10% (Erie County Comptroller, January 2026). Erie County gave $155,000 in 2020 and 2021 and $160,000 in 2022 (Erie County Comptroller); the museum credits the New York State Council on the Arts, SUNY Buffalo State, the National Endowment for the Arts, the City of Buffalo and private funders including the Baird, Cullen, Wendt, Joy Family and Rumsey foundations and M&T Bank (museum website).
w: Created in 1966 at the State University College at Buffalo as the Charles Burchfield Center, renamed the Burchfield Penney Art Center in 1994, and now an independent nonprofit on the Buffalo State campus with an ongoing relationship with the university (museum website). The Erie County Comptroller audited its county grants for 2020 to 2022 and found its documentation adequate (Comptroller report, 30 January 2026).

n: Memorial Art Gallery of the University of Rochester
f: Supported primarily by its members and the University of Rochester, with the New York State Council on the Arts; Monroe County makes half-price Thursday admission possible (museum website). In May 2026 it announced it had raised more than $9 million to make general admission free in 2027, including $3 million from Doug and Abby Bennett with the Sands Family Foundation, $2 million from Mary Ellen Burris and $1 million from Al and Lucy Levitan (University of Rochester).
w: Emily Sibley Watson gave it to the community in 1913 and it was free for its first 56 years; it is one of the few university art museums that also operates as a public museum (University of Rochester, May 2026). It is part of the University of Rochester, so its accounts are inside the university's.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Earned income carries most of the budget: the 2023 Form 990 shows $13,925,773 in program service revenue, $2,171,147 in investment income and $504,615 in contributions, against expenses of $18,584,785. Its programs are made possible by the New York State Council on the Arts with the Office of the Governor and the State Legislature (museum website). The founding wealth came from the Munson family's industrial interests (museum website).
w: Chartered in 1919 as 'an artistic, musical and social center' by Maria Williams Proctor, her husband Thomas R. Proctor and her brother-in-law Frederick Proctor, opened in May 1936 and renamed Munson in 2023; it runs a museum, performing arts and, with Pratt Institute, the Pratt Munson college programme (museum website).

f: Mostly donations and government support: the 2023 Form 990 shows $2,899,097 in contributions, $327,229 in program revenue and $58,935 in investment income against expenses of $3,070,374. Its supporters page lists Westchester County, the City of Yonkers and New York State, the Institute of Museum and Library Services ($50,000 to $99,999) and the Thomas and Agnes Carvel Foundation ($50,000 to $99,999) (museum website). A federal grant of $124,930 was terminated in April 2025 (museum website).
w: Founded in 1919 with the Yonkers Art Association and moved in 1924 into Glenview, a mansion built in 1877 and bought by the City of Yonkers (museum website). Its Institute of Museum and Library Services digitisation grant was terminated in April 2025 (museum website; HVNY).
nodes: Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA)

n: New Britain Museum of American Art
f: Donations and investments: the 2024 Form 990 shows $2,970,835 in contributions, $1,120,556 in investment income and $359,514 in program revenue against expenses of $5,884,776. The museum names Alix W. Stanley, who gave $40,000 for a wing in 1950 and funds for nearly 280 artworks, Grace Judd Landers, and the A. W. Stanley and Paul Zimmerman Funds (museum website).
w: It traces its roots to the New Britain Institute of 1853, began acquiring American art in 1894 and calls itself the nation's first museum devoted exclusively to American art (museum website).

f: Donations and investments: the 2023 Form 990 shows $2,829,536 in contributions, $530,516 in investment income and $398,159 in program revenue against expenses of $4,931,000, with assets of $33,154,429. The pages read named no individual funders.
w: Opened in 1988 in the former Bucks County prison in Doylestown and named for the novelist James Michener, born in the town in 1907; Bruce Katsiff was its first director (WHYY). Its collection centres on Pennsylvania Impressionism (WHYY).

f: Free admission is provided by Amanda and Glenn Fuhrman (museum website). It is part of the University of Pennsylvania and does not collect art; its two named directorships carry the names Daniel W. Dietrich II and DAJ (museum website). The pages read did not give its budget.
w: Founded in 1963 at the University of Pennsylvania as a non-collecting institution; Johanna Burton is the Daniel W. Dietrich II Director and appointed Sara O'Keeffe as DAJ Director and Curator of Public Engagement and Research in July 2026 (museum website).
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Revenue was $13,559,963 in the year to June 2023, of which $11,921,646 was contributions and $1,434,749 program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name its individual funders beyond the Teel family, whose name is on the 2010 pavilion.
w: A museum begun from the collection of Edwin and Margaret Crocker, whose gallery building and collection Margaret gave to the City of Sacramento in 1885. The 2010 Teel Family Pavilion more than tripled its size.

f: Revenue was $18,950,542 in the year to June 2022, with $7,716,448 in contributions and $1,823,205 in program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name individual funders; galleries and wings carry the names McCormick, Morton, Keck, Peck, Luria and Ridley-Tree.
w: Opened in 1941 in the former Santa Barbara Post Office. In January 2024 the Santa Barbara Independent reported that new director Amada Cruz cancelled a major exhibition on diversity grounds and eliminated the chief curator's post.

f: Revenue was $10,450,340 in the year to June 2023, with $5,593,724 in contributions and $2,883,223 in program service revenue (Form 990). The museum said in August 2026 that it received a $25,000 federal grant in 2025 and none since; the building belongs to the City of San Diego.
w: Opened in 1926 in Balboa Park; Appleton S. Bridges funded the building, which was transferred to the City of San Diego on opening. The Art Newspaper reported on 12 August 2026 that it laid off 11 employees on 5 August.

f: The pages read said the Timken family of Canton, Ohio, and the Putnam sisters were the main benefactors, with the Timken Foundation paying for a large part of the picture gallery. The pages read did not state amounts or a current budget.
w: Opened in 1965 in Balboa Park to house the Putnam Foundation's collection of European old masters, American art and Russian icons, set up in 1950 by sisters Anne and Amy Putnam.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Revenue was $6,708,179 in the year to June 2023, of which $5,223,313 was contributions and $239,861 program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name its individual funders.
w: A folk art and design museum in Balboa Park, founded in 1978 according to its site. Expenses ($8,343,740) exceeded revenue in the years to June 2022 and 2023.

f: Revenue was $3,272,330 in the year to June 2024, with $2,142,352 in contributions and $553,170 in program service revenue (Form 990). Its site names Bank of America and The Segerstrom Foundation as supporters; the Segerstrom Foundation provides free admission for children 12 and under.
w: Founded by local artists in 1918; collects California art from 1860 to the present, built almost entirely through gifts.

f: The Helen Diller Family Foundation is thanked on its site for supporting the Helen Diller Institute. The Chronicle-sourced KQED report of 18 March 2026 said expenses exceeded revenue by over $5.9 million in the year to June 2024 and that a bank-held construction-related loan accounted for $1.5 million of annual expenses.
w: Founded in 1984; Daniel Libeskind building opened 2008. It closed to the public in December 2024 for at least a year, cut staff, and announced on 18 March 2026 that it would sell the building.
why: Seven or more artists, including the group California Jewish Artists for Palestine, withdrew work from its 'California Jewish Open' in April 2024 after the museum refused demands over wall text and funding (KQED, 8 April 2024). Interim executive director Kerry King said the museum would not join the
nodes: Seven or more artists, including the group California Jewish Artists for Palestine, withdrew work from its 'California Jewish Open' in April 2024 after the museum refused demands over wall text and funding (KQED, 8 April 2024). Interim executive director Kerry King said the museum would not join the Palestinian Academic and Cultural Boycott of Israel.

f: Revenue was $4,868,575 in 2023, of which $4,553,431 was contributions and $190,583 program service revenue (Form 990). Its site says it relies on donors, members and grants from foundations, corporations and government, and names Kaiser Permanente as sponsor of Thrive @ MoAD.
w: Opened in 2005 on the ground floor of the St. Regis, San Francisco. KQED reported on 31 March 2020 that it laid off seven staff and cut the hours of the other 11 during the pandemic closure.

f: Revenue was $61,024,177 in the year to June 2023, with $24,434,650 in contributions and $30,146,997 in program service revenue (Form 990). A $300 million capital campaign paid for the Pier 15 building, which opened on 17 April 2013 (CBS News).
w: A San Francisco science museum on Pier 15 since April 2013, after about 40 years at the Palace of Fine Arts. In 2020 layoffs and hours reductions affected about 85% of employees (KQED, 1 April 2020).

f: Part of Stanford University. The Stanfords funded the original museum, which was not separately endowed; it is named for lead donors Iris and B. Gerald Cantor. The Capital Group Foundation gave more than 1,000 photographs.
w: Opened in 1894 as the Leland Stanford Jr. Museum, part of Stanford University; renamed in 1999. Admission is always free.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Revenue was $5,864,094 in the year to June 2023, with $5,003,408 in contributions and $279,703 in program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name individual funders.
w: An art museum in downtown San Jose run by the San Jose Museum of Art Association, a nonprofit filing Form 990.

f: Net assets were $58,658,604 in the year to June 2023, with $2,786,321 in contributions and $240,223 in program service revenue (Form 990). Erivan and Helga Haub gave their Western American art collection and $20 million for a building expansion in 2012.
w: Tacoma's art museum, whose Haub Family Collection of Western American Art came from the German couple Erivan and Helga Haub in 2012; Seattle Magazine (4 June 2024) reported criticism of the collection's imagery and the museum's [re]Frame response.

f: A unit of the University of Utah and the state's fine arts museum. The pages read did not state its budget or funders; a Mellon Foundation grant supported the joint Museum+Library Search with the Marriott Library (museum website).
w: A University of Utah museum that moved into the 74,000-square-foot Price building in 2001, with more than 22,000 original works.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: A division of the City of Albuquerque's Department of Arts and Culture. The pages read did not state its budget; the Albuquerque Museum Foundation Inc is listed as a separate nonprofit filer.
w: Established in 1967 in Old Town as a city museum of art, history and culture, with about 10,000 works of art and 35,000 historical objects.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Part of the New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs. A Henry Luce Foundation grant supported a November programme, and the Friends of Folk Art raise money through the Folk Art Flea; the pages read did not state amounts.
w: A state museum on Museum Hill, Santa Fe, built from the Florence Dibell Bartlett Collection and the Girard Collection given by Alexander and Susan Girard.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.
nodes: Friends of Folk Art raise money

f: Revenue was $3,515,673 in the year to June 2023, with $2,000,811 in contributions and $766,598 in program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name individual funders.
w: A museum in downtown Tucson covering art of the American West, Asian, Contemporary, Decorative, European, Indigenous, Latin American and Modern art.

f: Revenue was $19,826,011 in the year to September 2023, with $4,647,009 in contributions and $1,573,523 in program service revenue (Form 990). The pages read did not name individual funders.
w: Housed in the former Lone Star Brewery building; its site lists it as founded in 1981. Revenue swung between $9,389,383 and $19,826,011 across the filings read.

f: Revenue was $14,091,245 in 2023, with $8,977,307 in contributions and $2,557,539 in program service revenue (Form 990). The City of San Antonio Arts and Culture provides operations support; the New Witte was funded through a $100 million capital campaign.
w: Opened on 8 October 1926 with a bequest of $65,000 from Alfred G. Witte, matched by the City; it holds about 320,000 artifacts and specimens.

f: Founded and paid for by Trammell and Margaret Crow; the Crow family gave the whole collection to The University of Texas at Dallas in 2019. The pages read named no other funders and gave no amounts.
w: Opened in December 1998 as a free museum in the Dallas Arts District; since the 2019 gift it is part of UT Dallas, with a second site at the Edith and Peter O'Donnell Jr. Athenaeum in Richardson.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

n: Perot Museum of Nature and Science
f: Revenue was $29,850,477 in the year to September 2023, with $13,749,352 in contributions and $14,836,060 in program service revenue (Form 990). The Perot children gave $50 million in 2008; other named donors include the Rees-Jones Foundation ($25 million), T. Boone Pickens ($10 million), Hunt Petroleum ($10 million) and the Texas Instruments Foundation ($4.4 million).
w: Formed by a 2006 merger of three Dallas museums and named for Ross and Margot Perot after a $50 million gift from their five children in 2008; the Victory Park building opened on 1 December 2012 (museum website, History page).

f: Form 990 for the year to September 2025 shows revenue of $1,582,292, of which contributions were $933,357; the 1988 building was funded largely by gifts from the Blackmon family, Blount, Inc. and the Weil family. An endowment for American art came from the Ida Belle Young bequest in 2004.
w: Founded in 1930 by the artist John Kelly Fitzpatrick, Mrs. Harry S. Houghton and the Morning View Painters in a school building the City of Montgomery let for one dollar a year; it has stood in Blount Cultural Park since 1988. The pages read name private patrons, not a standing city or state grant.

f: In the year to June 2024 revenue was $7,081,600, including public support of $3,766,056 and government appropriations of $1,441,043 (annual report 2023-2024). The Jackson Advocate reported on 6 April 2026 that state bill SB 2189 sends $650,000 to the museum for projects and exhibitions.
w: It began as the Mississippi Art Association in 1911 and took its present name in 1978. Its own annual report shows government grants up 391 percent in 2023-24, and the state set aside $650,000 for it in a 2026 projects bill.

f: Form 990 data show revenue of $1,491,796 in the year to June 2025, down from $3,006,099 in 2022; contributions fell from $1,599,248 to $397,460 over the same years. The building at 900 Camp Street was gifted by Sydney Besthoff in 1999 (museum website, about page).
w: Founded by a collective of artists, with its own site giving 1976 in places and saying it officially began in 1977; it presents visual art and performance.

n: Reynolda House Museum of American Art
f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $5,516,565, of which contributions were $3,381,550 and program services $603,110, with net assets of $50,387,788. The museum is part of Wake Forest University; a Henry Luce Foundation grant paid for conservation of the collection (Reynolda website, about page).
w: The estate was built by R.J. Reynolds, who founded the plug tobacco factory that became the R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Company, and his wife Katharine; the house is now a museum of American art that is part of Wake Forest University. The pages read do not say what share of today's income comes from Reynolds family money.

f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $4,482,482, of which contributions were $1,191,875 and program services $734,977, with net assets of $73,273,668. WVTF reported on 6 March 2026 that the building was named for Nicholas and Eugenia Taubman after their lead gift, with the amount not stated.
w: It began in the 1950s as the Roanoke Fine Arts Center, was renamed the Art Museum of Western Virginia in 1992 and opened in its current downtown building on 8 November 2008. The pages read show no controversy.

f: The Mellon Foundation lists a $1,000,000 grant to Hampton University in 2023 under Humanities in Place, with earlier Hampton grants in 2020, 2018, 2017, 2015 and 2000. In January 2026 the university announced a gift of works valued at about $371,000 from T. Michael Todd.
w: Founded in 1868, it describes itself as the nation's oldest African American museum and is part of Hampton University. Its director is Dr. Vanessa D. Thaxton-Ward.

f: The pages read do not state the museum's budget. ProPublica lists a private foundation, the David Lloyd Kreeger Foundation, with revenue of $2,588,974 and net assets of $104,662,701 in 2024; the pages read do not say whether it operates the museum.
w: A museum of 19th and 20th century art in the former home of David and Carmen Kreeger, designed in 1963 by Philip Johnson and Richard Foster; the Kreegers bought most of it from 1959 on. It also sells admission and takes memberships and corporate memberships.

f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $28,220,542, of which contributions were $14,737,009 and program services $12,918,990, with net assets of $116,837,480. Washingtonian reported on 8 July 2026 that the theatre carries a $65 million debt load tied to its waterfront building.
w: One of the first regional theatres in the United States, led by Molly Smith for 25 years until 2023. Its artistic director Hana S. Sharif resigned in late June 2026; NOTUS and Washingtonian reported deficits, staff turnover and a board investigation, and Sharif said she and the board had differing visions.

f: Form 990 for the year to July 2025 shows revenue of $20,417,623, of which contributions were $8,009,990 and program services $10,834,462, against expenses of $25,021,598. A donor match of up to $100,000 before 31 December 2026 is advertised on its site.
w: It plays at Sidney Harman Hall (Harman Hall) and the Klein Theatre; Simon Godwin is its artistic director. The pages read show no controversy.

f: Form 990 for the year to August 2025 shows revenue of $54,686,743, of which contributions were $45,808,922. Its Music For All Campaign raised $173 million for the $140 million renovation and expansion of Powell Hall and for its endowment (SLSO release, 19 September 2025).
w: Founded in 1880, it is the second-oldest orchestra in the United States; Powell Hall reopened in September 2025 as the Jack C. Taylor Music Center after two seasons elsewhere. The pages read show no labour dispute since 2005.

f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $3,605,471, of which contributions were $2,784,121 and investment income $613,262, with net assets of $30,274,491. Admission is free.
w: A non-collecting museum in the Grand Center Arts District with free admission. Its board includes Rex A. Sinquefield and Michael Staenberg among other directors; the pages read do not name its funders.

f: The pages read do not state the museum's budget or funders. A WashU article from 2006 dates it to 1881 and says its first municipal tax levy in 1907 was never released to the university, and that the 2006 new facilities were designed by Fumihiko Maki.
w: Part of Washington University in St. Louis and described by the university as the oldest art museum west of the Mississippi. In 1945 curator H.W. Janson sold 120 paintings and more than 500 objects, about a sixth of the holdings, to buy modern works.

f: Form 990 for the year to August 2025 shows revenue of $5,934,733, of which contributions were $3,892,851 and investment income $1,642,479, against expenses of $8,182,793 and net assets of $67,366,597. Anna Sinton Taft and Charles Phelps Taft bequeathed the house and 530 works in 1927.
w: The museum is in a house built about 1820 and lived in by the Sinton and Taft families; the Tafts began collecting after Anna inherited her father's fortune in 1900. The pages read show no controversy.

f: Form 990 for the year to August 2025 shows revenue of $2,707,776, of which contributions were $2,653,323, against expenses of $4,416,697 and net assets of $23,183,381. Its director Christina Vassallo announced on 5 December 2025 she was leaving to lead the Pew Center for Arts & Heritage.
w: Founded in 1939 as the Modern Art Society by Betty Pollak Rauh, Peggy Frank Crawford and Rita Rentschler Cushman, and now housed in the Lois & Richard Rosenthal Center for Contemporary Art. Its 2025 accounts show a loss of $1.7 million.

f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $5,610,470, of which contributions were $2,300,818, investment income $1,532,415 and sales of assets $1,724,662, with net assets of $74,612,241. The Tribune Chronicle reported on 27 March 2025 that it bought Alfred Leslie's High Tea for $300,000.
w: A museum of American art in Youngstown led for over four decades by executive director Louis A. Zona. The Form 990 page lists reported conflict of interest transactions without describing them.

f: It is part of Oberlin College and admission has always been free. The pages read do not state its budget or funders.
w: Founded in 1917 on the Oberlin College campus to support teaching, with strong holdings in American, Asian, European and global contemporary art. The pages read show no controversy.
tn: No source outside the museum is recorded.

f: Form 990 for the year to June 2025 shows revenue of $9,288,576, of which contributions were $6,572,820, with net assets of $67,997,508. It is supported in part by the Genesee County Arts Education and Cultural Enrichment Millage, approved on 7 August 2018, and the Mott Foundation says it has granted nearly $292 million to Flint Cultural Center institutions between 1928 and 2025.
w: The second largest art museum in Michigan, on the Flint Cultural Center campus, with a community art school. The pages read show no controversy.

n: Charles H. Wright Museum of African American History
f: The audited accounts for the year to June 2025 show operating grants and contributions of $5,270,989 and capital grants of $5,107,160, with a fall in funding from the State of Michigan and the City of Detroit; the City contract paid $3,300,000. On 13 March 2026 the museum asked Detroit City Council for $11 million.
w: A city-owned museum founded by Dr. Charles H. Wright in 1965. It reported its first operating deficit in several years for FY2025, blamed on lower State funding, and said federal grants specific to Black museums have been eliminated.

f: Form 990 for the year to September 2025, filed as West Michigan Horticultural Society Inc, shows revenue of $38,055,994, of which program services were $18,458,521 and contributions $12,952,319. The related Foundation's endowment passed $200 million and provides more than 20 percent of the operating budget (annual report 2025).
w: Opened in 1995; the Meijer family, who founded a chain of superstores and markets in Michigan; The Art Newspaper reported in 2017 that a $115 million capital campaign was led by gifts from the Meijer family. The pages read show no controversy.

f: Form 990 for the year to September 2025 shows revenue of $5,022,607, of which contributions were $3,882,346, against expenses of $8,305,505 and net assets of $57,589,482. The Meijer Foundation pays for free general admission every Thursday from 5 to 8 pm.
w: It grew from the Art Association of Grand Rapids, formed on 1 June 1910, and has been in its downtown building since 2007. The pages read show no controversy.
